entries.title: What SuReSuite is
entries.text: What SuReSuite is The tool in one page — the problem it solves and what it produces. In short Model your supply chain, test a disruption, and compare cost and service under different responses. The results depend on your data and assumptions; the tool does not place orders or predict every real-world event. Read how it is designed , or try the worked example .

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — The problem it solves
entries.text: If a supplier loses capacity for four weeks, how much demand could you miss? Would more stock or a backup source reduce that loss enough to justify its cost? SuReSuite lets you compare those choices on the same modeled chain. Build a supply-chain model from suppliers, materials, products, demand and a bill of materials (BOM): the quantities of materials needed for one product. A policy is a rule for operating the chain, such as when to reorder. A scenario is the situation you test, including any disruption. SuReSuite builds a working model of your chain from the data you already have, then lets you break it on purpose and measure what happens. The three lenses on one network. Each layer has its own view in the app. Lens View What it answers Firm level Firm-Level Network Who supplies whom — suppliers, customers, the focal firm Product level Product-Level Network Which materials feed which products, and where a material has one source Process level Process-Level Network The steps that make each product, and where capacity and lead time bind

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — What it produces
entries.text: A model of your chain Built from files you already keep — suppliers, materials, products, the bill of materials, inbound and outbound lanes. Lanes connect suppliers to materials and products to customers. The simulation reads the modeled inputs; a graph can also contain relationships it does not simulate. A structural read on it Inspect connections and single-source exposure in the supplied network. Structural importance helps choose what to investigate; it is not proof of disruption losses. Answers to what-if Test a supplier capacity loss or another supported change. Repeated runs show variation in outcomes. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated result across those repeats, conditional on the model assumptions. A comparison between responses Holding more stock, qualifying a second supplier, expediting — each costs something and buys something. The comparison is the point; the simulation is how you get one. A figure you can defend Current version-bound runs identify the inputs, policies, scenario and engine build used. Keep those saved versions and run settings for reproduction; older records may be incomplete.

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — Who it is for
entries.text: Planners , who need to know which of this week's exposures is the one worth acting on. Supply chain managers , who have to justify the cost of resilience to people who see only the cost. Researchers , who need a model whose assumptions are written down and whose runs can be reproduced. The people who approve the tool , who want to know what runs where and what leaves the building before anyone uploads anything. That is System boundary .

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — What it is not
entries.text: SuReSuite supports experiments and decision review. It does not place operational orders. The engine advances in weekly steps around one focal production stage; it does not simulate every upstream company or individual factory operation shown in a graph. The engine is the software that calculates outcomes. Optional connectors can import data from business systems, so check how your project is connected. Read this before you rely on a number Every model leaves things out, and a manual that does not say which things is asking for a trust it has not earned. The omissions are listed on Known limits — one page, near the front, on purpose.

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — Where it comes from
entries.text: Horizon Europe Grant 101138269 ACCURATE SuReSuite is developed in part within the ACCURATE project, funded under Horizon Europe. Three industrial pilots — in aerospace, automotive and electronics — ground the stress-test scenarios and keep the architecture honest against chains nobody on the project team gets to simplify. That origin informs the transparency commitments: write down assumptions, mark substitutions where they are displayed, and publish results with the information needed to repeat them. What happens to your data explains those commitments and the gaps you should check today.

entries.title: What SuReSuite is — Where to go next
entries.text: How SuReSuite is designed — the architecture, and why it is shaped the way it is. Your first project — the end-to-end walkthrough, if you would rather start by doing. Known limits — what this tool does not model.

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed
entries.text: How SuReSuite is designed The six tiers as the journey your data takes, and the three laws that govern it. In short Your upload, accepted inputs, decisions and results have separate places in the system. This separation lets you review changes and compare runs made from saved versions. Follow the six tiers (stages in your data's life) below, then read one row's journey .

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — Six tiers: from your file to your result
entries.text: A tier is a stage in the life of your data. These numbers describe data responsibilities, not supplier tiers or separate servers. A bill of materials (BOM) lists the material quantities needed for one product. A lane connects a supplier to a material, or a product to a customer. Six numbered data tiers Six data responsibilities, numbered 0–5. Standard CSV uploads follow this path; node-list and deep-tier bulk uploads are exceptions. Historical records may lack source or version information. Tier 0 · Landing Keep the file as received. You can distinguish an original cell from the value later accepted by the model. Tier 1 · Staging Prepare rows for review. Staged means checked but not yet accepted: an upload can have valid rows and held rows without changing your model. Tier 2 · Accepted inputs (canonical) Canonical means the accepted working data, with consistent units and identifiers. Promotion is the step that applies reviewed rows here. This is where you correct the facts of your chain. Tier 3 · Computed views (derived) Build lanes, graphs and network measurements from inputs. Derived means calculated rather than supplied. After editing inputs, refresh or rerun the affected calculation. Tier 4 · Decisions Save policies and scenarios. A policy is an operating rule, such as how much to reorder. A scenario describes the conditions to test, including a disruption. Saved versions…

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — The three laws, and why they matter
entries.text: External data never lands below staging. Review an import before it becomes accepted input. Standard CSV uploads (spreadsheet-style text files) follow this path; node-list and deep-tier bulk uploads remain exceptions. Computed data is always rebuildable. A graph or measurement should be calculated again from its inputs, rather than repaired by typing a new output. Historical measurements can lack the saved inputs needed to reproduce them. Every decision remembers the data it was made on. A saved run uses identified input and policy versions. Check whether a saved validation still applies after editing the project. Older records can have incomplete version information. These are the design rules. Known limits explains where current or historical paths fall short; the diagram alone is not proof that every path follows them.

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — We never change your numbers silently
entries.text: That is the rule you should be able to check. Review the proposed changes before accepting an upload. On supported columns, rates and durations are converted to consistent units during promotion; keep the original units visible when checking the accepted value. A number may come from your data, a calculation, or a default. A default is a stated value used when an input is missing. A substitution should be marked where you read it. Inspect where a number came from and the run's conversion notes before relying on it. One written data description supplies the generated field references and upload rules. Automated checks catch some disagreements; explanatory pages still need review. A version identifies the inputs used, not whether your assumptions describe the real chain.

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — Where those stages run
entries.text: The browser is your workspace for uploading and reviewing data. Supabase is the hosted storage and request service. A simulation worker runs jobs on a server. The Python engine, scsim, calculates the outcomes. The app also has a browser execution path; System boundary explains what crosses between these components. Execution and control boundaries Illustration. The local verifier exercises the mapping and engine, not hosted authorization.

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — The limits to read before adopting the tool
entries.text: A stored version does not prove model validity or deployment parity. Not all ingestion paths use staging, and historical records can have incomplete provenance (the record of where a value came from). Known browser simulation authorization gap Source review identified incomplete caller authorization on the browser simulation endpoint. This path does not establish the caller's project role before dispatch. Interface restrictions must not be treated as a complete security boundary. The documentation changes do not fix this issue, and no production bypass test was run. See roles and capabilities .

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — Choose your next page
entries.text: New to the tool? Read How your data flows . Ready to try it? Follow Your first project . Reviewing a decision? Start with Reading your results . Looking for a table? Use the data model reference .

entries.title: How SuReSuite is designed — For engineers: developer setup
entries.text: Read the repository's README and CLAUDE.md. Install the lockfile dependencies with npm ci and start Vite with npm run dev . This serves the frontend; it does not create a local Supabase database or a Fly worker. The current Supabase client has project configuration in its source. Do not assume an arbitrary .env file redirects the application into an isolated backend. Arrange a dedicated backend before exercising writes from the full app. For an offline simulation check, install the Python dependencies and run python scripts/verify-manual-example.py . This checks the downloadable frozen-input example locally; it does not verify hosted upload promotion or browser-to-worker execution. For documentation changes, run npm test -- src/components/docs , npm run typecheck , npm run check:docs , npm run lint and npm run build . Edit source metadata or generators rather than generated references. Next: review the system boundaries or set up scoped API access .

entries.title: How your data flows
entries.text: How your data flows Upload, check, accept, compute, decide, simulate, stamp — follow one example row. In short Uploading a file does not immediately make it simulation input. Review and accept its rows, compute the views, then save decisions and run a scenario. The result records the versions used so you can inspect or repeat that comparison.

entries.title: How your data flows — Follow one bill-of-materials row
entries.text: A bill of materials (BOM) states how much material a product consumes. In the tutorial, P-CONTROL → M-CASE with consumption 2 means one control unit needs two housings. Follow that same row through the seven steps below. From upload to a stamped result The standard CSV journey, using two housings per control unit. Node-list and deep-tier bulk uploads follow separate paths.

entries.title: How your data flows — 1. Upload: keep the original file
entries.text: For standard CSV uploads, SuReSuite records the file as received. CSV is a spreadsheet-style text file with one record per line. The original cells remain distinct from the values prepared for your model.

entries.title: How your data flows — 2. Check: prepare rows for review
entries.text: Rows are staged: parsed and checked, but not yet accepted into the working model. The review shows new, changed, unchanged and held rows. A non-numeric consumption value can hold the BOM row while other valid rows remain eligible. File findings use error, warn and info. The simulation-readiness check uses block, warn and info. A file that can be read is not necessarily a model that can run: the product and material identifiers must also exist. See Uploading data .

entries.title: How your data flows — 3. Accept: apply the reviewed changes
entries.text: Promotion means accepting eligible staged rows into the canonical data: the project's accepted working inputs. A natural key is the combination of identifiers that distinguishes one record. Here, the product/material pair identifies the BOM line. Uploading P-CONTROL → M-CASE again with consumption 3 proposes a change from two to three housings, rather than a second independent requirement. Inspect the change preview before choosing Promote. The system checks the changes again against current inputs when accepting them. Rates and durations on supported columns convert to consistent units here. Some readers still convert older data, so check the accepted value and keep units explicit.

entries.title: How your data flows — 4. Compute: build views from the inputs
entries.text: The accepted BOM line helps build supply-chain lanes and graphs. Derived means calculated from inputs. With demand of 100 control units per week, consumption 2 implies a requirement of 200 housings per week. This arithmetic is a requirement, not proof that the supplier can deliver it. Refresh affected views or rerun analyses after an input change. Check freshness and provenance, meaning the record of where a value came from. Older derived measurements can lack that record. Some uploads follow another path Node-list and deep-tier bulk uploads do not share all the staging and original-file behavior above. A firm relationship drawn on a graph is supplied data, not a relationship proved by the drawing.

entries.title: How your data flows — 5. Decide: save how the chain will operate
entries.text: A policy is a rule for operating the chain, such as when to reorder or which supplier to use. Save your choices as a policy version. A scenario describes the conditions to test, such as a supplier losing capacity for four weeks. A dataset version is a saved copy of relevant model inputs. Frozen means that saved copy is fixed for a run; later edits to the project do not silently replace it. Keep the same input and policy versions when comparing a baseline with a disruption.

entries.title: How your data flows — 6. Simulate: run the saved combination
entries.text: The run binds the dataset and policy versions to the scenario and engine build. The engine is the calculation software. The current worker reads the frozen input and policy copies; an earlier run remains evidence about its earlier inputs. Validation checks model behavior under chosen settings; it does not certify a forecast. If inputs change, check whether the saved validation is stale, meaning it no longer covers the current model. Wait for a completed run before using its results.

entries.title: How your data flows — 7. Stamp: keep the evidence with the result
entries.text: The run record identifies the data, decisions, scenario and engine used. Replications are repeats with different random draws. Check the completed count, measurement period and conversion notes when reading an outcome. A hash is a content fingerprint used to identify a version. It cannot supply missing historical data or prove which build a live deployment ran. For handover, retain the input and policy exports, scenario, random seeds (the settings used to repeat draws), engine build and completed count.

entries.title: How your data flows — Where to go next
entries.text: Try the worked tutorial , learn about dataset versions and policy versions , or prepare verifiable exports .

entries.title: What happens to your data
entries.text: What happens to your data Five transparency commitments: sources, substitutions, limits, repeatable results and checked definitions. In short You should be able to tell whether a number came from your data, a calculation or a default. Saved versions make results checkable; published limits explain what those results cannot establish. Before sharing a result, check its sources and versions. Known limits records the gaps.

entries.title: What happens to your data — What makes a number worth using
entries.text: A simulation result is useful when you can explain its inputs and assumptions. These five commitments describe the standard SuReSuite aims to meet, and what you can check before making a decision.

entries.title: What happens to your data — 1. No number without a source
entries.text: A value should resolve to supplied data, a named calculation or an explicit default. For example, a material requirement can come from demand multiplied by its bill-of-materials quantity. A default is a stated value used when an input is missing. Follow the value's source marker and read the run's conversion notes; do not present an assumed value as a measurement. See Where a number came from . Historical derived records can have incomplete provenance, meaning the record of their source.

entries.title: What happens to your data — 2. Substitution is always visible
entries.text: If a missing input is replaced, the replacement should be marked where you read it. The data contract is the shared written description of field meanings, units and allowed substitutions. Generated references use it, and automated checks reject undeclared fallback rules in the paths they cover. Read When a value is missing before accepting an assumption.

entries.title: What happens to your data — 3. We publish our own blind spots
entries.text: A report should state the limits of its own computation. Read Known limits alongside the result. A company graph does not mean every upstream dependency is simulated. Missing measurements should be reported as unavailable, rather than as zero.

entries.title: What happens to your data — 4. Reproducible or not published
entries.text: A shared figure should name the data, policy, scenario and engine versions that produced it. A policy is an operating rule; a scenario is the situation tested; the engine is the calculation software. Their saved versions let another reader repeat a calculation on the same inputs. Keep the random seeds (settings for repeating random draws) and run settings too. Use the Reproducibility record and verifiable exports . Older records can lack these bindings; if you cannot recover the inputs, say the figure cannot be fully reproduced.

entries.title: What happens to your data — 5. Transparency survives handover
entries.text: Field definitions and automated checks should keep agreeing after the team changes. Table references are generated from the data contract; engine references come from the engine's own definitions. Build checks detect drift in those generated views. Explanatory prose and live deployment behavior still need review: passing a build is not proof that every promise holds in production.

entries.title: What happens to your data — Your data, access and removal
entries.text: Projects belong to an organization, and access depends on your account and project rights. These rights differ by operation. Roles and capabilities documents the known browser simulation authorization gap; do not assume the organization label alone guarantees isolation. Hosted storage and simulation services handle your data. When you use the AI assistant, project context can be sent to the configured model provider. Review System boundary before uploading sensitive information. Exports cover model inputs, decisions and results, rather than every record the system holds. Deleting a project also has retention exceptions. See Exporting and deleting your data for the practical scope. What you can check today The Audit log records administrative, data-change and access events, with coverage limits and the identity presented by the request. An audit row is useful evidence of a change; it does not by itself prove the caller's identity.

entries.title: What happens to your data — Where to go next
entries.text: Review what runs where , read the limits , or follow Your first project .

entries.title: System boundary
entries.text: System boundary What runs where — browser, Supabase, simulation worker, engine — and what crosses each line. In short You review data in the browser; hosted services store the model and execute server runs. The simulation engine, the software that calculates outcomes, receives prepared inputs rather than database access keys. Check access gaps and optional AI processing before uploading sensitive data. Then read Roles and capabilities .

entries.title: System boundary — Before you approve the tool
entries.text: This page explains where data is stored and which services handle it. The six data tiers describe stages in its life; the components below describe where work happens. A deployment is the running version of the application; it must be checked separately from a source-code description.

entries.title: System boundary — The four components
entries.text: What runs where The server-run path. Browser execution is also available. Hosted storage includes database rows and files; some worker paths keep temporary copies in memory. Access checks and optional AI processing need separate review. Your browser Displays the app, prepares edits and sends requests. Unsaved edits can be lost on refresh. The app also supports running the Python engine in the browser for validation and local execution; do not assume all computation happens on a server. Supabase The hosted database, file storage and server functions. Accepted inputs, saved policies, versions and run records live here. Database rules and request handlers govern access, with gaps noted below. Simulation worker A server process hosted on Fly.io. It receives a queued job, loads the run's saved input and policy versions, calculates outcomes and saves results. Some worker paths retain project data in memory between requests. scsim engine The Python library that calculates a weekly supply-chain simulation. It receives prepared model inputs. It does not need database credentials to perform that calculation.

entries.title: System boundary — What moves between them
entries.text: Browser → Supabase Uploaded files, saved edits and requests to read or run a project. Some paths carry an application-asserted identity rather than an authenticated Supabase user; access must be checked for the operation, not inferred from a sign-in screen. Request service → queue A job naming the project, scenario and saved versions. A queue holds work until a worker picks it up; it is not the permanent record of your model. Queue → worker → engine The worker loads saved versions and translates them into engine inputs. The engine returns calculated outcomes to the worker. Worker → storage → browser Saved result records and progress messages. The browser reads the result. Detailed series may use separate result-file storage, so storage is not limited to database rows.

entries.title: System boundary — Access and temporary copies
entries.text: The worker has elevated database access The worker uses a service credential that bypasses per-user database rules. Its request and execution code therefore matters to isolation. Hiding an action in the interface is not proof that the server refuses it. Some worker paths keep data in memory The worker's graph cache can retain project graphs and effective policies between uses. Its idle timer drops cached data after ten minutes by default. A current version-bound experiment reads frozen copies (saved for that run), rather than using later edits to the live project. Source review identified incomplete caller authorization on the browser simulation endpoint. This path does not establish the caller's project role before dispatch. The documentation changes do not fix the issue, and no production bypass test was run. Read the full access finding before treating the interface as a security boundary. The Audit log describes administrative, data-change and access events, including coverage and identity limits. A recorded identity is not always independently verified.

entries.title: System boundary — Optional processing, exports and deletion
entries.text: Hosted storage and execution involve the configured service providers. If you use the AI assistant, prompts and relevant project context can also be sent to the configured model provider. Review The AI assistant and your deployment's provider arrangements; this page does not establish those providers' retention or training terms. Exports leave the system when you download or share them. Project deletion removes project data through the supported deletion path, with exceptions for some files and account records. Read Exporting and deleting your data before assuming every copy disappears.

entries.title: System boundary — What to check next
entries.text: For an IT review, check the deployed services and credentials alongside Roles and capabilities . For a modeling decision, read Known limits . For the data path, return to How your data flows .

entries.title: Known limits
entries.text: Known limits The model, data and access limits to check before using a result for a decision. In short A result is evidence about the modeled chain and its assumptions, not a forecast of everything that can happen. Check the five limits below before recommending a response. If a missing mechanism could reverse your decision, test assumptions or gather more evidence. Then use Reading your results .

entries.title: Known limits — Five limits to check first
entries.text: The engine works in weekly steps around one focal production stage. A detailed process graph does not mean every intermediate stage is simulated. Company relationships show the network you supplied; they do not automatically become simulated upstream dependencies. Some upload paths and historical records have less review or provenance (the record of where a value came from). Missing information is not zero. A saved policy (an operating rule) may not affect the calculation. Ordinary app runs do not report the Resilience Index, a combined stress-test measure. Source review identified incomplete caller authorization on the browser simulation endpoint. The documentation changes do not fix it.

entries.title: Known limits — Model fidelity
entries.text: The engine uses weekly steps and aggregate quantities rather than tracking each individual item. It represents suppliers, materials, one focal production stage and customers. A bill of materials (BOM) lists component quantities; multi-level BOMs are flattened into total root-to-leaf material requirements for simulation. The engine can represent a product's production delay and work-in-progress (items started but not yet finished). It does not independently model intermediate inventories or subassembly capacities just because the process graph displays them. Timing within a week is outside this model. Company relationships in the deep-tier graph do not automatically become simulated upstream dependencies. Network centrality measures a node's structural position in the supplied graph; it is not measured loss or proof of how a disruption will spread. Three checks before a recommendation Illustration. If a missing assumption can reverse the decision, test or investigate it.

entries.title: Known limits — Data and mapping
entries.text: Standard CSV uploads have staging (checked rows waiting for acceptance) and promotion (applying reviewed changes). Node-list and deep-tier bulk uploads are exceptions. Missing optional values can use defaults, and computed values can differ from original cells. Inspect the change preview and run conversion notes. Changing accepted inputs can make analyses and validation stale: they describe older data. Current execution reads saved input versions, but older runs and derived records may not carry complete versions.

entries.title: Known limits — Policy support and results
entries.text: A policy is a rule for running the chain. Some controls are stored or reserved without affecting the current engine. Use the field's stage reference and engine status rather than inferring support from its presence. Finished-goods inventory controls apply to make-to-stock products, which build ahead of orders. Make-to-order products start from orders and do not use that finished-goods stock policy. The Resilience Index is a combined stress-test measure in the engine library; ordinary application runs do not emit it. Unavailable fill rate (the share of demand served), recovery time or a time series is not zero. Check the measurement period and whether recovery was still incomplete when observation ended.

entries.title: Known limits — Access-control and deployment limits
entries.text: Known browser simulation authorization gap Source review identified incomplete caller authorization on the browser simulation endpoint. Roles and capabilities distinguishes this from the scoped public API gateway. The documentation changes do not fix this issue, and no production bypass test was run. The reviewed source and a live deployment can differ. The tutorial's CSV validation and engine execution are local; hosted upload promotion and browser-to-worker execution remain unverified for the sample.

entries.title: Known limits — What the manual can establish
entries.text: Generated field references are checked against their source descriptions. Narrative guides still need review when behavior changes. A source check, a local example and a hosted run are different kinds of evidence; a page should say which it has.

entries.title: Known limits — What to report with a decision
entries.text: State the model boundary, data coverage, important assumed values, completed replication count, measured period and the factor you changed. A replication is one repeat of the model with its own random draws. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated result across those repeats. It measures simulation precision conditional on the model's assumptions; it does not certify real-world validity. When a limitation can reverse the decision, collect the missing evidence or test alternative assumptions before recommending action. Next: Reading your results and Experiments & comparison .

entries.title: The data model at a glance
entries.text: The data model at a glance Reference: every table in the system, grouped by the six numbered data tiers. In short This is a reference map of tables: stored lists of records with named fields. Use the six tier numbers (stages in your data's life) to distinguish inputs, computed views, decisions and results. New to the tool? Read the architecture overview first. Return here when you need a field reference.

entries.title: The data model at a glance — How to read this page
entries.text: Tiers are the stages data passes through, described on How SuReSuite is designed . A table's tier tells you what it is for and who writes it: tier 2 holds accepted input facts, tier 3 holds computed views, tier 4 holds decisions, and tier 5 holds version-bound results. The overview explains the rules and their current exceptions. 94 tables, of which 77 are described by the data contract (the shared definitions of fields and units) today — 1026 columns in all. Why the other tables are listed rather than hidden A page called “the data model” that showed only the 77 described tables would be making a false claim by omission. The remaining 17 are listed at the bottom of this page while their field descriptions are pending. You can see what exists, what is explained, and what is not yet — which is the whole of commitment T3 on What happens to your data .

entries.title: The data model at a glance — Looking for a specific column?
entries.text: This page is the map. The detailed index — every column of every described table, with its type, unit and constraints — is All tables , and Field index lists every field alphabetically. Start there for a field definition, unit or constraint. Reference data: contract 62a6e8587a37 , engine 0.8.3 . Generated definitions are checked separately from this page’s explanatory guidance.

entries.title: Your first project
entries.text: Your first project Build a small control-unit supply chain from example data, run a baseline, and measure what one disruption costs. In short A guided build: two suppliers, two materials, one product, one customer. You'll compare three runs — the baseline, a four-week board disruption, and the same disruption with a stock buffer. Every step ends in a checkpoint, so you know it worked before you move on.

entries.title: Your first project — Before you start
entries.text: Suppliers 2 Materials 2 Products 1 Customers 1 Demand 100 / week Use a new project for this, so nothing you do touches real work. You need rights to create a project, edit its inputs and policies, and run simulations. If a control is greyed out, check your project rights on your profile or ask the project owner. Opening the manual does not grant access to a project. All names and numbers are made up. The model has one production stage; it doesn't simulate individual factory operations or find suppliers for you. Download the control-unit example Seven CSVs for separate upload tabs. Protocol and verification JSON are for inspecting the local experiment; do not upload them as datasets. suppliers.csv materials.csv products.csv customers.csv bom_single_level.csv inbound_logistics.csv outbound_logistics.csv protocol.json verification.json One model, two controlled questions Illustration. Compare adjacent variants. A versus C changes both event and policy.

entries.title: Your first project — Create the project
entries.text: Open Project Manager › New Project . Name it Control-unit tutorial , set Plant to Assembly , and choose Curated data , Make-To-Order and Single Level BOM. Leave deep-tier exploration off, then choose Create Project . You should see the new project in your list. Select it before you upload anything.

entries.title: Your first project — Upload and accept seven files
entries.text: 1 Upload the four item lists Upload Data Suppliers, Materials, Products, Customers — each on its own dataset tab. These make the IDs easy to check. 2 Upload the three relationship files Upload Data BOM — single level, Inbound Logistics, Outbound Logistics. These are what actually connect the chain. 3 Review and accept each one Review Check new, changed, unchanged and held rows, then choose Promote N rows . Uploading alone is not accepting, and held rows are not accepted. Uploading data covers corrections. 4 Refresh if asked Project Manager Once the three core datasets are in, use Refresh Data if Project Manager asks you to finish building derived data. You should see two BOM lines, two inbound lanes and one outbound lane. P-CONTROL needs one M-BOARD and two M-CASE; C-ASSEMBLY wants 100 P-CONTROL a week.

entries.title: Your first project — Check the relationships
entries.text: Open the product view and search for P-CONTROL . Follow both materials back to their suppliers. At 100 products a week the BOM needs 100 boards and 200 housings a week. Supplier capacities are 150 and 300 units a week; product capacity is 150 a week — so there is headroom, for now. Weekly requirement against capacity, before and during the disruption. Item Needed per week Capacity per week During weeks 16–19 M-BOARD from S-BOARD 100 150 30 (80% cut) M-CASE from S-CASE 200 300 300 P-CONTROL at the plant 100 150 150 A link is missing? Check the IDs in the lane or BOM file, whether the rows were accepted, which project is selected, and any graph filters. A gap in the graph doesn't prove a gap in the real chain.

entries.title: Your first project — Save and validate the baseline
entries.text: 1 Supplier stage /policies On Policies , check S-BOARD supplies M-BOARD and S-CASE supplies M-CASE, each as the single primary source. Set Planning time unit to weeks where asked. Use min-max replenishment, 2 weeks of coverage and 0 days of Safety stock on both materials. Keep the uploaded opening stock: 200 boards, 400 housings. 2 Plant stage /policies P-CONTROL has finished-goods stock off (make-to-order) and capacity 150 a week. 3 Customer stage /policies C-ASSEMBLY / P-CONTROL has fixed demand of 100 a week, is supplied from the focal plant, and has backordering off. Demand is edited here. 4 Run & Validate /policies Save, then clear blocking findings and read every warning before acknowledging defaults. The tutorial protocol uses a 455-day horizon, 56-day warm-up, seed 42 and 3 replications. Choose Save Validated Model when the evidence is acceptable. You should see a saved Validated Model and a finished baseline. Note the settings and version IDs — you'll reuse them. Why these settings Three replications are a teaching setting for a fixed-demand example. They are not evidence that three is enough for a business study with uncertain demand. A primary-source choice satisfies the app's routing checks; the engine's actual sourcing also depends on its policy and lane data.

entries.title: Your first project — Add one disruption and run
entries.text: Open Simulation Lab , copy the validated baseline to a new scenario called Board disruption , and add one event in Recovery playbook : Target S-BOARD Type Capacity reduction, 80% When Week 16, for 4 weeks ( start_day 112, duration_days 28) Keep the same Seed, common random numbers, data, policy version, horizon and warm-up. Leave recovery levers off. Go to Run , review the gate, and dispatch. Wait for done with the expected replication count, and read the conversion notes before you trust the result. A queued or running result is preliminary; a failed run needs its error resolved before you retry.

entries.title: Your first project — Compare the runs
entries.text: Run 1 Baseline validated, no disruption ↓ → Run 2 Board disruption same settings + one event ↓ → Run 3 With buffer same event + 28-day stock The three runs. Change one thing at a time, so each comparison isolates one effect. In Compare , pick the baseline, then the Board disruption column. Only the disruption should differ. Read fill rate and lost sales together with the weekly trace. If the column is marked not like-for-like , read its reason — a seed mismatch, common random numbers off, a different engine or data version, or more than one change — and do not read its difference as the disruption's effect. To test a response, save a second policy version with 28 days of material safety stock and run the same disruption under it. Extra stock has a cost; don't call better service a net win until you've checked it.

entries.title: Your first project — What you should get
entries.text: Engine 0.6.1 results for the downloadable protocol, 52 measured weeks after an 8-week warm-up. Run Fill rate Lost-sales value Cost of resilience Baseline 100% 0 0 Board disruption 95.9615% 12,600 12,600 Same disruption, with buffer 100% 0 2,400 At 100 products a week and a selling price of 60, measured demand is worth 312,000. The disruption loses 12,600 of it: 1 − 12,600 / 312,000 ≈ 95.96%. The buffer avoids that loss in this fixed example while adding holding cost. What has and hasn't been verified The downloadable files pass the repository's CSV parser and contract validator, and the exact protocol runs locally through the worker's frozen-input pipeline. Its output records the engine version, KPIs and conversion notes. Database promotion, browser-to-worker dispatch and a hosted app run have not been executed for this tutorial. UI defaults may differ from the protocol, so record what your run actually used. All three replications are identical because the inputs are fixed. That is not a statement about real-world certainty. Next: read the evidence behind the numbers , then design a controlled comparison .

entries.title: Projects
entries.text: Projects The container everything else belongs to — and the decisions you make once, at the start.

entries.title: Projects — What a project is
entries.text: A project is one supply chain around one plant: the suppliers feeding it, the materials they supply, the products it makes, and the customers it serves. Every dataset you upload, every policy you set and every result you produce belongs to exactly one project. A project is also a boundary. Nothing in one project reads anything in another, so you can keep a real chain and an experiment side by side without either contaminating the other. Projects live at Project Manager .

entries.title: Projects — The fields you set when you create one
entries.text: Name The project's title, as you type it. Names are not identifiers here — renaming a project breaks nothing, because everything else refers to it by a stable internal reference rather than by its name. Plant name The plant this project models. It is more than a label: the lane and bill-of-materials tables carry the same plant name, and it is how their rows are matched to this project. Changing it after uploading data is not a cosmetic edit. Supply chain model Make-to-stock or make-to-order. Make-to-stock builds finished goods against a forecast and serves demand from inventory; make-to-order starts production when an order arrives. It changes what the simulation is doing at the plant, so it is worth getting right before you run anything. BOM level Whether the project uses a single-level bill of materials (products consume materials directly) or a multi-level one (materials consume other materials, to any depth). This decides which bill-of-materials dataset is read and which uploader you are offered. Start single-level unless you genuinely need the depth. Simulation window The first and last day of the horizon the project simulates. Optional at creation and editable later. Deep tier Whether the project models tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers as well as your direct ones. Leaving it off keeps the model to the chain you have contracts with; turning it on unlocks the deep-tier datasets…

entries.title: Projects — Completion
entries.text: A project is marked complete when it has the datasets it needs to simulate. You do not set this — it is maintained for you as data arrives, and it is what the simulation screen checks before offering to run anything. An incomplete project is not a broken one. It means something a run would need is not there yet, and the project screen will tell you which dataset it is waiting for.

entries.title: Projects — Ownership and access
entries.text: A project has an owner — the person who created it — and belongs to one organization. Those two facts decide who can read it and who can change it: the organization decides who can see it at all, and ownership decides who can edit it, alongside administrators. Organizations and members covers the organization side, and Who can see your data answers the question directly.

entries.title: Projects — Demonstration projects
entries.text: A project records whether its data was uploaded by a person or generated for demonstration. It is worth checking which kind you are looking at before drawing a conclusion from it — a synthetic project is there to show how the tool behaves, not to describe anyone's real chain.

entries.title: Projects — Where to go next
entries.text: With a project created, the next step is Uploading data . If you want the whole sequence in one page, Your first project walks it end to end.

entries.title: Uploading data
entries.text: Uploading data Get a CSV into your project, check what changed, and accept the rows that are right. In short Upload one CSV per dataset from Project Manager › Upload Data . Start from that tab's template. Nothing changes in your model until you accept the rows. Rows with errors are held back. Uploading again updates rows with the same IDs — it never deletes the rows you left out.

entries.title: Uploading data — Upload a file
entries.text: 1 Upload file kept as sent ↓ → 2 Review rows checked and compared ↓ → 3 Promote reviewed rows accepted ↓ → 4 Verify check the model The upload path for a standard CSV. Nothing is accepted until step 3. 1 Open Upload Data /project-manager In Project Manager , select the project you mean to change and choose Upload Data . 2 Pick the dataset tab and download its template Upload Data Use CSV, one dataset per file. Renaming an XLSX file to .csv does not convert it. The template is a filled example: overwrite the rows, keep the headers. The deep-tier network also has a JSON path with different handling. 3 Upload, then read the review Review Every row lands in one of five groups: new , changed , unchanged , superseded or held . Open a row to see the value you sent beside the value that was parsed. You should see a count for each group, and held rows listed with the finding that held them. 4 Choose Promote N rows to accept them Review Rows with errors stay held. Fix them in the original CSV and upload it again — don't edit around them. You should see the accepted table shows the row counts you expected. Review a correction before accepting it Illustration. This is an illustrative correction, not a change required by the tutorial. Practising first? Use the control-unit files from Your first project . They are small enough to check by eye.

entries.title: Uploading data — Which file does what
entries.text: Item lists describe things. The BOM and the two logistics files connect them. A model that can run needs both kinds, plus economics, demand and capacity — having every table present is not the same as being ready to run. Item lists Suppliers, Materials, Products and Customers. Their IDs must match the BOM and logistics files exactly, after trimming spaces. A supplier on its own creates no supply relationship. Products also accept optional production lead-time columns ( production_lead_time with production_lead_time_unit , and a shape); a blank unit means weeks. BOM How much of each material one product uses — units per unit, not a percentage. In the tutorial, P-CONTROL uses 1 M-BOARD and 2 M-CASE. Inbound logistics Which supplier delivers which material. volume is a rate in time_unit ; lead_time has its own lead_time_unit . Optional columns ( lead_time_dist , lead_time_cv , lead_time_min , lead_time_mode , lead_time_max ) give the lane its own lead-time shape; a lane with none follows its material's. Outbound logistics Which customer buys which product. volume and time_unit set the demand rate; unit_price is the selling price. Product-level and customer/product overrides may change the demand the simulation uses. Optional Node locations (for maps), deep-tier firms (for exploration) and a multi-level BOM (for projects set up for one). None of these proves an upstream relationsh…

entries.title: Uploading data — If something goes wrong
entries.text: A number was rejected Use a decimal point. Currency signs and thousands separators are not removed for you. A header wasn't recognised An extra column doesn't add a new parameter to the simulation. Check the dataset's reference page for the columns it accepts. A blank cell was filled in A blank optional cell supplies no value and may trigger a default. Required headers and required values are separate checks. A zero was refused Some fields accept 0 and some don't. BOM consumption must be above zero; a customer priority of 0 is allowed and means lowest priority. The comparison isn't ready Until the review has compared rows, don't read them as all new. Recompute the comparison, then decide. There's no Promote button That is usually your project rights, not the file. Send the project owner the exact message and the project name — uploading again won't help. A warning doesn't stop a row An inbound unit_price of 0 is accepted with a warning, and the simulation reads it as 1.0. Read the warnings before you accept, and check the held rows even when the promotion succeeds.

entries.title: Uploading data — Uploading the same file again
entries.text: Rows with the same IDs are updated , and new IDs are added . Rows you leave out of the new file are not deleted . A blank cell is not a reliable “keep the old value” — if you mean to keep a value, include it. The columns that identify a row, read from the data contract. Same key means update; a new key means insert. Dataset Row identified by BOM — single level product_id + material_id Inbound Logistics supplier_id + material_id Outbound Logistics customer_id + product_id Materials material_id Products product_id Suppliers supplier_id BOM — multi level material_id + higher_level_component_id + level Demand Forecast customer_id + product_id + period_start How this works: which columns identify a row Each dataset has a natural key — the IDs that pick out one row within your project. Multi-level BOM and forecast files add hierarchy or period fields to it, so they are not interchangeable with a single-level BOM or static demand. The node list and the deep-tier network use a separate upload path with no review step. Don't assume they keep the raw file or replace rows the same way — export a copy and read the network-table page before you replace them. A column one row supplies is written for every row in that upload, which is why a blank cell can still change a value.

entries.title: Uploading data — After you accept
entries.text: Check the accepted table, refresh derived data if you're asked to, then run input verification . Check relationships as well as counts: two rows with the wrong IDs still describe the wrong model. Re-validate your policies after a data change. Results from before the upload still describe the earlier inputs. An upload error, a row that fails validation and a permission denial need different fixes — capture the exact message. Never delete the project to fix one bad file. Next: follow a file through its life , or open the field references .

entries.title: Inbound Logistics
entries.text: Inbound Logistics Supply lanes: which supplier delivers which material, at what price and lead time.

entries.title: Inbound Logistics — What this file is
entries.text: One row per supply lane — a supplier who can deliver a material. It is the file that tells the model where a material can come from, so a material with no inbound row is a material nothing can supply, and the simulation will say so. Lanes are not the same thing as suppliers. This file says this supplier can deliver this material, at this price, in this time ; the Suppliers file says what is true of the supplier regardless of what they are delivering. Upload both. Tier 2 canonical — the only tier humans edit One supply arc as the user uploaded it: this supplier can deliver this material to this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. UNIQUE on natural_key_intended since WP 3.3 ( 20260916000018 ): a second upload of the same arc UPDATES it rather than adding a row, and the promotion is the upsert that does so (D5 closed). Uploaded as inbound_logistics from /project-manager. You never type project_id or plant_name — the server sets them from the project you are in, so a file cannot land in somebody else's project by naming it. A row is identified by project_id + plant_name + supplier_id + material_id . The database enforces it, so uploading the same file twice updates those rows rather than doubling them. Writing to it needs project role editor or above, and every write records who made it. Who can see your data is the honest version of what that role check does and d…

entries.title: Inbound Logistics — The template
entries.text: Download inbound_logistic.csv — the same file the upload wizard offers under Inbound Logistics . It is a filled example, not an empty header row: overwrite the rows, keep the headers. supplier_id,material_id,volume,time_unit,lead_time,unit_price,lead_time_unit,lead_time_dist,lead_time_cv,lead_time_min,lead_time_mode,lead_time_max 12 columns, of which 3 are required: supplier_id, material_id, lead_time. Column order does not matter — the parser reads the header row, not the position. The wizard links csv-upload-guide.md beside this dataset. It is a short format note, not a substitute for this page. Column order does not matter — the parser reads your header row and binds by name. A column we do not recognise is kept in the record of the file and mapped to nothing, and you are told which. A column the server supplies is different: a file carrying project_id or plant_name is refused , because its author expected those values to be used and they will not be. Upload it from Project Manager . Uploading data describes what the wizard checks before anything lands.

entries.title: Inbound Logistics — Rules the database itself enforces
entries.text: These run on every write, from any source. A row that fails one is refused — not corrected, not warned about. CHECK (lead_time_unit IS NULL OR public.unit_days(lead_time_unit) IS NOT NULL) CHECK ( (lead_time_dist IS NULL OR lead_time_dist IN ('deterministic', 'normal', 'lognormal', 'gamma', 'triangular', 'uniform')) AND (lead_time_cv IS NULL OR (lead_time_cv >= 0 AND lead_time_cv <= 1)) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_min >= 0) AND (lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_mode >= 0) AND (lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_max >= 0) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_min <= lead_time_mode) AND (lead_time_mode IS NULL OR lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_mode <= lead_time_max) AND (lead_time_min IS NULL OR lead_time_max IS NULL OR lead_time_min <= lead_time_max) )

entries.title: Inbound Logistics — What reads this file
entries.text: Almost every economic default in the model traces back to this file. When cost is blank on a material, the engine values it at the average unit_price of its lanes here, each weighted by that lane's volume — so what you pay most for counts most, and a cheap lane you barely use does not set the material's cost. With no volumes anywhere on a material, the cheapest quoted price is used instead. When a supplier's share of a material has to be worked out, it comes from the same volume columns. So an inbound file with placeholder prices does not produce a model with placeholder prices in one place — it produces one with placeholder economics throughout, and the provenance dots in the policy grid are how you see which numbers those are.

entries.title: Inbound Logistics — Related
entries.text: Suppliers · Materials · Outbound Logistics · Units and time periods · Supply Chain Data , which is what we derive from this file. 7 more columns the system fills in id Surrogate row identifier. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid. created_at When the row was inserted. Server-set. updated_at When the row last changed. Server-set. ingest_run_id The ingestion run that last wrote this row (WP 3.3), and through it the project, the source kind and who approved the promotion. NULL for every row that predates the CSV landing path, and for rows whose run has since been deleted — a null here means the provenance is UNKNOWN, never that there was none. Set by ingest_apply_run and by nothing else. source_row_id The tier-1 staged row this was promoted from (WP 3.3). Its source_row_number is the physical line of the uploaded file, header = line 1, so a person can be shown the line rather than told a file name — which is what extends A4 down to the source. ON DELETE SET NULL and DEFERRABLE: staging is deleted with its run, and a canonical row belongs to the project rather than to the run that last wrote it. entries.title: Outbound Logistics
entries.text: Outbound Logistics Demand lanes: which customer buys which product, at what price and lead time.

entries.title: Outbound Logistics — What this file is
entries.text: One row per demand lane — a customer who buys a product. It is the mirror of Inbound Logistics : that file is where material comes from, this one is where product goes. It is also the file that decides how much demand the simulation sees. If demand_mean is blank on a product, the demand for it is the sum of its outbound volumes, normalised to weeks. Most projects never fill demand_mean in at all and are driven entirely from here. Tier 2 canonical — the only tier humans edit One demand arc as the user uploaded it: this customer buys this product from this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. UNIQUE on natural_key_intended since WP 3.3 ( 20260916000018 ): a second upload of the same arc UPDATES it rather than adding a row (D5 closed). Uploaded as outbound_logistics from /project-manager. You never type project_id or plant_name — the server sets them from the project you are in, so a file cannot land in somebody else's project by naming it. A row is identified by project_id + plant_name + customer_id + product_id . The database enforces it, so uploading the same file twice updates those rows rather than doubling them. Writing to it needs project role editor or above, and every write records who made it. Who can see your data is the honest version of what that role check does and does not buy you.

entries.title: Outbound Logistics — Demand per customer and product
entries.text: Each row may state its own demand: a distribution with its mean and variation, or a forecast series uploaded as a Demand Forecast . A product's demand is then the sum of its rows. A row that states nothing keeps the product-level demand, split by volume — so a file without these columns runs exactly as it always has. Every value can be overridden per row on the Customer stage at /policies ; the upload is never changed by that. expected_lead_time is stored, validated, and read by nothing The contract records no engine field for it — the entry is empty, not omitted. The column is required, it must be a positive number, it is kept on the row and it appears in exports. It does not reach the simulation, so changing it changes no result. We are stating that rather than leaving you to infer it from a run that does not move. This is §5.3 T3 — a published blind spot — and it is the honest answer until either the engine grows a customer-side lead time or the column is retired.

entries.text: Demand Forecast The forecast per customer × product, per week or per month — the centre the run draws demand around.

entries.title: Demand Forecast — What this file is
entries.text: One row per bucket : from period_start , for one week or one calendar month, this customer is expected to take quantity of this product. A row's buckets in date order are its forecast series. The plan reads the forecast. The simulated world draws actual demand around it. A forecast is the centre of the row's demand, week by week. The row's distribution and variation — set on Outbound Logistics or on the Customer stage at /policies — decide how far actual demand strays from it. With no distribution, the row's demand is exactly its forecast. A row is identified by project_id + customer_id + product_id + period_start . The database enforces it, so uploading the same file twice updates those rows rather than doubling them. entries.title: Demand Forecast — A month is spread evenly over its weeks
entries.text: When the file is promoted, each bucket's quantity is spread evenly over its own days and stored as a weekly rate: 1 000 over a 30-day November is 233.33 a week, over a 31-day December 225.81. The review screen of the upload says so. The run lays every row's buckets on one calendar: week 0 starts on the project's earliest period_start , and each simulated week takes the days it shares with each bucket — so a week that straddles two months takes some of each. A day no bucket covers counts as zero demand, and the pre-run check warns about it. Past the end of the series A forecast shorter than the run is used to its end; after that the row plans on its demand_mean if it has one, else on the forecast's last value. The pre-run check warns before the run and the run itself says which it used. Setting the row's Demand mode to model on the Customer stage sets the series aside.

entries.title: BOM — single level — What this file is
entries.text: The recipe, flattened. One row says: to make one unit of this product you consume this much of this material. Nothing between the two — no sub-assemblies, no intermediate stages. entries.title: BOM — single level — Single level or multi level?
entries.text: Use single level when every material you buy is consumed directly by a finished product, which is most planning models. Use multi level when a material is consumed by something that is itself consumed by something — and you want the intermediate stage to exist in the model rather than being folded away. They are separate files and separate tables. A project can hold both; the engine collapses the multi-level tree into the same product-to-material rows the single-level file states directly, so the two describe the same thing at different resolutions.

entries.title: Materials — What this file is
entries.text: One row per material — an item master . It holds what is true of a material wherever it comes from: what it costs, what it costs to keep, the smallest order anyone will take, and how variable its lead time is. Every column except the identifier is optional, and every one of them has a documented answer for what happens if you leave it out. That is the point of the file: you fill in what you know and the model tells you what it assumed for the rest. Tier 2 canonical — the only tier humans edit One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing. entries.title: Products — Finished-goods policy and opening stock (make to stock)
entries.text: A make-to-stock product keeps finished goods, and five columns say how much. Each is optional; a product that sets none runs exactly as before. All levels are end-of-week finished-goods targets, in units. fg_policy picks the rule: base_stock builds up to fg_base_stock (S) every week; min_max builds up to S only when the stock left after the week's demand falls below fg_reorder_point (s), and builds nothing otherwise; days_of_cover targets fg_cover_days (D) days of the projected weekly demand — D/7 × demand — so the target rises and falls with the forecast. Empty is base-stock with the derived target: one week of forecast, plus the finished-goods safety stock when that is switched on. A level you type is the target: the safety-stock buffer is never added on top of it, so nothing is counted twice. Planned production is the policy's requirement, plus any backlog, capped at the product's capacity. fg_initial_on_hand is the stock the run starts with — empty starts it at the policy target. An incomplete policy (min-max without both levels, or with s not below S; days of cover without D) runs as base-stock, and the run's mapping report says so. A make-to-order product holds no finished goods and ignores all five. Each can also be set per product on the Plant stage , as an override.

entries.title: Suppliers
entries.text: Suppliers Capacity and reliability, beyond the lanes that connect a supplier to materials.

entries.title: Suppliers — What this file is
entries.text: One row per supplier. Inbound Logistics says what a supplier can deliver and at what price; this file says what is true of the supplier across everything they deliver — how much they can ship in total, and how often they deliver as promised. Tier 2 canonical — the only tier humans edit One supplier in one project: what the simulation needs to know about them beyond the arcs that connect them to materials. Uploaded as item_master_suppliers from /project-manager. You never type project_id — the server sets it from the project you are in, so a file cannot land in somebody else's project by naming it. A row is identified by project_id + supplier_id . The database enforces it, so uploading the same file twice updates those rows rather than doubling them. Writing to it needs project role editor or above, and every write records who made it. Who can see your data is the honest version of what that role check does and does not buy you.

entries.text: Units and time periods Which column a period applies to — the question that costs people a run.

entries.title: Units and time periods — The one rule
entries.text: A period column governs the column the contract says it governs, and nothing else on the row. It is never “the units for this line”. Several of the input files carry two quantities with a period in them, and readers reasonably assume one setting covers both. It does not, and the two are not even the same kind of thing: one is a rate over a period, the other is a duration. time_unit governs volume; lead_time is weeks The two columns are unrelated. This is the misreading that costs people a run. time_unit is about volume. Lead times are weeks. On an Inbound Logistics row, time_unit says what period volume is quoted over — 500 a month, 500 a week. lead_time on the same row is fixed at weeks by the contract, and has its own optional override, lead_time_unit . So time_unit=month, lead_time=2 means 500 a month, delivered in two weeks . If the supplier quoted fourteen days , write lead_time=14 and lead_time_unit=day — leaving it out makes it fourteen weeks, and nothing will object, because fourteen weeks is a perfectly valid lead time.

entries.title: Units and time periods — Quantities quoted over a period
entries.text: These columns are rates . Their unit is not fixed: another column on the same row names the period, and two rows are only comparable once both have been converted to the same one. time_unit demand_forecasts Sets the period for quantity on the same row. Nothing else. lead_time_unit inbound_logistics Sets the period for lead_time , lead_time_min , lead_time_mode , lead_time_max on the same row. Nothing else. time_unit inbound_logistics Sets the period for volume on the same row. Nothing else. time_unit outbound_logistics Sets the period for volume , demand_mean , demand_min , demand_max on the same row. Nothing else. production_lead_time_unit products Sets the period for production_lead_time , production_lead_time_min , production_lead_time_mode , production_lead_time_max on the same row. Nothing else. time_unit tier2_suppliers Sets the period for volume on the same row. Nothing else. time_unit tier3_suppliers Sets the period for volume on the same row. Nothing else.

Writing to it needs project role viewer or above, and every write records who mad…

entries.title: Supply Chain Data — The three numbers worth understanding
entries.text: weighted is the volume on this edge after unit normalisation — always per week, whatever period the uploaded row was quoted in. That is what makes two rows comparable, and it is why a monthly volume and a weekly one can sit in the same graph without either being rescaled by a reader. sourcing_ratio is this edge's share of everything flowing into its destination. A share, so it is dimensionless and adding two of them is meaningful. material_consumption_rate is carried through from your bill of materials rather than recomputed, so it means exactly what it means there.

entries.title: Supply Chain Data — Every column, and who wrote it
entries.text: id uuid Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. from_location text The upstream end of the edge — a supplier, a PURCHASED material, or a finished product, depending on which lane produced it. THIS SENTENCE IS WHY §4 D127 EXISTS: the column carries no role, so every consumer infers one at render time and eight of them disagree. The role is authored once now, on node_list.echelon , and read rather than inferred. entries.title: Dataset Versions
entries.text: Dataset Versions A frozen copy of your data, and the fingerprint that identifies it.

entries.title: Dataset Versions — Why a version exists at all
entries.text: A result is only meaningful with the data that produced it. A run that names a dataset version can be reproduced; one that does not, cannot. So freezing a version does two things. It keeps the actual rows — not a pointer to rows that may since have changed, the rows themselves — and it computes a fingerprint over them. Two runs with the same fingerprint saw the same world. Tier 3 derived — a pure function of tier 2 One frozen snapshot of a project's tier-2 data, with the hash that identifies it. The trust anchor: a run that names a dataset_version can be reproduced, and one that does not cannot. This table is outside the ingestion contract Nothing lands it in staging, nothing diffs it against what is already there, and nothing promotes it under review — the four steps How your data flows describes are skipped. Written when a version is frozen, from the tier-2 tables as they stand at that moment. Nothing uploads it and nothing edits it afterwards — that is the point of it. Writing to it needs project role viewer or above, and every write records who made it. Who can see your data is the honest version of what that role check does and does not buy you.

entries.title: Dataset Versions — The fingerprints, and why there are three
entries.text: One hash would answer “did anything change”. Three answer “did anything that matters to this question change”, which is a more useful thing to know when you are trying to work out whether a stored result is still good. graph_hash The fingerprint of the snapshot. Two runs with the same graph_hash saw the same world; two with different hashes did not. hash_inputs SHA-256 over the inputs domain of the snapshot — the tier-2 tables a SIMULATION reads. When this moves, a run stamped with the old composite cannot be reproduced. hash_network SHA-256 over the network domain — tier2_suppliers , tier3_suppliers , multi_tier_supply_chain , and since schema_version 3 the deep-tier topology itself: the six columns the two prominence RPCs return from network_nodes and network_edges . When this moves a multi-tier or deep-tier ANALYSIS is stale; no simulation changes. hash_product SHA-256 over the PRODUCT level (WP 10.1, §4 D235): suppliers, materials, products, customers, the single-level BOM and the inbound / outbound lanes — every column the inputs domain hashes except the multi-level BOM. A projection of facts already hashed; the composite does not include it, so adding it moved no graph_hash . NULL never — computed for every snapshot that has inputs . hash_process SHA-256 over the PROCESS level (WP 10.1): bom_multi_level and multi_tier_supply_chain whole, plus the endpoints and quantities…
