entries.title: How policies work
entries.text: How policies work A policy is a rule for running the chain — when to reorder, where to source, how to treat demand you can't meet. In short Your data describes the chain. Policies decide how it behaves. Same data, different policies, different results. Each field resolves on its own: your override, then the uploaded value, then a stated default. There's no single ladder. A value only matters if the simulation reads it — check the stage reference for each field.

entries.title: How policies work — What a policy changes
entries.text: Inputs describe demand, the BOM, lanes and capacities. Policies decide replenishment, sourcing, production and what happens to demand you can't meet. On Policies , work through the Supplier, Plant and Customer stages, then Run & Validate . The three stages, with fields used in the tutorial. Stage Decides Example fields Supplier Where materials come from and how they are replenished Primary source · replenishment type · coverage · safety stock · lead-time override Plant What is made and whether finished goods are stocked Finished-goods stock (make-to-stock / make-to-order) · capacity Customer Demand and how it is served Demand · fulfilment source · backordering Each cell shows where its value came from: an unsaved draft, a saved override, a project default, or your upload. Those are different states. Two fields, different resolution paths Illustration. These examples are not a universal precedence ladder.

entries.title: How policies work — Where a value comes from
entries.text: 1 Saved override on the policy row ↓ → 2 Uploaded value item master or lane ↓ → 3 Derived value e.g. from lanes ↓ → 4 Stated default marked as such A master-backed field, such as material cost, resolves left to right. Other fields have their own chains. Look at each field on its own. For a cost read from the item master, a saved override replaces the uploaded value; with neither, a value derived from lanes or an explicit default applies. Demand, lead time and finished-goods fields follow their own chains, listed on the stage references. An example M-BOARD costs 20 in the tutorial master. An override of 25 changes the simulated valuation and leaves the master at 20. Removing the override restores 20; re-uploading the master doesn't remove it. Blank isn't zero A blank can mean no override, derive a value, or use a default. Zero opening stock starts empty; zero safety-stock days asks for no fixed buffer. Check the field's limits before you type 0. Lead time The Supplier-stage cell can override a lane without changing the lane. An override wins; otherwise the lane, or a two-week default if the lane has none. The exception is a lane whose lead-time shape is triangular or uniform: the run plans on the mean of its bounds, the cell shows that mean as a derived value, and a lead time typed on the row is not read. How this works: lead time and finished-goods targets Lead-time entry uses…

entries.title: How policies work — Replenishment types, briefly
entries.text: A reorder point or target you type is an absolute level — nothing is added on top. Leave it empty to use the formula and its buffer. MRP takes replenishment from the plan. Notation: s, S, T and (R,Q) A typed material reorder point s or target S is an absolute level; the engine does not add safety stock to it. Periodic replenishment reads its review period T. An (R,Q) row needs a positive lot Q, on the row or inherited from the project; it has no coverage κ control. A parameter stored for a previous type is dropped by the conversion, with a warning.

entries.title: How policies work — Try it: test a stock buffer
entries.text: 1 Start from the tutorial baseline /policies Min-max replenishment, 2 weeks of coverage, 0 days of safety stock, explicit opening quantities. At 100 products a week the BOM needs 100 boards and 200 housings a week. 2 Change one thing Supplier stage Set Safety stock to 28 days on the material rows. Don't touch demand, opening stock or the disruption. 3 Save a new version and rerun Run & Validate Keep the baseline version, rerun the same supplier disruption, and compare service and holding cost together. You should see two policy versions you can compare side by side. The 28-day figure is illustrative. A buffer can improve service and still cost more than it saves.

entries.title: How policies work — Drafts, versions and Validated Models
entries.text: Draft An edited cell that isn't saved yet. Save, and check that no unsaved marker remains. Policy version A saved set of policies, captured for a run. Preset A reusable starting point — not evidence that it suits your chain. Validated Model Binds policy and dataset versions to validation evidence and adopted simulation settings. It can go stale when inputs or policies change. When the run button offers Save version and run , it's asking to bind your edits to a version. Read the credibility message; an old validation may not cover a new scenario.

entries.title: How policies work — Saved isn't the same as simulated
entries.text: The simulation doesn't use every field Transport-family settings and routing flags can be saved and shown without being simulated. Disabled milestone controls describe planned support. The Supplier , Plant and Customer references mark each field. The engine models one focal production stage; a multi-level BOM display doesn't add sub-assembly capacity or work in progress. After a significant change, read the conversion notes and effective values. Version history › Export maps a saved policy through the same path as a run. Its Read me sheet says whether it used the latest run's dataset and scenario or the current project data — check that before treating it as evidence for a particular run. Next: versions and presets , then model validation .

entries.title: How planning works
entries.text: How planning works From the demand your customers state, to what the plant builds, to what it buys, to who gets served.

entries.title: How planning works — The flow, end to end
entries.text: The plan always starts from future finished-good demand — and it never reads demand that has not happened. 1 · Demand per customer row. Each customer × product row states its demand: a forecast series (uploaded as a Demand Forecast ) or a mean, a variation and a distribution. A row that states neither takes its product's demand split by volume. The plan uses the forecast or the mean; the run draws actual demand around it. See Customer stage . 2 · Planned production = min(requirement, capacity). For a make-to-order product the requirement is the projected demand plus any backlog; for make-to-stock it is what the finished-goods policy asks for — base-stock, min-max or days of cover — plus any backlog. The plan looks ahead as far as the longest material lead time planned by MRP. See Plant stage and Products . 3 · Materials. A material on MRP is ordered from the plan: the BOM times planned production over its lead time, net of stock and what is on the way, rounded up to the MOQ. A material on a reorder-point type is ordered from consumption, as before. Both can sit in one project. See Policy types . 4 · Fulfillment per row. When supply is short, the project's one allocation rule splits each product's units across its rows — by priority, fair share, price or service target. Each row decides for itself whether what it does not get waits (backorder, within its window, at its cost) or…

entries.title: How planning works — One rule for the plan and for fulfillment
entries.text: When the plan sees a week it cannot build in full, it splits the shortfall with the same allocation rule fulfillment uses, and carries forward only the share of rows that allow backorder. A lost-sales row's shortfall leaves the plan the week it leaves the order book, so the plant never builds — and MRP never buys — for an order a customer has already cancelled. What the plan cannot know The plan reads the forecast, not the future. A change that is in your forecast is planned for before it arrives; a change nobody forecast is met only by what is on hand and your safety stock. The validation study measures both, with the same demand and disruption on both sides: docs/research/mrp-vs-reorder-point.md .

entries.title: How planning works — Where each setting lives
entries.text: Demand and fulfillment per row: the Customer stage. The FG policy and opening stock per product: the Plant stage. MRP per material: the Supplier stage's policy type. The allocation rule and the backorder defaults: the Customer rules line above the Customer grid; the FG safety buffer: the line above the Plant grid. All on /policies ; the uploads are the base each cell overrides.

entries.title: Plant stage — One row per product
entries.text: What the plant can make, what it costs to make it, and — where the product is made to stock — how much finished inventory to keep. The rows come from your Products master and the outbound lanes that name a product. Each row's FG inventory switch — the product's fulfillment_mode — decides how much of this stage applies to it. A make-to-order product holds no finished goods, so its row shows no FG policy at all. For a make-to-stock product the FG inventory band reads like the Supplier stage's inventory band: the FG policy is the policy type, and one Replenishment parameters cell holds only the levels that policy reads — S for base-stock, s and S for min-max, D for days of cover — then the opening stock. They decide how much to build: planned production is the policy's requirement plus any backlog, capped at capacity. How much finished stock to keep is said once, on the row: an empty S is one week of the projected demand, and a typed S is used as typed. Demand is not set here: it is set per row on the Customer stage , and a row with no demand of its own inherits the product's mean from the item master, then the outbound volume. 17 columns, across 1 policy family — production . Every column on this stage reaches the simulation.

entries.text: Customer stage Per customer × product: sourcing firm, price, backorder handling. Demand comes from product data. Demand and fulfilment are set here, row by row Each customer and product row carries its own demand — mode (forecast or model), distribution, mean, variation and, for a triangular row, its bounds, with the uploaded forecast beside them — and its own fulfilment: whether it backorders, for how long and at what cost, and the priority, price or service target the project's allocation rule reads. The supplier stage has 25 columns and the plant stage 17; this one has 16.

entries.title: Customer stage — One row per customer and product
entries.text: What happens at the demand end: which firm serves this customer, what they pay, and what the model does with an order it cannot fill. The rows come from your Outbound Logistics upload. A row's demand comes from its own spec when it has one — uploaded on the outbound file or as a Demand Forecast , and overridable in the cells here — and otherwise from its product's demand, split by volume. Products covers the product-level shape. 16 columns, across 2 policy families — fulfillment , demand . 2 of them do not reach the simulation Each is marked below with what is actually happening to it. They are not broken settings you should avoid — they are settings that are stored, versioned and shown back to you while the run ignores them, which is a different and more misleading thing. We would rather say so here than let you discover it by changing one and seeing no difference.

Nothing reads this value at all is read by NO consumer anywhere — not scsim, not the frozen legacy engine, and by nothing in the product beyond the grid that renders it. Editable, stored, versioned and hashed into policy_hash , and the only thing that ever happens to the value is that it is shown back. This is §4 D18's exact shape. The chain is unwritable only because nothing DECLARES that, so a reader cannot tell it apart from a field the engine forgot. Evidence: src/hooks/useStageRows.tsx:785, src/hooks/useStageRows.tsx:800. entries.title: Customer stage — What is per row, and what is per project
entries.text: One allocation rule per project; everything that rule reads, and every backorder setting, per row. The allocation rule — priority, fair share, proportional, revenue maximising or SLA tiers — is set once, on the Allocation line above the grid — shown only when two or more customers want the same product, because only then is there anything to share — at /policies . Allocating between customers is a rule the chain applies across rows, so a per-row version would be several rules competing to be the rule; the engine reads one. What that rule reads is per row: a row's priority , its price and its service target . Each column appears only under the rule that reads it. So is backorder : one row can wait for supply while another of the same product loses what cannot be shipped, each with its own backlog, window and cost. When supply falls short, each product's units are split across its rows by the project's rule, a row's oldest backlog first. A project that sets none of this per row runs exactly as before, with that line's settings for every row. The base under these cells is your data: the Outbound Logistics row (demand, price) and the customer's own row in the customers upload (priority weight, segment, contracted floor). An edit here is an override on the row; the upload is never changed.

entries.title: Policy types
entries.text: Policy types Min-max, base stock, (R, Q), periodic review and MRP — and which parameters each one actually uses.

entries.title: Policy types — What a policy type is
entries.text: A replenishment policy answers two questions: when do we order , and how much . Different types answer them differently, and each one needs a different set of numbers from you. Choosing the type is what decides which parameters appear. The types, their parameters and every default below are read from the engine's own export. If the engine gains a parameter, it appears here without anyone editing this page. Four rules, one demand The shapes are what you are choosing between. The marks are which of the numbers you type actually reach the simulation — and on three of the four types, none of the sizing parameters do.

entries.title: Policy types — Inventory / replenishment
entries.text: Everyday replenishment rule (min-max / base-stock / (R,Q) / periodic). The baseline shock absorber every chain already has; quantifying it prevents over-buying dedicated resilience. Min-max (s, S) implemented type = min_max Parameters this type uses Reorder point (s) reorder_point A number. If you leave it blank: 50 , the registry's declared default · accepted range 0 to ∞ Order-up-to (S) order_up_to A number. entries.title: Policy types — MRP — ordering from the plan
entries.text: The four reorder-point types order from consumption : when stock runs down, refill it. MRP orders from the plan . Each week it looks at what the plant will build over the material's lead time — planned production, which comes from your customer demand — multiplies it out through the BOM, and orders the difference between that need and what is already on hand or on the way: order = need over the next lead time + safety stock − on hand − on the way, rounded up to the MOQ when it is positive, sent to the material's primary supplier. It has no level of its own to type. Its buffer is the row's safety-stock days, counted once. A demand step that is in your forecast is ordered for before it arrives; one that nobody forecast is caught only by what is on hand — the plan never reads demand that has not happened. MRP and reorder-point materials can sit in one project, and an inspection run shows each MRP material's record week by week: need, on hand, on the way, net and order.

entries.title: The policy catalog — How to read this page
entries.text: 23 policies, of which 12 are implemented and 11 are planned. Engine 0.8.3 . A planned policy is in the catalog and not in the engine. It is listed rather than hidden so that the answer to “does this tool model X” is a fact you can read rather than a silence you have to interpret. Nothing on this page is a roadmap commitment; it is the state of the engine's own declaration. This page is generated, and that is the point The archived manual carried a hand-copied policy catalogue, and it drifted from the engine within a quarter. This one is read from the engine's export, so a policy that is added, implemented or renamed changes here with no one editing a page.

entries.title: The policy catalog — Customer — 4
entries.text: P-C.1 unmet demand handling implemented What happens to an unservable order: it dies (lost_sales — competitive markets), waits (backorder — contractual B2B), or splits (partial_backorder). entries.title: Where a number came from
entries.text: Where a number came from Every number in the grid carries a mark saying where it came from. This is how to read them.

entries.title: Where a number came from — The promise this keeps
entries.text: No number without a source. Every value you see resolves to your data, a named rule, or an explicit default — there is no fourth possibility, and the mark tells you which. The mark is on the cell, not in a log. That is deliberate: a substitution you would have to go looking for is a substitution most people never find, and a model built on numbers nobody checked is the failure this product is designed around. The marks, on a real grid The dot colours are the grid's own. Five marks cover eight states, and the ninth — a bundle default — has no mark and no legend entry, so it looks exactly like a plain cell.

entries.title: Where a number came from — The marks
entries.text: Edited You have just changed this and not saved yet. Nothing else has seen it. Saved override You changed this and saved it. It stays until you remove it, and a re-upload does not touch it. From project data It came from a file you uploaded, unchanged. From item master It came from one of your item master files — materials, products or suppliers. Suggested by ranking your uploaded volumes — not an uploaded value; confirm it We ranked your uploaded volumes and put the leader here. It is a starting point, not something you told us — confirm it. Derived fallback (≈) — the engine computes this from your inbound/outbound uploads We worked it out from your other uploads, because the field it belongs to was empty. The number is real; the choice to use it was ours. Imputed project average — verify An average across your project stood in for a value nothing supplied. Verify these. Empty — the schema declares what that means The cell is empty, and empty MEANS something here. The token shown is the declared meaning, not a number we invented. Bundle default (no dot) Nothing in your data resolved it, so the policy bundle's default applies. One of them has no dot, and that is a real gap A bundle default renders with no mark at all. So a cell showing a number nothing in your data produced looks exactly like a cell showing a number you supplied — unless you know that an unmarked cell is the d…

entries.title: Where a number came from — When empty is an answer
entries.text: A few columns mean something specific when they are blank. A supplier with no capacity_per_week is an unlimited supplier, not one that can ship nothing. Those cells render the declared token with its own mark rather than a made-up number — because rendering 0 there tells the reader the exact inverse of what the model believes. Suppliers has the full story of that one, including where the grid still gets it wrong.

entries.title: When a value is missing — The rule behind this list
entries.text: A substitution that is not on this page does not exist in the software. The list is generated from the same declarations the code reads, so it cannot be incomplete by oversight. 67 substitutions across 19 tables. Each says what triggers it, what goes in, and how it is marked when you look at the value. A substitution is not an error. Most of them are the answer you would have given: the price you actually pay across your own inbound lanes, the demand your own outbound lanes imply. What matters is that you can tell one from a number you supplied — which is what the provenance marks are for. 22 of them do not say where you would see them The contract records what these substitutions do and not where the substitution becomes visible. In practice most are marked in the grid like any other; what is missing is the declaration, so this page cannot promise it for them. They are the rows below with no “you see it here” line.

entries.title: Policy versions & presets
entries.text: Policy versions & presets Saving a set of decisions, reusing it, comparing two — and why a preset is not a set of numbers.

entries.title: Policy versions & presets — Why a policy set is versioned at all
entries.text: A result is only meaningful with the decisions that produced it. If the policies can change after a run, then a chart from last week is a chart of something nobody can reconstruct. So a saved policy set is a version : a fixed thing a run can point at. The version is what makes “rerun exactly this” a question with an answer.

entries.title: Policy versions & presets — Versions
entries.text: Saving the grid writes a version: every override, as it stood, with a fingerprint over the contents. Two versions with the same fingerprint are the same decisions, whatever they are called and whenever they were saved. Comparing two runs starts with comparing their versions. If the fingerprints match, the policies are not what changed — which is usually the first thing worth ruling out.

entries.title: Policy versions & presets — What a version records beyond the values
entries.text: A version carries a label and free-text notes , the person who saved it by name and email, and a pointer to the version it was saved from . So a project's versions form a chain rather than a pile, and “what did this change” is answerable against its parent rather than against whichever version happens to be next to it in a list. It also stores the previous snapshot beside the new one. That is what makes the difference between two versions readable without re-deriving it, and it is what an automatic restore uses when an applied change has to be undone. Write the notes. The label tells you which version; the notes tell you why there is one, and six weeks later that is the whole value of the record.

entries.title: Policy versions & presets — Presets — 8, and none of them is a set of numbers
entries.text: A preset is a recipe, not a saved configuration. It computes its values from your project's own measurements every time you open it. Two projects applying Sustainable get different numbers, because the preset reads what their chains actually look like first. Between them the 8 presets read 6 measured facts: how variable that demand is your average daily demand how variable those lead times are your suppliers' average lead time whether the project is modelled make-to-stock or make-to-order your highest-volume supplier, by name Which means a preset applied to an empty project is not the preset. With no data loaded there is nothing to measure, and the dialog says so — it tells you the values shown are schema defaults rather than derived ones. Upload first, then apply. Make-to-Stock supplied with the product Produce ahead of demand, hold FG inventory, ship from stock. Sets 7 policy families. Derived from how variable that demand is, your average daily demand, your highest-volume supplier, by name. Make-to-Order supplied with the product Zero FG stock, lot-for-lot production, long backorder window. Sets 7 policy families. Derived from how variable that demand is, your average daily demand, your highest-volume supplier, by name. Lean / JIT supplied with the product Minimal inventory, daily review, single-source, FTL — fast & cheap when stable. Sets 7 policy families. Derived from ho…

entries.title: Policy versions & presets — Applying one is a review, not a button
entries.text: The dialog shows a diff before anything is written: every field the preset would change, its current value struck through beside the proposed one, grouped by policy family with a count on each. You choose which families to take. Each group has its own checkbox and the apply button counts what you selected — so taking a preset's inventory posture without its sourcing strategy is one click rather than an edit afterwards. A family already matching the preset does not appear at all. Every proposed value carries a reason, on the information icon beside it. That is where a derived number explains itself — “max(14, 2 × lead-time variability × lead time)” rather than “14 days” — and it is the only place the reasoning exists. It is not written to your project. The reasoning does not survive the apply Applying writes overrides exactly as if you had typed them. Nothing downstream can tell a preset's value from one you chose, which is deliberate — a preset is not a third kind of provenance. But it means the why is gone the moment you click. If a derived value matters, put it in the version's notes before you save, because that is the only field on this page that keeps a sentence. These two tables are not yet described in the contract Everything else in this manual's reference sections is generated from a per-table description — every column, unit, constraint and substitution. policy_versi…

entries.title: Verify your inputs
entries.text: Verify your inputs What is checked before a run, what stops it, and how to clear each finding.

entries.title: Verify your inputs — What verification actually asks
entries.text: One question, per field the engine reads: does this resolve to your data, to a named substitution rule, or to nothing? It is not a schema check — the upload already did that. This asks whether the model you have built can be simulated, and how much of it would be running on defaults if it were. Run it from /policies , on the Run & validate stage, before launching anything.

entries.title: Verify your inputs — The three severities
entries.text: The grading follows the engine's own rule, so a finding here means the same thing it would mean to the simulation. block The run cannot start. Either the engine would fail outright, or a field it requires resolves to nothing at all. There is no number we could put there that would not be an invention. warn The run will start, using a neutral constant. A value is missing and the fallback is a flat default — a price of 1.0, a lead time of two weeks. It is not derived from anything you uploaded, so the result is a shape rather than a quantity. You can acknowledge these and proceed. info The run will start, using something worked out from your data. A value is missing and the fallback is derived from what you did upload — the average price you pay across a material's inbound lanes, the demand your outbound lanes imply. Usually what you meant, and still worth reading. The difference between warn and info is where the number came from Both mean “you left this out and we filled it in”. A warn was filled with a constant nothing in your project produced; an info was filled with something computed from data you did upload. That distinction is the whole difference between a model of your chain and a model of a chain.

entries.title: Verify your inputs — Clearing a finding
entries.text: 1 Read which rows it names /policies Every finding lists the entities it applies to, up to twenty-five of them. A finding on two rows and a finding on two thousand need different responses. 2 Decide whether the fallback is wrong An info finding is often correct — if what you pay on your own inbound lanes is the price, there is nothing to fix. When a value is missing lists what each substitution actually does. 3 Fix it where it belongs A missing master value goes in the item-master file or the grid cell; a missing lane goes in the logistics upload. Fixing it in the policy grid when it belongs in a file means the next upload does not carry it. 4 Re-verify The gate is recomputed from the data as it stands, not from what it said last time.

entries.title: Verify your inputs — The one finding that always blocks
entries.text: A material in your bill of materials with no supplier that can deliver it cannot be simulated at any level of approximation — there is no chain. This blocks regardless of how it got there, and it is the most common reason a first run will not start. It is usually a mismatch rather than an omission: a material_id spelled one way in the BOM and another in the inbound file. Compare the two files before adding rows.

entries.title: Verify your inputs — What the engine asks for before any policy does
entries.text: 7 fields the simulation reads regardless of which policies you have chosen. A policy you enable can add more. Each carries the engine's own level and, where there is one, the rule that stands in when it is absent. materials.cost required Inventory valuation and holding cost — the terminal default of 1.0 makes every cost KPI meaningless. If nothing supplies it: volume-weighted average inbound unit_price across the material's supply lanes; the cheapest quoted price when no lane carries a volume products.sell_price required Revenue and lost-sales valuation — the terminal default of 1.0 makes revenue KPIs meaningless. If nothing supplies it: demand-weighted average outbound unit_price products.demand_mean required Demand generation — with neither source the product is never ordered (zero demand). If nothing supplies it: Σ weekly outbound volume products.production_capacity recommended With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds. If nothing supplies it: production policy capacity_units_per_day × 7 × utilization inbound_logistics.unit_price recommended Purchase cost per sourcing arc — a missing price defaults to 1.0 and distorts procurement spend. If nothing supplies it: nothing does — this is the blocking kind. inbound_logistics.lead_time recommended Supplier lead time per sourcing arc — missing values default to 2 weeks. If not…

entries.title: Data Trust Report
entries.text: Data Trust Report Coverage, freshness, ingest history and known limits, for one project, in one place.

entries.title: Data Trust Report — The question it answers
entries.text: Is this model built on good data — and where is it not? Verify your inputs tells you whether a run can start. This tells you what the run would be standing on. They are different questions and a model can pass the first while failing the second badly. Open it beside the pre-run gate at /policies .

entries.title: Data Trust Report — What is in it
entries.text: Headline One line. It is never better than the limits below it allow — a report with unexplained rows does not say “all clear”. Dataset fingerprint The hash of the data this report was computed against. Two reports with the same fingerprint describe the same project state, whatever their timestamps say. Coverage Per field the engine reads: how many entities got a value from your data, how many from a named substitution, and how many from nothing. The third number is the one that blocks. Substitutions The same list, filtered to where a rule stood in for you, with the rule's own wording. When a value is missing has the catalog. Freshness Per table: how many computed rows still describe the data you are holding. Ingest history The recent loads into this project — where each came from and who applied it. Known limits What this report cannot tell you. Some entries are true of every project; some carry a count from yours. A limits block that never changes is a disclaimer, and this one is meant to change. Freshness has three states, and unknown is not stale fresh — the row was computed from the data you are holding now. stale — the row was computed from a different version of this project. Any figure that depends on it describes a project state that no longer exists. unknown — we cannot tell. The row was written before provenance existed, so it carries nothing saying which data produ…

entries.title: Data Trust Report — The finding that is not about display
entries.text: Most stale rows affect what you read. One kind affects what runs: a policy override seeded from data the project no longer holds. The engine reads overrides, not the grid. So a stale seeded override means the simulation uses a number that is not the one on screen. It is called out separately in the report for that reason. How policies work explains why a row-level value and a bundle value behave differently on a re-upload, which is the mechanism behind it.

entries.title: Data Trust Report — What it does when it cannot compute a section
entries.text: It says so, and renders nothing else. A trust report that quietly omitted the part it could not calculate would be claiming a clean bill it never checked — which is precisely the failure the whole transparency standard exists to prevent.

entries.title: Model validation
entries.text: Model validation Checking the model against what actually happened — and the badge every run carries because of it.

entries.title: Model validation — What validation means here
entries.text: A model that reproduces last quarter is a model you can argue about next quarter with. Verify your inputs asks whether the model is complete. This asks whether it is right — whether, run over a period you already know the outcome of, it produces something close to what you observed. The two are independent. A model can be fully populated, pass every gate, and still be wrong about your chain, because nothing in the input data says whether your assumptions about behaviour are correct. It happens on Policies → Run & validate, and what it produces is a card .

entries.title: Model validation — A card is not just a verdict — it adopts two numbers
entries.text: The warm-up length and the replication count a validation settles on become the defaults every scenario created under it inherits. This is the part that changes your work rather than recording it. Validating a model decides how long it takes to reach steady state and how many replications the statistics need, and a scenario created afterwards starts with both already set — marked as inherited until you change one. The warm-up is found by one of 3 methods, and the card records which: engine , welch or mser5 . Two different methods can settle on two different weeks for the same model, so the method is part of the claim rather than an implementation detail.

entries.title: Model validation — A verdict is bound to what produced it
entries.text: What a verdict is tied to This is the one place in the product where a result already carries everything that produced it. The badge is what that binding buys you. This is the one place in the product where a stored conclusion names all four of the things that decided it. A card records the 4 components below, each by identity and by fingerprint. Identity says which one; the fingerprint says whether that one has since changed. It also names the run that was the evidence, so the verdict points at a result rather than standing alone. dataset dataset_version_id · graph_hash The data it ran on, by version and by fingerprint. policy policy_version_id · policy_hash The policy set, by version and by fingerprint. scenario scenario_hash · scenario_fingerprint The scenario's conditions, fingerprinted. engine engine_fingerprint The engine build that produced the evidence. That binding is what makes the credibility badge possible, and the badge is the reason this page matters to somebody who will never open the validation screen.

entries.title: Model validation — The badge on every run and every scenario
entries.text: Wherever you see a credibility badge — beside a scenario in the list, on a run's results — it is this card being compared against your project as it is now. Three states, and the middle one is the useful one. unvalidated No active card for the policy version you are on. Not a criticism of the model — it means nobody has checked this particular version of the decisions. validated A card exists for this policy version, its verdict is positive, and none of the fingerprints has moved. stale A card exists and something underneath it has changed. The badge names which — policy, data, scenario or engine — so “the validation no longer applies” is actionable rather than a warning to dismiss. Unsaved policy edits count as drift immediately, before you save anything. The engine component is checked only after a run, because it compares the build that produced a result against the build that produced the evidence. A live screen cannot know it yet, and does not pretend to.

entries.title: Model validation — What a verdict can say, and what a card can become
entries.text: A verdict is validated or rejected , on one of 2 bases: statistical or face . A statistical basis is a comparison against observed outcomes; a face basis is a knowledgeable person judging the behaviour reasonable. Both are recorded as what they are , which matters when somebody later asks how hard the check was. A card is active , superseded or revoked . Superseding points at the card that replaced it, and revoking is a status change rather than a delete — so a validation that turned out to be wrong leaves a record that it was made and withdrawn, which is the whole reason to store one. The card also keeps the tests that were run and the findings as they stood at the time. A verdict given while a model had known gaps records those gaps beside itself rather than leaving a reader to reconstruct them. The binding is on this card, not on every result A validation names its dataset, policy set, scenario and engine. An ordinary run's results do not yet leave the system as one artifact carrying the same four — that is the reproducibility record, and it is owed. So the honest reading is: a validated model is reproducible; an arbitrary figure is not yet. Reproducibility record says exactly what is in place and what is missing. This table is not yet described in the contract model_validations has no per-column description. So this page has no column reference to link you to, and will not…

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment
entries.text: Simulation Lab — running an experiment Run a controlled scenario from a saved model, then inspect completion and compare.

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment — Before you run
entries.text: Start with a completed baseline from Policies → Run & Validate and a saved Validated Model. In Simulation Lab , the pinned baseline is inspected and copied; its validation is managed on Policies. Copying a scenario copies settings, not completed runs. Select the intended project and scenario. Check your permission to run simulations. A scenario identifies horizon, warm-up, replication settings, seed, objective, disruption schedule and recovery configuration; the dispatched run binds these to saved input and policy versions. Five stages, one gate The gate is the only place the sequence can stop. The readout, the stage label, the button and its reason are one state, so they cannot disagree.

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment — Setup and Recovery playbook
entries.text: In Setup , inspect the horizon, seed, common random numbers and replication count. Choose an objective the run actually reports, such as fill rate. The horizon is not the same as the engine's analysis window; use the window summary and conversion notes. In Recovery playbook , set a supported event and any intended response. For the control-unit tutorial , target S-BOARD with an 80% capacity reduction starting at week 16 for 4 weeks. Leave recovery levers off for the first disrupted run. An empty disruption schedule is appropriate for a baseline. A stage's completion marker is a workflow hint, not proof of a correct experiment. Supplier and plant targets must resolve to entities the engine supports; a material shown in a graph is not automatically a supported direct disruption target.

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment — Run: findings and save state
entries.text: In Run , clear every blocking finding. Read warnings before ticking the acknowledgement to run with defaults. A warning can describe a meaningful substitution, and accepting it records your choice; it does not make the input accurate. Inspect the saved policy version. If edits are pending, use Save version and run where offered; if no version exists, save one first. A not permitted state needs the project owner's help, not a different numerical setting. Checkpoint: the submitted run has an ID, version bindings and a visible status. Clicking Run alone is not completion.

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment — Queued, running, done, failed or cancelled
entries.text: A queued run is waiting for execution. A running run can show preliminary results as replications arrive. Wait for done and confirm the completed count before using the full experiment. Closing the browser does not cancel a remote worker job. Use the run's Cancel control to request cancellation and verify its final status. For a failure, retain the run ID and error, inspect conversion notes and input findings, then correct the cause before retrying. Do not repeatedly dispatch the same blocked model. Add replications only when the run controls support it and the existing model/protocol is still the one you intend. Reuse can return an existing compatible completed result. Check its run record and bindings rather than treating a fast response as evidence that new computation occurred.

entries.title: Simulation Lab — running an experiment — Results and Compare
entries.text: Open Results to review completion, conversion notes, KPI distributions and weekly traces. Then open Compare and select a completed, non-exploratory baseline. Comparable scenarios appear together; select one to inspect its paired comparison. Preserve common random numbers and the seed, and change exactly one comparison component: policy, world or disruption schedule. For baseline versus Board disruption, hold data and policies fixed. For a buffer response, keep the same disruption and vary only the policy version. The comparison checks several identities but does not replace your review of dataset versions, warm-up, measurement windows and assumptions. Next: reading results and comparison design .

entries.title: Scenarios
entries.text: Scenarios Saving a set of conditions so two runs can differ in exactly one way — and every setting that makes one up.

entries.title: Scenarios — What a scenario is
entries.text: The conditions a run happens under, separated from the model it happens to. Your data describes the chain. Your policies describe how you run it. A scenario describes the world it is running in — how long the window is, how precisely you want to measure, and what goes wrong. Keeping the three apart is what makes a comparison mean something. If you change the scenario and the policies at once, the difference in the result is not attributable to either.

entries.title: Scenarios — Every setting, and what it starts as
entries.text: Days in, weeks out The form takes days; the chain's physics are weekly. Two start dates six days apart can be the same run, and nothing on the form says so. Stage 1 of Simulation Lab , in three groups. The value in the right-hand column is what a brand-new scenario carries before you touch anything — so a setting you have never opened is that one. Run window Planning horizon the project's planning unit 364 How long the simulated window is. Everything the run reports is measured inside it, so a horizon shorter than your longest lead time measures a chain that never finished replenishing. Stored as horizon_days . Steady state starts at the project's planning unit 14 The point at which the model stops filling its pipes and starts counting. Weeks before it are simulated and excluded from every measure — which is why a result can look nothing like the first ten weeks of its own chart. Stored as warmup_days . Warm-up detection "auto" On auto, the engine detects where the model settled and reports the week it chose. On manual you fix it yourself, and typing a warm-up switches this to manual for you rather than silently overriding your number. Stored as warmup_mode . Precision Replications runs 10 How many times the same world is run with different random draws. This is the single biggest lever on how much you can trust a difference between two scenarios. Stored as replications . Comm…

entries.title: Scenarios — Templates and the saved library
entries.text: A template is a scenario worth starting from rather than a scenario you ran. Applying one fills in the conditions and drops you on the disruption editor; from that point it is an ordinary scenario and nothing downstream treats it differently. Duplicating one of your own scenarios copies its settings and not its runs, which is the right way to test one change: duplicate, change the one thing, run both, compare. Change one thing at a time The discipline this feature exists to support: run a baseline, save it, then change exactly one condition and run again. Two runs that differ in one scenario setting produce a difference you can attribute. Two runs that differ in three produce a number. Leave Common random numbers on while you do it. Without it the two runs also differ in every random draw, and the difference you measure includes noise you did not ask for.

entries.title: Disruptions
entries.text: Disruptions What fails, when, for how long — and the two different ways this system records that. Read this first: the simulation reads the scenario's own schedule, and the two tables below are history The simulation runs off a disruption schedule stored on the scenario itself — the list you edit on stage 2 of Simulation Lab , and the one a stress preset fills in for you. That schedule is sent with the run and is the only disruption the engine ever sees. The two tables described below are a different thing. One is a single row per affected node; the other splits a disruption into a profile, its targets, its effects and its settings. Neither reads the other, nothing migrated the rows from the first into the second, and nothing marks either as retired. And no run reads either of them : the worker loads the item masters, the logistics, the BOM, the customers and the scenario, and no disruption table is in that list. Until September 2026 a disruption added from a network map's dialog was written to the second table set and to a new scenario — and the table half never changed a simulation. The dialog now writes only the scenario's schedule , to a new scenario started from the validated baseline or to one you already have, and it checks the target first: the engine disrupts a supplier of the project or the plant, and says so before anything is saved. So the product writes one model,…

entries.title: Disruptions — The one the engine reads: a scenario's own schedule
entries.text: A list of events on the scenario, each naming what is hit, the day it starts, how many days it lasts and how hard it is. It travels with the run and is the only disruption the engine acts on. Everything about how those four numbers are interpreted — which targets resolve, how days become weeks, what a magnitude at or above 100% does, and the five-event cap — is on Stress tests , because that is the page a reader arrives at with a schedule already written for them. Read it before you write one by hand. A start can be entered three ways — a run week, an ISO 8601 calendar week (weeks start Monday; some years have a week 53) or a date — and all three go through the project's simulation start, which is run week 0: run week t is the seven days from the start plus 7· t . The engine runs whole weeks, so a date lands in the run week that contains it, and the line under the field always states all three readings. What you typed is kept beside the run week; if the project start later changes, the event says so and offers to keep its run week or move to what you entered — it never moves by itself. Without a simulation start only the run week can be entered. The engine has a second calendar for demand — the earliest forecast period — and the editor says when the two differ. A run records the date of its week 0 when it is dispatched, so later edits to the project start never re-date it. Run…

entries.title: Disruptions — The first table — one row per affected node
entries.text: One disruption applied to one node of one project: a capacity cut, a delay, or both. The ORIGINAL disruption shape, superseded in design by the disruption_scenario_* profile/target/effect/setting split but never migrated — both are live and neither reads the other. Everything about one disruption lives on one row: which node, how much capacity is lost, how much delay is added. It is the simpler thing to write and the harder thing to extend — a disruption that hits an edge rather than a node has nowhere to go. id uuid Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. project_id uuid The project this row belongs to. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. plant_name text The plant this scenario belongs to, by display name. A project has one plant_name, so this is a denormalised copy of projects.plant_name rather than a second identity. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. node_id text The node the disruption is applied to, by its display id — the same string the network pages use. Not a uuid and not a foreign key: a scenario may name a node that no longer exists in the graph, and deleting it silently would …

entries.text: The same idea, normalised. A profile is the disruption; three tables under it say what it hits, what it does, and how it is simulated. A profile deleted takes all three with it, so one action by a person removes rows from four tables. disruption_scenario_profiles the header — what the disruption is called, when it starts and ends id uuid Surrogate key. The natural key is below; this is what the child rows reference. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. project_id uuid The project this row belongs to. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. plant_name text The plant this scenario belongs to, by display name. A project has one plant_name, so this is a denormalised copy of projects.plant_name rather than a second identity. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. scenario_name text What the person called this profile. Not unique — two profiles may share a name, and the surrogate id is the key. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. status public.disruption_status draft , active or archived , as the disruption_status enum. entries.title: Recovery playbooks
entries.text: Recovery playbooks What the chain does once something has already gone wrong — the six levers, which of them reach the engine, and how a playbook is reused.

entries.title: Recovery playbooks — Recovery is a different question from resilience
entries.text: A resilient chain absorbs a shock. A recovery playbook is what you do when it did not. Most policy decisions are about standing posture — how much stock, how many suppliers, how much slack. A playbook is conditional: if this happens, do that . It costs nothing while nothing is wrong, which is exactly why it is easy to leave un-thought-through. A playbook lives on stage 2 of Simulation Lab , beside the disruption schedule it responds to. The master switch above the strategies turns the whole thing off: with it off, disruptions hit raw and nothing mitigates. 1 of the 5 strategies do not reach the engine Safety stock can be switched on, can carry parameters, are saved with the scenario and are shown as enabled — and the model mapper has no branch for it, so it changes no number in the run. This is not a guess about implementation depth: the same list on the policy grid was already narrowed to what the engine maps, and neither of these is on it. Two screens, two lists, and nothing comparing them until this page did. Several of the built-in policy presets turn Safety stock on. A preset is not wrong for doing so — the intent is recorded — but a run under one of them is not running the lever the preset's note describes.

entries.title: Recovery playbooks — The 5 strategies
entries.text: Which levers reach the engine Two of the six change no number in the run, and two of the engine's plugins cannot be reached from this screen at all. The lists disagree in both directions. Each one is a switch, and turning it on reveals its own parameters. The parameters are what the strategy costs or how fast it works — they are not thresholds for when it fires, which is the trigger block above them. Backup supplier reaches the engine While a supplier is disrupted, reroute its materials' orders to another qualified supplier (P-S.1). Backup supplier lead time weeks · starts at Leave blank to use each backup lane's own lead time; a number overrides every backup's (Ts') Safety stock saved, not simulated Hold extra cover for the disrupted supplier's materials between two weeks, its holding cost charged only then (P-P.3). No parameters — it is on or it is off. Overtime production reaches the engine Activate overtime shifts when the revenue gain exceeds the overtime cost (P-P.5). Overtime cost % of product price · starts at 5 Additional cost per unit produced during overtime shifts (Cop) Material reallocation reaches the engine Revenue-maximising material allocation LP over a rolling planning horizon during a disruption (P-P.9). Planning horizon weeks · starts at 4 Rolling window for the material-allocation LP (W) Annual planning labor cost € · starts at 6240 Indirect labor cost for…

entries.title: Recovery playbooks — Saving one as a playbook
entries.text: The set of strategies and their parameters is a playbook , and a playbook is reusable across scenarios. The picker above the strategies offers system playbooks — supplied with the product, not editable — and your project's own. Once a scenario is linked to a playbook, the picker tracks whether the scenario still matches it and marks it modified when it does not. From there you can save the changes back into a playbook you own, save as a new one, or reset the scenario to the playbook. Somebody else's playbook, and every system one, is read-only: you save a copy rather than editing theirs. Project-level recovery settings sit underneath all of this. A scenario's settings are overlaid on the project's, so a scenario that has never been touched inherits the project's posture rather than starting empty — and the stage rail's lever count is the count of the merged result, not of the scenario's own overrides. The engine declares the playbook policy and does not implement it yet P-X.1 is planned in the engine's own catalog. Firms execute SEQUENCED responses — detect → expedite → backup → overtime — gated by triggers and budget. Composes enabled policies; replaces flat recovery lists. Hook: PH-20 (evaluation) + delegated. That is a separate question from the 4 strategies above, which do reach the engine through their own plugins. It is read from the catalog rather than stated here, so t…

entries.title: Experiments & comparison
entries.text: Experiments & comparison Ask one question per comparison and preserve the evidence needed to attribute the difference.

entries.title: Experiments & comparison — Choose the question first
entries.text: Baseline versus disruption estimates the disruption's impact. Disruption without a buffer versus the same disruption with a buffer estimates the buffer's effect. Comparing baseline directly against disruption plus a new policy changes two causes and does not isolate either. Keep the comparison attributable Illustration. A passing comparison gate still requires a review of inputs and assumptions. The control-unit tutorial follows this three-run design. Duplicate a scenario, change one factor, retain the original and give the new scenario a name describing its difference.

entries.title: Experiments & comparison — What the comparison checks
entries.text: Open Simulation Lab → Compare and choose a baseline from scenarios with completed, non-exploratory results. Every other scenario with results becomes a column in the comparison matrix, checked against that baseline separately. Use the chips to include scenarios, rank by a KPI, and select a column to inspect its full table. On a phone, use the ranked list. If every run is exploratory, first run a Validated Model through Policies → Run & Validate. A column is a paired experiment when four conditions hold: common random numbers are enabled with matching seed specifications; both runs record the same engine, or two versions whose change record says results unchanged for every version between them (a note names both); both runs record which data they read; and exactly one of four components differs — the data version, the policy version, the world fingerprint (horizon, time step, demand model) or the disruption schedule. Its cells are CRN-paired differences, and only such a column can be marked best. Any other pair — a different engine version, a different data version together with new policies, mismatched seeds — is still compared, but marked not like-for-like on its chip, its column and its full table, and listed beneath the matrix with every reason: which components differ (and, for the world, which fields), how the engines differ and what the change record says lies between th…

entries.title: Experiments & comparison — Check what the screen cannot decide for you
entries.text: Confirm dataset versions and the exact inputs behind each run. A changed price, BOM or capacity is a model change even when the label looks familiar. Use the same warm-up and measurement window for a policy-effect question. Confirm the event and enough recovery time are inside the window. Use completed replications with matched seeds. Read the actual paired count; the requested count can differ from the completed count. Review conversion notes on both runs. A new fallback or clamped setting may be another changed factor. Specify the practically important difference before choosing more replications. Do not keep sampling solely until a preferred result becomes significant.

entries.title: Experiments & comparison — Read the difference and its interval
entries.text: The comparison uses measures present on both sides. Paired differences compare matched replication results before summarizing their uncertainty. They can be more precise than subtracting two unrelated run means. Overlapping intervals on the two means do not by themselves decide the paired test. Each scenario–KPI cell is a separate test. Looking across many cells increases the chance of a chance finding; select the primary outcome in advance and confirm a promising response with an independent experiment. The matrix does not directly test challengers against each other. A winner is meaningful only for a measure with a defined direction and a paired interval supporting that direction. Inventory and utilization are trade-offs, not quantities always improved by increasing or decreasing them. An unpaired, independent or inconclusive result should be reported as such. For a toy example, B serving five additional units every week may improve service, but if the response adds large holding cost the commercial decision can still be unattractive. Report service, loss, cost and the assumptions used to value them.

entries.title: Experiments & comparison — Application workflow versus engine library
entries.text: This guide describes the reachable baseline-versus-many view, whose tests remain pairwise. The repository also contains an experiment-designer component and engine-library stress/synergy functions; their presence alone does not make them application features. Use the documented application controls or the separately documented Python interfaces. Next: seeds and precision , KPI definitions and exporting evidence .

entries.title: Seeds, replications & confidence
entries.text: Seeds, replications & confidence Separate random-run precision, startup effects and uncertainty about the real supply chain.

entries.title: Seeds, replications & confidence — Seeds and common random numbers
entries.text: A seed identifies a random stream within a particular implementation. Keep the engine build, inputs and protocol as well as the seed; the seed alone is not a promise of identical output across every version and environment. Common random numbers help compare alternatives under coordinated demand and supply draws. Keep the same seed specification in both scenarios. The comparison panel checks this before presenting a paired result. Why one run is not an answer The same model, different draws. The band is the answer; the line alone is not — and where two bands overlap, the better-looking mean is not yet a better model.

entries.title: Seeds, replications & confidence — How many replications?
entries.text: A replication is one simulated realization. Replications measure variation caused by the model's random inputs. More replications can improve precision, with additional compute cost, but there is no universally sufficient count. Use the convergence view and adopted validation settings. Decide what difference matters for your decision, then ask whether the interval is narrow enough to distinguish it. For a deterministic teaching model, three identical replications exercise the workflow but add no empirical evidence about real-world variability.

entries.title: Seeds, replications & confidence — Warm-up and the measurement window
entries.text: Opening inventory and an initially empty pipeline can influence early weeks. Excluding warm-up can help study ongoing operations. If the question is specifically about startup or recovery from an empty system, excluding it can remove the phenomenon you wanted to study. The application supports adopted validation settings and manual warm-up. Keep the same adopted window across controlled variants unless window length is the experimental factor. Inspect the actual engine window: it is distinct from the full horizon and can be limited or shortened.

entries.title: Seeds, replications & confidence — What the interval means
entries.text: A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated model quantity from finite replications. The min/max range instead describes observed extremes in those replications. Neither is a complete prediction interval for every possible future business outcome. Precision is not validity A narrow interval can coexist with a wrong demand mean, missing common supplier, incorrect BOM or unrealistic capacity. Review inputs and conversion notes, compare against observations where available, and test plausible alternative assumptions. A zero-width interval in the deterministic tutorial reflects its assumptions. If time to recover is censored because recovery was not seen before the window ended, report that limit; do not replace it with zero. If no demand exists in the measured window, fill rate is unavailable. Next: model validation and controlled comparison .

entries.title: Stress tests
entries.text: Stress tests Seven one-click scenarios — what each one fills in, and which of them your engine will actually act on. Read this first: 5 of the 7 presets cannot reach the engine yet, and the drawer says so The engine disrupts suppliers and the plant — not materials, customers or lanes. A preset whose schedule names one of those ( material:critical , customer:all , edge:inbound , node:nexus ) is disabled in the drawer with this reason rather than launchable: a run whose event was dropped would report the undisrupted baseline under a stress-test name. supplier:primary is different — it is a placeholder the launch resolves to the supplier carrying the largest share of your weekly inbound volume (the resolution is written into the scenario's description), and a project with no inbound lanes gets a refusal, not a hollow scenario. A hand-edited schedule can still name an unresolvable target. The engine drops it and says so in the run's mapping warnings — …targets cannot be disrupted yet (land later in M7) — event skipped for a target kind it does not support, or no supplier or plant named '…' in this project's data — event skipped for a supplier id the project does not have — and that line is the difference between a stress test and an expensive repeat of your baseline. Read the mapping warnings on every stress run before you read its KPIs. A preset whose event was dropped produces r…

entries.title: Stress tests — What clicking a preset does
entries.text: A preset does not run anything. It creates a scenario with the disruption already filled in, and leaves you on the editor for it. Open Simulation Lab and expand the stress-test drawer above the scenario list. Clicking one creates a new scenario named after the preset — they all begin [Stress] , so they sort together in your list — writes the preset's schedule into it, selects it, and opens its Disruption & recovery pane. You then run it like any other scenario. The new scenario inherits the warm-up length and replication count from your model validation, the same as a scenario you create by hand: a disruption is excluded from the run fingerprint, so a stress scenario shares the baseline's world rather than starting a new one. That is what makes the comparison meaningful — see Seeds, replications & confidence .

entries.title: Stress tests — The 7 presets
entries.text: Each row below is exactly what the preset writes into the scenario. There is no prose behind it — the schedule is the description, so it is printed rather than summarised. Day numbers count from the start of the simulated window , warm-up included. Single-supplier outage single_supplier_outage Top-volume supplier (resolved at launch) offline for 14 days from day 120, past the default warm-up. supplier:primary starts day 120 lasts 14 days 100% resolved at launch to your top-volume supplier Plant shutdown plant_shutdown Plant production halted for 14 days starting on day 120, past the default warm-up. node:plant starts day 120 lasts 14 days 100% reaches the engine Material shortage material_shortage Critical material inbound capacity reduced 50% for 21 days. material:critical starts day 120 lasts 21 days 50% preset disabled — the engine cannot hit this target yet Lead-time shock lead_time_shock Inbound lane lead time extended 200% for 28 days. edge:inbound starts day 120 lasts 28 days 200% preset disabled — the engine cannot hit this target yet Demand surge demand_surge Aggregate demand +40% for 21 days starting on day 120. customer:all starts day 120 lasts 21 days 40% preset disabled — the engine cannot hit this target yet Multi-hit (compound) multi_hit Supplier outage on day 120, demand surge on day 135. supplier:primary starts day 120 lasts 14 days 100% resolved at launch to …

entries.title: Stress tests — Making a preset actually bite
entries.text: Click the preset, then edit the target in the scenario's Disruption & recovery pane before you run it. Two kinds of target resolve today: A supplier id from your own data Exactly as it appears in Suppliers or in the supplier_id column of Inbound Logistics . A supplier: prefix is optional — everything before the last colon is discarded, so supplier:ACME-01 and ACME-01 are the same target. It must match the id character for character; there is no fuzzy matching and no lookup by supplier name. The plant Written plant , node:plant or plant: anything. A project models one focal plant, so the engine does not need to be told which. Materials, customers and lanes are not targetable yet. A schedule naming one is accepted by the editor, saved to the scenario and dropped at run time — which is why the warning line matters more here than anywhere else in the product.

entries.title: Stress tests — What the three numbers actually do
entries.text: The editor takes days and the engine runs in weeks, so each number is converted on the way in, and the conversion is worth knowing before you tune one. Start day → a whole week, rounded Day 30 becomes week 4, and so does day 28. Moving a start by a day or two usually changes nothing at all; moving it by four days can move it a whole week. The earliest a disruption can start is week 1. Duration → whole weeks, 1 to 52 14 days is two weeks; 21 days is three. Anything under about four days rounds to the minimum of one week rather than to nothing, and anything past a year is clamped to 52. Magnitude → a capacity cut below 100%, a full outage at 100% or above Under 100% the target keeps that share of its capacity — 40% means it loses 40% and keeps 60%. At 100% or above it becomes a full outage instead , so the Lead-time shock preset's 200% is not “twice the lead time”: it is a total loss of that target for the window. A partial cut also needs the target to have a finite capacity to cut — a supplier with a blank capacity_per_week is unlimited, so the engine turns the partial cut into a full outage and says so in the warnings. Five events per scenario, and the sixth is dropped A scenario's schedule is read up to five events. A sixth is discarded with a warning naming how many were dropped. Only Multi-hit (compound) ships more than one event, so you will meet this limit only if you bui…

entries.title: Stress tests — What these are not: a sweep
entries.text: Each preset is one disruption at one severity for one duration. It answers “what happens to this chain if that fails”. It does not answer “which failure matters most”, which needs the same run repeated across every supplier, or every severity, and the results ranked. There is no sweep in the product. Comparing a handful of stress scenarios side by side in Experiments & comparison is the nearest thing, and it is a manual one: you create the scenarios, you run them, you read the table.

entries.title: Stress tests — The engine's own battery — a library, not a feature
entries.text: The simulation engine ships a separate stress module declaring 7 sweeps, ST-1 to ST-7, of which 2 have implementations. Nothing in this product calls them. They are importable from the scsim Python package by a researcher running the engine themselves, and there is no screen, endpoint or job that reaches them — so you will not find ST-1 anywhere in the application. They are listed here because the engine is open to anyone who wants to run it directly, and because an earlier version of this page presented them as the product's stress feature. If you are reading this to plan work inside SuReSuite, the seven presets above are the whole of what exists. ST-1 implemented in the library Supplier outage sweep (manuscript): each supplier × LT-extension × Δt {5,8,10}. ST-2 implemented in the library Supplier capacity-cut sweep: each supplier × φ {0.75,0.5,0.25,0} × {4,8} wks. ST-3 declared, no implementation Material shortage sweep (M7: material-scoped capacity). ST-4 declared, no implementation Edge/lane shock (M7: edge split). ST-5 declared, no implementation Demand surge (M7: demand-side events). ST-6 declared, no implementation Compound: ST-1 ∩ ST-5 (M7). ST-7 declared, no implementation Nexus-node attack: top-k ML-critical (M7; ml-service integration).
