entries.title: Product-Level Network
entries.text: Product-Level Network Inspect which suppliers and materials each finished product depends on.

entries.title: Product-Level Network — Read the four roles
entries.text: The product view groups suppliers, purchased materials, finished products and customers. Edges follow the supplied lane and BOM relationships through these roles. Echelon colors identify roles; they are not risk ratings. Each edge is labelled with its weekly flow and drawn wider as that flow grows. The flow is the same number the process view shows for the same lane: a supplier's share of its material's demand, a material's demand propagated down the BOM to each finished product, and a product's outbound volume, each summed over every plant. It is computed from demand, not an independently measured shipment. The Labels button hides the labels. The control-unit chain Illustration. Synthetic sample; links read top to bottom. Both BOM depth and units matter. Layout and node size support legibility. Read the legend, selected-node details and numerical metric before interpreting visual prominence as economic importance.

entries.title: Product-Level Network — Find P-CONTROL in the tutorial
entries.text: Use the control-unit example . Search for P-CONTROL and follow M-BOARD and M-CASE back to S-BOARD and S-CASE, and forward to C-ASSEMBLY. The BOM requires one board and two housings per product. At demand of 100/week that implies 100 boards and 200 housings/week. These are BOM-implied requirements. Inbound volumes describe supplied rates and help determine sourcing shares; they are not proof of actual transactions or a second independent measure of demand. Avoid summing edges across different material units as if they were all the same commodity.

entries.title: Product-Level Network — What this view can answer
entries.text: Use it to identify products sharing a purchased material, materials with only one recorded supplier and the customer demand connected to a product. Focus a node to inspect its supply path; restore the full view before concluding that a missing connection does not exist. A second supplier only represents an available alternative if the underlying data and operating assumptions support it. Two supplier nodes also do not prove independent upstream sources.

entries.title: Product-Level Network — When an edge is missing
entries.text: Check selected project, active filters, identifier spelling, promotion status and whether derived data needs refreshing. A master row does not create a lane or BOM line. A disconnected material may be deliberately unused, incorrectly identified or awaiting relationship data. For multi-level data the product view collapses internal BOM structure into purchased-material to finished-product dependencies. Use the process view to inspect intermediate components.

entries.title: Product-Level Network — What reaches simulation
entries.text: The engine maps accepted BOM, supplier/material lanes and customer/product demand into its model. The graph's screen layout, node size and computed centrality are not simulation parameters. The current engine has one focal production stage; displaying a multi-level BOM does not create intermediate stock, capacity or processing time. Next: inspect BOM depth , then set operating policies . Read conversion notes after the run to confirm the input mapping.

entries.title: Process-Level Network
entries.text: Process-Level Network Inspect BOM dependencies and distinguish component depth from actual production operations.

entries.title: Process-Level Network — What a process node means here
entries.text: This view expands component relationships using the multi-level BOM when available. It displays suppliers, materials and subassemblies, finished products and customers. It is a BOM-oriented view, not a routing model of individual machines, processing steps or labor stations. The control-unit chain Illustration. Synthetic sample; links read top to bottom. Both BOM depth and units matter. Role and depth colors help distinguish levels; each edge is labelled with its weekly flow and drawn wider as that flow grows. A component that goes into several finished products carries the sum of all of them, in every plant. The Labels button hides the labels; select a node for its totals. Screen position and size are not evidence of process duration or capacity.

entries.title: Process-Level Network — The same control unit at two depths
entries.text: The tutorial uses a single-level BOM: one board and two housings feed P-CONTROL. Its process view therefore adds little depth beyond the product view. This is expected; a deeper-looking drawing would require additional BOM data. As a separate illustration, suppose a board assembly needs two chips and the product needs one board assembly. A multi-level BOM can show chip → board assembly → product. Two chips per assembly times one assembly per product implies two chips per product. This illustration is not included in the executable single-level sample.

entries.title: Process-Level Network — BOM level is not company tier
entries.text: BOM depth counts component relationships. Company tier counts organizational relationships relative to a focal firm. A board supplier may be a tier-one company even when its board is several BOM levels below a finished product. Do not transfer one kind of depth onto the other.

entries.title: Process-Level Network — Follow a dependency without losing context
entries.text: Search for a component, focus its upstream and downstream path, and restore Show all before assessing overall connectivity. The top-flow filter is useful for readability, but a low-volume component can still stop every product that needs it. If a component is isolated, inspect higher-level component identifiers, product roots, consumption rates and the selected BOM configuration. Check filters and derived-data freshness before editing source data. Do not add a speculative edge just to make the picture connected.

entries.title: Process-Level Network — From graph inspection to a scenario
entries.text: Add disruption event can create or update a scenario from a supported target. Supplier and plant targets are supported by the engine path; a material or subassembly needs an appropriate supplier target where offered. Confirm the resolved target in the scenario and conversion notes. Displayed depth is not simulated production depth The worker currently flattens multi-level BOMs to root-to-leaf requirements for the single-stage engine. Intermediate inventory, work-in-progress, lead time and capacity are not independently simulated. Use this view for structural inspection; do not report a subassembly bottleneck experiment as verified without a model that represents it. Next: company relationships and disruption configuration .

entries.title: Firm-Level Network
entries.text: Firm-Level Network Explore supplied company relationships and the evidence gaps around them.

entries.title: Firm-Level Network — A separate company graph
entries.text: The firm view reads deep-tier nodes and edges. A node identifies a company; an edge records the supplied src_uid → dst_uid relationship. The layout draws connections without arrowheads, so use edge details and the source/destination identifiers when direction matters. Company depth and seed status drive tier classification. Operational data is not a deep-tier graph Illustration. The operational relationships here summarize the sample; they are not uploaded firm-graph edges. Revenue and relative-revenue attributes are separate from physical material quantities. A displayed weight can include a fallback when revenue data is missing; inspect data coverage before interpreting it as money or purchasing share.

entries.title: Firm-Level Network — Why the tutorial may have no firm graph
entries.text: The control-unit files describe S-BOARD and S-CASE supplying materials to Assembly, and Assembly serving C-ASSEMBLY. They do not include deep-tier company-node and company-edge files. An empty firm graph after completing that tutorial does not mean its product network failed. To extend it, collect and document company relationships with stable company identifiers and evidence, then upload the corresponding deep-tier files. A company name, directory listing or manufacturing capability alone is not proof that it supplies a named buyer. Keep possible suppliers separate from established relationships in your research data.

entries.title: Firm-Level Network — Questions this graph can support
entries.text: Look for recorded shared upstream dependencies, concentration in industries or locations, and companies with many supplied connections. A common upstream firm can suggest correlated exposure, but only within the observed network and evidence quality. Low connectivity can reflect a genuinely sparse chain, incomplete data collection, unresolved company identities, missing endpoints or filtering. 'No shared supplier found' is not equivalent to 'the suppliers are independent'. Report coverage and missingness with any conclusion.

entries.title: Firm-Level Network — Review deep-tier files before importing
entries.text: Deep-tier uploads use bulk paths distinct from the staged CSV workflow for BOM and logistics. Do not assume a raw-file archive or a promotion diff. Keep the previous export, verify every edge endpoint has a node, and review Deep-Tier Nodes and Deep-Tier Edges before uploading. Check tier and direction conventions against the data source. Do not use BOM level as a company tier or fill unknown weights with invented transaction values.

entries.title: Firm-Level Network — What this graph does not simulate
entries.text: The ordinary worker's frozen-input model reads operational supplier, material, product, BOM and demand tables. Deep-tier company edges do not automatically become capacity-constrained upstream production stages. A central firm in this graph is a research lead, not a measured simulation impact. Next: network measures for structural interpretation, or the operational product graph .

entries.title: Interactive Network Space
entries.text: Interactive Network Space Exploring the chain without a fixed layout.

entries.title: Interactive Network Space — What it is for
entries.text: The other three network views each answer a question by fixing a layout: materials flow left to right, manufacture stacks by level, firms arrange by tier. A fixed layout is what makes those views readable, and it is also what stops you seeing anything the layout was not designed to show. This one fixes nothing. You move nodes, pull a cluster apart, and look at the shape you get. It is for the question you have not formed yet — if you know what you are looking for, one of the structured views will answer it faster. Explore without confusing views Illustration. A workflow illustration, not an application screenshot.

entries.title: Interactive Network Space — What you can do here
entries.text: Drag anything Pull a node out of a cluster to see what it is actually attached to. Dense regions in an automatic layout hide their own structure, and separating them by hand is often the fastest way to read one. Search and focus Find a node by name and highlight what it reaches. On a large graph this is the difference between a picture and a diagram. Turn labels off Labels make a small graph readable and a large one unreadable. Without them the shape comes through — clusters, bridges, isolated pieces. Work by level The level counts tell you how the graph is distributed in depth before you start moving things, so you know whether you are looking at a broad shallow chain or a narrow deep one. A layout you arrange is not saved, and is not evidence Moving nodes changes what you are looking at and nothing else. The arrangement is not stored, is not part of any run's provenance, and cannot be exported as a result — so a picture from this screen is an illustration, not a finding. It also means an arrangement you spent time on is gone when you leave. That is worth knowing before you spend the time: if a layout is telling you something, capture the conclusion rather than the picture. Anything you intend to quote should come from a measure with a run behind it — Network science metrics — or from a simulation result, which carries the data version that produced it. entries.title: Network science metrics
entries.text: Network science metrics Centrality, prominence and critical-node prediction — what each one means and where it comes from.

entries.title: Network science metrics — What these numbers are
entries.text: They are statements about the structure of your chain, not about its performance. None of them is a simulation result. A centrality asks a question about the graph — how connected is this firm, how much traffic passes through it — and answers it from the shape alone. That is their strength and their limit: a firm can be structurally critical and commercially trivial, and the graph does not know the difference.

entries.title: Network science metrics — They do not agree, and that is not a fault
entries.text: Each measure asks a different question of the same graph, so each can name a different firm as the most critical one. None of them is the right answer on its own — the right question is which failure you are worried about. Four answers, one graph The most critical firm is a property of the question, not of the chain. Ask a different measure and a different firm comes back.

entries.title: Network science metrics — The measures
entries.text: prominence written by calculate-node-prominence (and calculate-network-science-metrics) A composite score combining the measures above with the firm's own size. What it is good for: One number to rank by when you want a shortlist rather than five separate views. What the contract says about this column ANALYSIS OUTPUT — calculate-node-prominence 's composite score. Dual-written into analysis_results since WP 4.3, so it can be read with the run, the input hash and the code version that produced it. WP 5.3 drops the column once every reader has moved. degree_centrality written by calculate-network-science-metrics How many other firms this one is directly connected to. What it is good for: A high-degree firm is a hub. Losing it disconnects many relationships at once. What the contract says about this column ANALYSIS OUTPUT — calculate-network-science-metrics . Dual- written into analysis_results since WP 4.3. weighted_degree_centrality written by calculate-network-science-metrics The same count, weighted by how much of the relationship's revenue each edge carries. What it is good for: Separates a firm with many small relationships from one with a few large ones. What the contract says about this column ANALYSIS OUTPUT — degree weighted by relative_revenue . Dual- written since WP 4.3. eigenvector_centrality written by calculate-network-science-metrics How well connected this firm…

entries.title: Network science metrics — The analyses that produce them
entries.text: 8 kinds of analysis are declared, each with the code that computes it, the version of that code, and every parameter it takes. A parameter absent from this list does not exist — a declared parameter no code reads is exactly the defect this catalog was corrected for. combine_etl computed by combine-project (migrated in WP 4.3, as §11 names it) combine_etl@wp43.1 Produces one result per project . Takes no parameters. Why this one is the way it is REGISTERED BUT NEVER SKIPPED. combine_etl 's output is rows in supply_chain_data , not entries in analysis_results , so "already computed" means "those rows are still there" — which the store cannot see, and a row deleted by hand would make a hit skip an ETL the project needs. WP 4.3 records the run for its identity; WP 4.4 owns staleness and is the package that may turn a hit into a skip. critical_nodes computed by predict-critical-nodes (migrated in WP 4.3) critical_nodes@wp43.1 Produces one result per supply_chain_row . plant_name (string) — default none The plant filter the request carried, or null for every row of the project. It is part of the key because two plants of one project are two different analyses over two different row sets. NOTE that plant_name is NOT project-scoped, which is why the function derives the project from the rows it loaded and refuses a set spanning two. Why this one is the way it is NO topology_digest , a…

entries.title: Network science metrics — On the Product-Level Network
entries.text: The Product-Level Network's analytics table uses the same measures on a different graph: the one that page draws — suppliers, purchased materials, finished products and customers, with the bill of materials collapsed. It lists the purchased materials. Edges are weighted by their weekly flow rather than by revenue, and the table's Weekly flow column is the finished-goods demand propagated down the BOM to each material. Betweenness there counts every shortest path, not a sample. The result is stored with the version of the lanes it was computed on, so a change to a price leaves it current and a change to a bill of materials or a volume marks it out of date. What these measures cannot see They are computed over the deep-tier graph you supplied, so a firm you have not discovered has no centrality and does not lower anyone else's. An incomplete graph produces confident numbers about the part of the world it contains, and says nothing at all about the rest. The measures are also purely structural: none of them reads a price, a lead time or a capacity. A supplier with an alarming betweenness may be trivially replaceable, and nothing here would tell you.

entries.title: The AI assistant
entries.text: The AI assistant What it can see, what it can do, what the picker actually changes, and what it cannot do without you.

entries.title: The AI assistant — What it is for
entries.text: A conversation about your project, with the project in front of it. You can ask what your data says, what a policy would change, or what a result means, without leaving the tool and without knowing which screen holds the answer. It can read and it can propose. It cannot change your project on its own — every change it suggests arrives as something you approve or discard.

entries.title: The AI assistant — The two modes, and the third one that is switched off
entries.text: Beside the model picker is a mode switch. It is per thread, and it decides whether the assistant may draft a change at all. Ask Decision Support — answers and analyses only; nothing about the project changes Review default Accept edits — agents draft; every change is a proposal card you approve Auto disabled Visible and not selectable. Its tooltip states the conditions under which it could ever unlock, and they are reproduced word for word below rather than summarised. What would have to be true before anything runs unattended Auto isn't available. It unlocks only after: ≥ 3 consecutive months of per-agent accepted-proposal rate ≥ 0.9 AND an org explicitly requesting it AND resolved principals (server-verified identity) — and then as a per-org opt-in designed as a new decision, scoped first to deterministic diffs. Until then every change is a reviewable proposal. Quoted exactly. A commitment about when software may act without a person is the last thing a manual should paraphrase, and the point of printing it is that you can hold the product to it. A new thread starts in Review . The mode switch is behind a deployment setting, so where it is not turned on you will not see it and every thread behaves as Review — the server enforces the mode regardless of what the control shows.

entries.title: The AI assistant — The 5 personas — and what picking one actually changes
entries.text: A persona is a sentence added to the prompt. It is not a different assistant. All 5 share one tool surface, one model and one prompt body. The only difference is a preference — prefer the risk tools first — so a question the Risk Analyst can answer is a question the Logistics Planner can answer, slightly less eagerly. Pick one to steer, not to unlock. Risk Analyst Supplier & network risk, single-source exposure, criticality. Simulation Modeler Design scenarios, stress tests, and recovery playbooks. Inventory Strategist Safety stock, MOQ, service level, and working capital trade-offs. Logistics Planner Lead times, routing, in-transit inventory, expediting. General Assistant no project needed Open-ended supply-chain conversation. No project required.

entries.title: The AI assistant — The 9 specialists, which you do not choose
entries.text: Behind the conversation is a router. It reads what you asked and hands the work to one of 9 specialists, each with its own prompt, its own narrowed set of tools and its own kind of proposal. None of them is in the picker , and the picker's names map onto none of these — so the way to reach the policy configurator is to ask about a policy, not to select a persona. data-steward Completes and corrects item-master data (materials, products, suppliers) as reviewable diffs. cost-estimator Estimates missing item-master economics with method-cited values and uncertainty intervals where the data alone cannot supply them. network-cartographer Maps the supply network beyond tier 1 from user-provided documents and registered external sources, as evidence-cited reviewable graph extensions. disruption-sentinel Assesses disruption events on demand against registered sensing feeds and files corroborated, simulation-sized risk alerts for the project's network. policy-configurator Turns natural-language intent into a reviewable policy-configuration change (defaults + overrides). vv-analyst Interprets verification & validation evidence and drafts model-validation cards. experiment-designer Compiles decision questions into reviewable, gate-checked experiment specifications. explainer Answers "why did the model do that?" from recorded decision traces with mandatory citations. report-builder Turns …

entries.title: The AI assistant — Conversations and folders
entries.text: Threads are kept, so a line of enquiry can be picked up later, and can be organised into folders when there are enough of them to need it. A thread belongs to a project — asking the assistant about one project from inside another is not something the tool lets you do by accident. The mode is a property of the thread , not of your account. A thread you started in Ask stays in Ask, which is the right way to keep a read-only line of enquiry read-only.

entries.title: Plans and proposals
entries.text: Plans and proposals Review before apply — nothing changes because a model suggested it.

entries.title: Plans and proposals — The shape of it
entries.text: The assistant proposes; you apply. Those are two separate events, and the second one is always yours. A plan is what the assistant intends to do, written out before it does any of it. A proposal is a specific change waiting for your decision. Neither touches your project until you say so, and a proposal you never look at simply stays a proposal.

entries.title: Plans and proposals — How it goes
entries.text: 1 You ask for something “Set safety stock to four weeks on everything from this supplier.” 2 It writes a plan What it would change, on which rows, and why. You can read the plan and stop there. 3 It proposes the change The concrete edit, as values. It is stored as a proposal, against the state of the project it was computed from. 4 You apply it — or you do not Applying writes the same overrides you would have typed, through the same path. Nothing downstream can tell the difference, which is deliberate: an applied proposal is your decision, not a third kind of provenance.

entries.title: Plans and proposals — The 9 kinds of change, and who may file each
entries.text: One specialist, one kind of artifact. The pairing is enforced by the database, not by convention. A proposal names both the agent that drafted it and the class of change it is, and the two are checked against each other when it is stored — so a tool with a bug cannot file a policy change under the data steward's name. There is no agent that can propose anything it likes. item_master_diff data-steward Changes to the economics on your materials, products or suppliers — a cost, a lead-time shape, a capacity. The agent behind it completes and corrects item-master data (materials, products, suppliers) as reviewable diffs. policy_bundle_diff policy-configurator Changes to your policy defaults and overrides, the same values you would type into the grid. The agent behind it turns natural-language intent into a reviewable policy-configuration change (defaults + overrides). model_card_draft vv-analyst A validation card — a warm-up length and replication count, with the evidence for them. The agent behind it interprets verification & validation evidence and drafts model-validation cards. experiment_spec experiment-designer A design for a set of runs: what varies, over what range, measured against what. The agent behind it compiles decision questions into reviewable, gate-checked experiment specifications. trace_explanation explainer An answer to “why did the model do that?”, cited to the…

entries.title: Plans and proposals — Every proposal declares one of 3 provenances
entries.text: The card says on its face where its values came from, and this is the first thing to read on one. It is not a confidence score — it is a statement about who chose the numbers. deterministic computed by named code. The model packaged the result and did not choose the numbers, so the values are as checkable as anything else the product computes. llm_drafted the model selected or derived this content. It is the class that needs your eyes: the card says so on its face rather than leaving you to assume. user_supplied the values came from your own message, verbatim. The proposal is a way of applying what you already said, not a suggestion.

entries.title: Plans and proposals — The states a proposal moves through
entries.text: Six states, one clock Four of the six you choose and one the agent chooses. The sixth is what happens when nothing is decided, and that is deliberate. draft proposed approved applied rejected expired A rejected card stays in the thread , faded rather than removed, because the record that you said no is the point — and it is the one state above that you can reach and then do nothing further with. A proposal expires after 14 days if nothing happens to it. That is not a nag: a change computed against a project you have since edited is a change that should be redrafted rather than applied late. Asking twice for the same thing does not stack two cards. A re-drafted identical request converges on the card that already exists, so a conversation that went round the houses leaves one decision to make rather than four. An apply that fails shows you the server's reason and offers a retry, rather than disappearing. Where an apply half-succeeded and then hit a blocker, the previous policy version is restored — so the failure leaves your project where it was, and the attempt stays in the history.

entries.title: Plans and proposals — Plans are the other half, and they have states too
entries.text: A plan is the sequence the assistant intends to work through, kept so a long piece of work can be picked up rather than restarted. It is active , done , failed , abandoned or expired , and like a proposal it expires after 14 days. abandoned and failed are different states on purpose: one is you changing direction and one is the work not working. Both stay visible, which is what makes a plan an account of what happened rather than a to-do list that quietly empties. A proposal knows which data it was computed from A proposal is grounded on a version of your project. If the data moves underneath it — you re-upload, or an analysis recomputes — the proposal is marked as describing a state that no longer holds, rather than silently applying to a world it never saw. That is the same anchor Dataset Versions describes, used to stop an old suggestion looking current. Applying is as reversible as any other edit, and no more An applied proposal becomes ordinary policy overrides. You can change them back the way you change any override, and there is no “undo this proposal” button that reaches into your project and lifts it out. The before state is stored on the proposal, and the automatic restore above is the one place it is used — a failure compensating for itself. It is not offered to you as an action. If a proposal is large, saving a policy version first is what gives you a point to ret…

entries.title: Project memory
entries.text: Project memory What the assistant remembers between conversations, how a memory gets written, and who can read one.

entries.title: Project memory — What memory is here
entries.text: Context about the project that survives a conversation ending — not a copy of your data, and not a record of your results. Without it, every conversation starts from nothing and you spend the first three messages re-explaining which plant you care about and why the numbers for one product are odd. With it, that context persists and the assistant opens further along.

entries.title: Project memory — Nothing is remembered unless you say so
entries.text: The model is never in the loop that decides to save. Two paths, both yours. 1 Say “remember …” A message beginning remember — with or without “please”, “that” or a colon — saves what follows it, verbatim. That phrasing is the consent, and it is matched by a fixed pattern rather than judged by the model. 2 Or click the chip it offers A message that sounds like a decision — “we decided”, “we're going with”, “from now on” — produces an offer , not a write. Nothing is saved until you click it. 3 Or add one yourself /project-intelligence → Project memory Typing it into the sidebar panel is the consent, in the same way. A memory is capped at 500 characters and is stored as typed. Longer than that is truncated rather than refused, so a very long “remember …” keeps its beginning and loses its end — say the important part first. The whole feature is behind a deployment setting. Where it is off, nothing is written and nothing is recalled.

entries.title: Project memory — The 3 kinds, and how one is chosen
entries.text: The kind is classified from the words you used, not asked for. It is a label for reading the list back, and it changes nothing about how the memory is used. fact the default Something true about the project that is not in the data — why one plant is treated differently, what a code in your ids means. preference How you want things done. Phrasing like “always”, “never”, “by default” or “going forward” lands here. decision Something you settled. “We decided”, “we're going with”, “from now on” lands here.

entries.title: Project memory — A memory can go stale, and it is still used
entries.text: A memory saved while your project had a known policy and data fingerprint carries both. If either moves — you re-upload, you change a policy — the memory is shown marked [stale — saved against older project data] . The marker is a label, not a filter A stale memory is still handed to the assistant , with the marker text attached. It is told the note may be out of date; it is not prevented from using it. So a stale memory can still shape an answer. If something you asked it to remember is no longer true, archive it rather than relying on the marker — that is what the archive control on each row is for, and archiving is the only thing that takes a memory out of the conversation. A memory saved when no fingerprint was available carries none, and can never be marked stale — because nothing anchors it. Those are the ones to re-read yourself. Memories are handed over newest first up to a fixed budget, so a long list is truncated rather than summarised: the oldest entries simply stop being included. Archiving what no longer matters is what keeps the ones that do inside the budget.

entries.title: Project memory — Scope, and who can read one
entries.text: Memory belongs to a project. The assistant reads only the memories of the project you are in, so nothing remembered about one project appears in a conversation about another. The rows themselves are not project-scoped at read time That project scoping is done by the query . The table's own read rule permits any signed-in client to select any row, so a memory is not private to your project the way your uploaded data is — it is private to the extent that the surfaces reading it filter. Write it as though a colleague elsewhere in your organization could read it, because architecturally they can. Who can see your data is the rest of that picture, and it is the page that explains why we state this rather than smoothing it. Writes go the other way: there is no direct write path at all. Every memory is created and archived through a single server function, so the consent check cannot be bypassed by talking to the table. It is context, not record Nothing in memory is evidence. It carries no run, no engine version and no result. Anything that has to be right is in your data, your policies or a run — all three of which carry the version they came from. This table is deliberately outside the data contract project_memory is in the register of tables the contract does not describe, under WP 5.2, and the reason is a positive one rather than a backlog: it carries no simulation input and no e…

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits
entries.text: Models, budgets and limits Which models run, what they cost, and who is allowed to use them.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — Three separate questions
entries.text: Which models exist · what they may spend · who may use them. They are configured separately and they fail separately. A model can be available and unusable because a budget is spent. A user can be entitled to a model that is not configured. Reading “it does not work” usually starts with deciding which of the three is in the way.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — Budgets
entries.text: A budget is a ceiling, and usage is recorded against it as work happens. When it is reached, requests stop rather than continuing silently at cost — which means a stopped assistant is sometimes the budget working rather than a fault. A budget is set at one of 3 scopes — user , org or project — over a daily or monthly window. So “the budget” is rarely one number: a person can be inside their own and stopped by their organization's. Each one can cap 4 different things at once: money, tokens, and requests per minute and per day. Being stopped on requests per minute is not the same as being out of budget , and the two feel identical from the conversation — if the assistant recovers after a minute, it was rate rather than spend.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — What gets recorded about each call
entries.text: Every request the assistant makes records the model, the provider, the tokens in and out, the cost, how long it took, and whether it succeeded. Failed calls are recorded too, with their error, which is what makes “it stopped working at four o'clock” answerable. The status vocabulary is worth knowing because the third value is not an error: success , error , blocked . blocked means a limit refused the call before it was made — it cost nothing and it is not a fault. A run of them is a budget or an entitlement, not an outage. Cost is computed from the model's own per-thousand-token input and output prices, which are configured per model rather than looked up from a provider. A price set wrong makes every figure on the usage screen wrong in the same direction, and nothing external contradicts it.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — Who may use what
entries.text: Per-user entitlements decide which models a person can pick, which one a new conversation starts on, and which one is used when the first is unavailable. allowed_model_ids The models this user may use, as ai_models.id . An allow-list, but read as one only when it is non-empty. Clearing the allow-list grants every model. It does not revoke them. This is the one thing on this page that will surprise an administrator, and it surprises them in the dangerous direction. The list of permitted models is treated as an allow-list only while it has entries in it . An empty list — and a user with no entitlements row at all — means no restriction: every configured model is permitted. So the intuitive way to take someone's access away is the exact way to give them all of it. To restrict a user, list the models they may use. To stop them using a particular model, remove that model from a list that still contains the others. The behaviour is deliberate — it is what every user had before entitlements existed, and changing it would silently lock out everyone who has no row. What was missing is a warning at the moment of the action, and until the admin screen carries one, this page is it.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — Checking your own access
entries.text: Your account page has an “AI models you can use” block, and it is the only place you can see your own entitlements without an administrator. It says one of three things, and the first one is the one to read carefully. “All enabled models are available to you.” This is what you see both when somebody deliberately granted you everything and when nobody has ever set an entitlement for you — including when an administrator cleared your list intending to take access away. The page cannot tell the three apart, because the stored state is the same. A list of named models Somebody restricted you on purpose, to exactly these. The block also names the model a new conversation starts on and the one used when that is unavailable. “No AI models are enabled for your account.” Not an empty entitlement — the models themselves are not enabled in this deployment. This is an administrator's question, not yours.

entries.title: Models, budgets and limits — Where this is set
entries.text: Models and budgets at /admin/models and /admin/usage ; per-user entitlements on the user's own page under /admin/users . All three need an administrator — Admin screens covers what each one controls.

entries.title: Connecting an ERP / MRP system
entries.text: Connecting an ERP / MRP system Linking a project to a system of record, so the data comes to you.

entries.title: Connecting an ERP / MRP system — What a link is
entries.text: A standing permission to read from your system, attached to one project. Once linked, a sync can be requested: the rows arrive into staging, diffed against what you already have, and wait for somebody to approve — unless the link's own auto-apply threshold lets them through. Reviewing and applying a sync is that half, and it is where the threshold's consequences are. One system is supported today and it brings across products. Your other tables — lanes, bills of materials, materials, suppliers, the deep-tier network — are files whether or not a link exists. CSV or connector sets out what that means for how you build a model. A link belongs to one project. Connecting a system does not connect it to your organization, and a second project needs its own link — which is deliberate: a connector that silently spanned projects would put one project's data in another.

entries.title: Connecting an ERP / MRP system — Every column
entries.text: id uuid Surrogate key. The link's identity for every run that used it. Free text, not CHECK-constrained, and that is the one place this table still assumes a single vendor: ingest_runs.source_kind is the closed vocabulary WP 3.1 added, and it is the one a reader should trust. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. external_company_id text The company/tenant identifier IN THE EXTERNAL SYSTEM. Part of the natural key with the project and the system: one project may link one company of one system exactly once. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. external_company_name text The company's display name, cached for the picker and refreshed on each sync. entries.title: Reviewing and applying a sync
entries.text: Reviewing and applying a sync Seeing exactly what would change, before any of it does. Read this first: an ERP sync is not the CSV path with a different front door The review screen, the run record and the role check below are shared. What is not shared is the promotion: an ERP sync stages into its own table and is applied by its own function, which does not re-diff and does not take the contract's column rules with it. Three consequences, and each has its own box further down: a link can apply itself with nobody looking; the run's diff counts do not mean what the same words mean on an upload; and only two fields of a product actually cross.

entries.title: Reviewing and applying a sync — The shape of a sync
entries.text: A sync fetches, stages and diffs before anything changes. Whether a person approves it is a setting. Rows are fetched from the connected system, mapped into staged rows, and held with a diff against what you already have. Applying is a separate act — and it is the person with the review screen open, unless the link carries an auto-apply threshold. The review screen, the run record and the warnings are the same ones an upload produces, which is why the two feel alike. The rules underneath are not the same, and the sections below say where they part. A link with an auto-apply threshold does not wait for you When a link has a threshold above zero and a sync's change is small relative to the live table — and nothing failed to map — the run applies itself . No review screen is opened and no approval is given at the time. It is attributed rather than anonymous: the write records the person who created the link and set the threshold, because that is when the authorisation happened. The run records that it was triggered automatically rather than by somebody present. Set the threshold to zero if you want every sync reviewed. A link whose creator has no recorded identity cannot auto-apply at all — the promotion refuses an unattributed write, and the run is left staged for a person instead, with the reason on the run.

entries.title: Reviewing and applying a sync — A run is the unit you approve
entries.text: Rows belong to a run , and approval is a decision about the run rather than about a row. So a sync is all-or-nothing: you cannot accept half of it and leave the rest staged, because half a consistent set of rows is not a consistent set of rows. id uuid Surrogate key. Not the grain: a run is identified by what it did, and nothing joins to this except the staging rows and the landed files. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. link_id uuid The ERP link this run used, or NULL for a source that has none. NULL means 'this source needs no link', never 'the link was lost' — a CSV upload and an API push have no credential to point at. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. triggered_by text manual or scheduled. A manual run was asked for by a person; a scheduled one was started by the cron sweep against the link's sync_schedule_cron . Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. triggered_by_user_id uuid The person who asked for a manual run, in auth.users . NULL for a scheduled run, where there is no person — stated rather than back-filled to a service account, because 'nobody asked, the schedule did' is the true answer (G4). Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this colu…

entries.title: Reviewing and applying a sync — The diff, and why it is computed twice
entries.text: 1 At landing Every staged row is compared against what is in your data now, and marked as new, changed or unchanged. 2 On demand Recomputed whenever you open the review, because your data may have moved since the rows landed. 3 Inside the promotion Computed again , in the same transaction that writes. This is the one that counts: the review screen shows a decision, and the promotion verifies the decision still describes what it is about to do. The two answers are cross-checked against each other, and a disagreement raises rather than reporting a promotion that did something else. That is the upload path. An ERP sync's diff is computed once, at landing, and the promotion does not recompute it — so the counts you approve are the counts as they were when the rows arrived. On an ERP sync, “changed” does not mean anything changed The sync's diff asks one question per row: have we seen this external id before? If not it is new ; if so it is changed . No values are compared. So a sync that pulls a completely unmodified catalogue reports every row as changed, and the unchanged count is always zero. Read the number as “rows we already had” rather than as “rows that differ”, and do not use it to decide whether a sync is worth reviewing. This is also what an auto-apply threshold is measured against, so a first sync of a large catalogue will always be far over any sensible threshold and a…

entries.title: CSV or connector — which to use
entries.text: CSV or connector — which to use The trade-off, stated plainly — including the three things that are not the same. They are not two doors into one room It is tempting to read a connector as “the same upload, automated”. It is not, and the differences all point the same way: the file route is the one with the full set of guarantees behind it.

entries.title: CSV or connector — which to use — What each one can actually load
entries.text: The file route loads 11 datasets. The connector loads one. Uploading covers your whole chain — lanes, bills of materials, item masters, the deep-tier network. The ERP connector brings across products , and nothing else. Every other table is a file, whether or not you have a connector configured. So this is not really a choice between two ways of loading your data. It is a choice about one table, made against a background where everything else arrives as a file.

entries.title: CSV or connector — which to use — The trade
entries.text: A file You control exactly what goes in, and you can edit it before it does. Good for a first model, for a one-off study, and for any situation where the data needs judgement applied before it is loaded. It goes stale the moment you export it. A connector The product data comes to you and can be refreshed without anybody exporting anything. Good for a model that is kept current. It carries whatever your system of record carries, including the parts you would have cleaned up by hand.

entries.title: CSV or connector — which to use — What is genuinely the same
entries.text: Both routes stage before they change anything, both produce a run you can look at with a count of new, changed and unchanged rows, and both record what was substituted on the way in as mapping warnings. Neither writes over your tier-2 data without a staged copy existing first. Both also name the person who applied the change, and the tier-2 write records them. For a sync that applied itself, that person is whoever created the link and set the threshold — attribution to who authorised the automation, not to somebody present at the time. The run records which of the two it was.

entries.title: CSV or connector — which to use — What is not
entries.text: Where the routes diverge Both end in your data, and almost nothing between is shared. The branch with nobody on it is the one to know about. A sync can apply itself, and an upload cannot A link with an auto-apply threshold applies its own run when the change is small relative to the live table and nothing failed to map. That is the setting doing what it says — but it means a connector can change your data with nobody looking at the diff , and an upload never can. Set the threshold to zero if you want every sync reviewed. No file is kept for a sync An upload keeps the bytes you uploaded, so “what exactly did we load in March” is answerable from the file itself. A sync has no file — what it fetched is reconstructed from the staged rows, and only for as long as they are kept. The two paths are different code An upload is parsed and validated from the data contract itself, so a column rule changes in one place and both the uploader and the documentation follow. The sync maps its own fields. They agree today; nothing makes them agree tomorrow. The honest answer for most people is both Connect products if your item master genuinely moves and you have the connector. Upload the rest, and upload the things you decided — which materials are in scope, how the bill of materials is modelled. A model is not a copy of your ERP, and the parts of it that are judgement do not belong in a sync. …

entries.title: Reading your results
entries.text: Reading your results Check the run first, then the assumptions, then read service, cost and how sure you can be. In short Before quoting any number, confirm the run finished and which data, policy and scenario versions it used. Read the conversion notes — they say where the engine used a default, clamped a value or ignored one. A narrow interval means precise for this model. It doesn't mean the model is right.

entries.title: Reading your results — Start with the run record
entries.text: 1 Run record status · versions · count ↓ → 2 Conversion notes defaults · clamping ↓ → 3 KPIs mean · interval · range ↓ → 4 Interpretation assumptions stated Read a result in this order. Each step can stop you before the next. 1 Open the finished run /simulation-lab › Results In Simulation Lab › Results , or the shared results panel in Policies › Run & Validate . 2 Confirm what it is Run record Status, completed replication count, the credibility badge, and the exact dataset, policy and scenario versions. A preliminary estimate can move as replications finish; a failed or cancelled run with some rows is not the experiment you asked for. 3 Read the notes before the numbers Engine conversion notes Notes can describe defaults, clamping, unsupported values or a target that couldn't be used. Write down anything that matters to your question. You should see a completed run, its versions, and no surprises in the notes. Read the evidence in this order Illustration. Ordinary application runs do not produce the library Resilience Index.

entries.title: Reading your results — What each panel answers
entries.text: KPI summary Mean, confidence interval, standard deviation, range and count across replications. Rows follow the measures the engine actually returned; labels and directions come from the KPI catalog. A measure the engine didn't return is unavailable — never zero. Convergence plot Whether the running estimate has settled — the simulation's precision, not whether your demand, capacity or BOM are right. One replication cannot give an interval between replications. Replication & seed explorer The weekly trace. Find when the shock starts, whether stock delays its effect, and whether service recovers within the measured window. Inventory and capacity Materials and finished goods, read separately. Average inventory is a level averaged over the window, not a weekly sum. Utilization alone doesn't show whether capacity refused production; check the binding measures too. Per-item inspection Product or material detail, from an inspection run. A missing series isn't evidence of zero stock or zero demand. Utilization heatmap — removed The former panel depended on a per-node capacity_utilization series that the engine did not produce. Its removal does not mean capacity is unlimited. Use the returned aggregate capacity measures and binding indicators described above.

entries.title: Reading your results — Reading the tutorial result
entries.text: The tutorial needs 100 boards and 200 housings a week. An 80% capacity cut takes S-BOARD from 150 to 30 a week. Opening stock and replenishment can delay the customer impact, so service won't drop the same week the event starts. Compare baseline against disruption to measure the shock. Compare the same disruption under two policy versions to measure the buffer. Read lost sales, service and cost together. The example's demand and lead times are fixed, so identical replications and a zero-width interval are expected here. Don't count a loss twice Cost of resilience already includes lost-sales cost, among its engine-defined parts. It isn't just the cash spent on extra stock.

entries.title: Reading your results — Know what's being measured
entries.text: Fill rate is fulfilled demand value divided by demand value in the measured window — value-weighted, so expensive products count for more. No demand means no fill rate. A missing recovery figure can mean recovery didn't happen inside the window. The engine separates the total horizon, the excluded warm-up and the measured window. A longer horizon doesn't always lengthen the measured part by the same amount — read the run-window summary, and check that the disruption and recovery both fall inside it. Warm-up excluded ↓ → Measured window KPIs computed here ↓ → Rest of horizon if any Only the measured window counts toward a KPI. Check that the disruption and recovery fall inside it.

entries.title: Reading your results — What a result can support
entries.text: A narrow interval is precision given the model. It says nothing about missing suppliers, wrong BOM quantities, uncertain forecasts or policy mapping errors. For a management conclusion, write down those assumptions, test plausible alternatives, and say where the conclusion changes. Resilience Index The engine's stress-battery library defines one; ordinary runs don't produce it. Don't infer a score from an empty field. The KPI reference has the formula and normalization. Next: controlled comparisons and verifiable exports . Keep the inputs and protocol with the result, not just a screenshot of a mean.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index
entries.text: KPIs & the Resilience Index Every measure the engine reports, what it is for, and its unit.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index — How to read this page
entries.text: 12 measures, from engine 0.8.3 . The definition under each one is the engine's own, read from its export rather than restated. The definitions below come from the committed engine registry export. Regeneration checks help keep the reference aligned; the run record identifies which engine actually produced your result.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index — Window, units and availability
entries.text: Ordinary run KPIs use the engine's analysis window after warm-up, not necessarily the whole requested horizon. Fill rate is fulfilled value divided by demand value; higher is better, and no demand produces an unavailable measure. Lost sales and resilience costs are monetary amounts; lower is generally better when the service comparison is held fixed. Inventory is averaged over the window. Utilization has no universally preferred direction. The registry also defines library measures that ordinary application runs do not emit. In particular, the Resilience Index below is calculated by the engine's stress-battery library, not the standard Results dashboard.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index — Resilience Index: formula and worked arithmetic
entries.text: RI = 100 × [0.35(1 − L) + 0.25(1 − R) + 0.15S + 0.25(1 − C)]. L is service-loss area divided by window weeks; R is recovery weeks divided by window weeks; S is survival weeks divided by window weeks; C is resilience cost divided by clean-baseline revenue. Each normalized component is clipped to [0, 1]. The implementation guards the window denominator with at least 1 and revenue with at least 10⁻⁹. Illustrative arithmetic only: a 20-week window, service-loss area 2, recovery time 4, survival time 3 and cost 10 against clean revenue 100 give L=0.10, R=0.20, S=0.15 and C=0.10. The default weighted score is 76.25. These are invented teaching inputs, not a simulation result. Weights sum to one; their choice encodes priorities. Changing the window, clean baseline or weights changes the meaning of the score. Compare underlying measures alongside it. A near-zero clean revenue makes the guarded ratio numerically defined but economically difficult to interpret.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index — Three of them are shapes, not numbers
entries.text: ttr_weeks , tts_weeks and service_loss_area are defined on the fill-rate trace itself. Reading their definitions as sentences is possible; seeing them is faster, and the three-week rule in particular does not read as load-bearing until you watch it disqualify a week. Three measures as regions Three of the engine's measures are regions on this picture rather than facts about a single week. The three-week rule is why the first week that looks fine is usually not the recovery.

entries.title: KPIs & the Resilience Index — The measures
entries.text: fill_rate FR in % The headline service measure. Weighted by value, so missing an expensive product hurts more than missing a cheap one. The engine's definition Value-weighted served demand: Σ u_p·served_p / Σ u_p·D_p over the analysis window (Eq. 10); weekly FR[t] recorded in the trace. NOT MEASURED (NaN → null) when the window holds no demand — never a perfect 100%; a week with no demand keeps FR[t] = 1. lost_sales_value in € What the unserved demand was worth. The number a commercial reader will ask for first. The engine's definition Σ u_p · L_p over the window. cost_of_resilience C^res in € The engine-defined sum of resilience-cost components, including lost-sales cost. Review the components before treating it as extra cash expenditure. The engine's definition mat-SS holding + backup premiums + multi-sourcing premiums + expediting + overtime + lost sales + allocation labor + FG-SS holding (MTS) + backorder penalties (Eq. 23). delta_cost ΔC^res_i in % How much a strategy changed the cost of resilience, against the baseline. The engine's definition 1 − C^res_i / C^res_S0, CRN-paired per replication (Eq. 24-style); positive = cheaper than do-nothing. delta_revenue ΔR_i in % How much it changed revenue, against the baseline. Read with delta_cost, never alone. The engine's definition Σu_p(Q_i − Q_S0) / Σu_p(D − Q_S0), CRN-paired (Eq. 25-style); share of S0's lost revenue recover…

entries.title: Per-item time series
entries.text: Per-item time series Every material's and every finished good's stock, week by week, ranked by risk and downloadable to Excel — and the switch you have to throw before the run to get it. You have to ask for this before the run, and only a single-replication run can give it Per-item series are off by default and cannot be produced afterwards. A run that did not keep them has to be run again to get them — which costs time and nothing else, because the same seed reproduces the same world exactly. The switch is Inspection mode , on Policies → Run & validate → the Single tab. It is not in Simulation Lab, and it is not on the multi-run tab, because the engine only writes item series for a run with exactly one replication . Ask for it on a run with more and the request is dropped with a warning rather than honoured. Simulation Lab shows the explorer for such a run and, for any other, links to where one is started: a Lab scenario carries its own replication count, so the Lab cannot start one without writing a scenario.

entries.title: Per-item time series — Why the weekly view is usually the finding
entries.text: An average tells you the level. A series tells you the shape, and the shape is what a decision is made about. A 94% fill rate can be 94% every week, or perfect for forty weeks and 40% for ten. The first is a chain running slightly short; the second is a chain that failed and recovered. They need different responses and the aggregate cannot distinguish them. The shape the average hides Same average, different businesses. The mean cannot tell them apart.

entries.title: Per-item time series — The 18 measures, and what each one is a count of
entries.text: Every value is one week's worth , in the item's own units — pieces, kilograms, whatever the quantities in your files are in. Nothing here is a rate or a percentage, so a number is directly comparable with the volumes you uploaded. A material and a product carry different measures, because they are different halves of the chain: a material is something you hold and replenish, a product is something you promise and deliver. A material — 7 lines On hand on_hand How much you were holding at the end of that week. The line that hits zero is the stockout, and it is the last event rather than the first. In transit in_transit How much was ordered and not yet arrived. Read beside on hand: inventory falling while this stays flat means replenishment stopped, and inventory falling while this rises means it did not stop, it is just too slow. Orders placed orders How much you ordered that week. This is the policy speaking — it is the only one of the three that is a decision rather than a consequence, so it is where a policy change shows up first. MRP need (next lead time) mrp_need MRP on hand (after production) mrp_on_hand MRP on the way mrp_on_the_way MRP net mrp_net A product — 11 lines Demand demand How much was asked for that week. This is the draw the rest of the chain is answering, and on a stochastic demand model it is different on every seed. Projected demand (plan) projected_demand …

entries.title: Per-item time series — The two tables, and how they are ranked
entries.text: The explorer opens on Materials ; the switch beside it shows Finished goods . Each table has every item of the run, riskiest first, and leaves out the weeks before the warm-up ends. Materials : suppliers, average and minimum on hand, weeks at zero, the first week it ran out, average in transit, average use per week, minimum cover in weeks (minimum on hand over average use) and the total ordered. Ranked by weeks at zero, then by the thinnest cover — the order notebook 04 uses. Finished goods : fulfillment mode, average and minimum finished-goods stock, average target, weeks with no stock while demand was waiting, the first such week, weeks of cover, fill rate (everything delivered over everything demanded, so backlog served late counts), average backlog and lost units. Ranked by the largest shortfall — lost units plus average backlog — then by weeks out of stock, then by the lowest fill rate. That puts make-to-stock and make-to-order products on one scale. What the tables cannot say Use is derived, not measured. It is each product's production (units started) times its bill of materials, flattened through sub-assemblies. The engine consumes materials at production start, so it is the consumption it booked — but it is computed for this view, and so is minimum cover. A sub-assembly has no row. The engine holds stock per leaf material and per finished good; an intermediate compone…

entries.title: Per-item time series — Using the explorer
entries.text: 1 Run with Inspection mode on /policies → Run & validate → Single Set the seed you want — the series you get are that seed's world, and writing the number down is how you come back to the same one. The panel appears under the run once it finishes. 2 Choose materials or finished goods Two buttons, and two different tables. The header tells you how many of each this run has. The search box filters by id or name. 3 Tick the items you want to see Each ticked row draws its own chart below the table, in the order you ticked them, up to twelve at once. A material shows on hand and in transit with a marker on every week it ran out, and below it orders placed as bars with use as a line (and the MRP record, when it has one). A finished good shows its stock against its target with stockout markers, and below it demand, production and fulfillment with the backlog as an area, plus the plan's projected demand and planned production. 4 Download Excel For the selected items, or for all of them. The workbook opens with the run's reproducibility record — the dataset, policy, scenario, seed and engine that produced these numbers, and their limits — then the materials and products tables, one weekly sheet per selected item, and a long weekly sheet (week, kind, item, measure, value) for every item in the download. It needs the Export right on the project. 5 Read the chart against the warm-up line …

entries.title: Per-item time series — Reading one
entries.text: Start at the week the aggregate went wrong and read backwards. A stockout is the last event in a sequence — on-hand falling, in-transit not arriving, demand unchanged — and the useful question is which of those moved first. A material's two charts share their weeks on purpose. If on-hand is falling while orders placed are flat, the policy is not reacting; if orders are rising and in-transit is not, the supply is not answering. Those are different problems with different fixes, and the charts distinguish them at a glance in a way the KPIs never can. A material the disruption did not touch, used less: production stopped for want of another one. One seed, one world — there is nothing here to average An inspection run is one replication . The chart is one possible world, not the expected one, and a spike in it may be that seed rather than your chain. You cannot check it against the other seeds on this screen, because this run has none. The way to tell them apart is to change the seed and run inspection again. If the spike moves, it was the seed; if it stays in the same week, it is structural. Seeds, replications & confidence is why one run is never the answer on its own. An inspection run that could not store its series fails rather than reporting green The series are the entire point of asking for one, so a run whose item rows fail to persist is marked failed — not completed with…

entries.title: Performance & caching
entries.text: Performance & caching Why a second run is faster, and when the answer is recomputed instead.

entries.title: Performance & caching — The rule that decides a reuse
entries.text: An answer is reused when it was computed from the same data, with the same parameters, by the same version of the code. Not when it is recent. That is the whole design, and it is the opposite of the usual one. A cache keyed on freshness is a bet: probably nothing has changed in the last hour . This is keyed on identity — two requests carrying the same three things are asking the same question, so answering from the store is not an optimisation with a risk attached, it is the same answer. The consequence a user feels: change your data and the next request recomputes, every time, without you having to remember to clear anything. Change nothing and it returns immediately, however long ago it was computed. A result you are shown always knows what it was computed from Because reuse is keyed on identity, every stored answer carries the identity it was keyed on — which data, which parameters, which code version. That is what lets the Data Trust Report sort a project's computed rows into current, out of date, and we cannot tell . In practice the store is empty, and that is worth knowing The mechanism is shipped and correct. What has not happened is that anybody has run an analysis since it shipped — so every computed row that exists predates it and carries no identity at all, and none of them can be reused. The first analysis you run fills it in for the rows it writes. Until then, eve…

entries.title: Performance & caching — Why a particular run is slow
entries.text: The simulation cost scales with the size of your chain, the length of the window and the number of replications — and only the last of those is free to change. Halving replications halves the time and widens every interval, which is a trade to make deliberately rather than to discover. Replications are independent, so they parallelise; a single replication does not, and is deterministic for that reason. A run that is slow because the model is large will not get faster on a bigger machine per replication — it gets faster because more of them run at once. Uploading a large network is one recomputation, not one per row Loading a deep-tier graph used to trigger a full recomputation of the whole graph for every row inserted — thousands of identical requests, none of which could reuse another because each one saw a slightly different graph. That is fixed: a bulk load is one statement and triggers one recomputation.

entries.title: Reports & files
entries.text: Reports & files Rendered reports, who can open them, how long they last, and what they are worth later.

entries.title: Reports & files — What a rendered report is, and where it comes from
entries.text: A report is produced by the assistant, from a proposal you approved — not by a button on a results screen. You ask the project assistant for a decision report. It proposes one: a title, a template and a list of sections. Nothing is rendered until you approve that proposal, and what is rendered is exactly what you approved. Plans and proposals is that review step. At render time every section is resolved against live data — the runs and readings it cites, as they are now. A report is therefore current at the moment it is rendered rather than at the moment it was proposed, and a section citing a run that has since been deleted makes the render fail rather than quietly drop the section.

entries.title: Reports & files — What you get
entries.text: Three choices, and two of them give you two files. XLSX only The data pack: one sheet per section, numbers and narrative as cells. This is what you want if the report is going to be worked on rather than read. PDF — which always brings the XLSX too Ask for a PDF and you get two files, the document and the data pack behind it. That is deliberate and it is the same principle as the verifiable workbooks: a rendered document never circulates without the numbers it was made from. Asking for “both” gives you the same two files. The PDF drops characters the XLSX keeps The PDF is written with the standard Latin-1 fonts. Em dashes, curly quotes and ellipses are converted to plain equivalents, and anything outside Latin-1 — Greek, Cyrillic, Chinese, most accented non-European characters — is replaced. So a product or supplier id in a non-Latin script reads correctly in the XLSX and is mangled in the PDF. If your item names are not Latin-1, circulate the XLSX.

entries.title: Reports & files — Who can open it
entries.text: A file belongs to the person who created it. Your colleagues cannot see it, even on a project you share. user_files is read under one rule — the row's owner — plus a super-admin rule for platform operations. Project membership does not grant access to a file, and there is no sharing control. To give somebody a report, you send them the file. Downloading is the only way out, and it goes through a server action that checks the file is yours and then mints a link good for one hour . The storage bucket is not public and there are no permanent URLs — a link you pasted into a chat yesterday does not work today.

entries.title: Reports & files — How long a file lasts
entries.text: 1 Fourteen days, by default Every rendered file expires 14 days after it is created. The sweep deletes the row and the stored object together, so an expired file is gone rather than orphaned. 2 Mark it Keep to stop the clock A retained file is never swept. This is the one action that decides whether a report exists in three weeks, and it costs one click at the time you make it. 3 500 MB of retained files per person The cap is on what you keep, not on what you render, and it is enforced when you press Keep — so you are told at that moment rather than losing something later. An expired file stops appearing in your list before it is physically swept, so the list never shows you something you can no longer download. A report is not a verifiable export A rendered report shows results. The three verifiable workbooks show results and the inputs and fingerprints they were computed from , which is what lets somebody else check them. Send a report to explain. Send the workbooks to be believed. The whole file workspace is a deployment switch Reports, the file list and downloads exist only where the file workspace is turned on for the deployment. Where it is off, the assistant cannot store a report and every download answers with a service-unavailable message rather than a broken page. If you cannot find the file list at all, that is the likeliest reason, and it is an administrator's sett…

entries.title: Verifiable exports
entries.text: Verifiable exports Three workbooks that let someone check your model without access to this software.

entries.title: Verifiable exports — What makes an export verifiable
entries.text: It carries what it was computed from, not only what was computed. A spreadsheet of results is a claim. A spreadsheet of results, plus the exact inputs, plus the fingerprint tying the two together, is something a reviewer can check — by recomputing the fingerprint, by reading the inputs, or by rerunning the model elsewhere. That is the whole difference, and it is why there are three files rather than one: they answer what did you decide , what did you decide it on , and what came out .

entries.title: Verifiable exports — The three workbooks
entries.text: Policy snapshot The saved policy version: every family, every override, every cell. Stamped with: the policy fingerprint What makes it checkable: Under every value row sits a provenance row grading the cell — set (differs from the schema default), equal to the schema default, override, or inherited. So a reader can tell a decision you made from a default you never touched. And what it admits: Storage cannot distinguish “never touched” from “deliberately set to the default value”, and the export says so rather than picking one. Dataset The exact canonical rows the dataset fingerprint was computed over, one sheet per table the engine reads. Stamped with: the dataset fingerprint What makes it checkable: Not “the rows as they are now” — the rows as they were when the version was frozen, taken from the snapshot itself. Someone can recompute the fingerprint from the sheets and get the same value. And what it admits: A sheet the fingerprint does not cover would be a sheet a reader would wrongly believe was verified, so the workbook carries the snapshot and not a fresh query. Run results Per-run metadata, aggregate KPIs with confidence intervals, one row per seed, and a weeks-by-seeds sheet per stored series. Stamped with: the run's own provenance What makes it checkable: The per-seed sheet is what makes the confidence interval checkable: a reader can recompute the spread rather than …

entries.title: Verifiable exports — Where to get them
entries.text: From the policy screen at /policies , against a saved policy version . A version is required rather than optional: an export of unsaved decisions would carry a fingerprint over something nobody could return to.

entries.title: Reproducibility record
entries.text: Reproducibility record The stamp that lets someone else rerun exactly what you ran — and what is honestly in place today.

entries.title: Reproducibility record — What a reproducibility record is
entries.text: Four things, bound to one result: the data it ran on, the decisions it ran under, the scenario it ran in, and the version of the engine that ran it. With all four, a figure can be handed to somebody else and recreated. With any one missing, it cannot — a number reproduced against different data is a different number that happens to look the same. This record does not exist yet, and this page will not pretend it does The single artifact binding all four is not built. It is the next substantial piece of work in this area, and until it lands the honest statement is that a result is reproducible in pieces rather than as a record . What you can do today: export all three verifiable workbooks for the same run. Between them they carry the dataset fingerprint, the policy fingerprint and the run's own metadata, and a reader can confirm the three belong together. That is most of the record, assembled by hand, with nothing checking that you assembled it completely. One conclusion already has all four, and it is the exception worth knowing. A model-validation card records the dataset, the policy set, the scenario and the engine build it was reached under — each by identity and by fingerprint — and names the run that was its evidence. So a validated model IS reproducible today. What is missing is the same binding on an ordinary figure.

entries.title: Reproducibility record — What is in place
entries.text: Every computed row is able to say which version of your data it came from. The columns exist on 4 tables, the analyses that write them fill them in from the run rather than from a parameter — so a row cannot name a world its run never saw — and a check compares the stored values field by field against the run store. network_nodes node_list network_summary supply_chain_data One table deliberately has no such column: the deep-tier edges, because every column of it is uploaded. A provenance stamp no writer could fill would be a promise rather than a fact. And every derived row that exists today carries no stamp The mechanism is shipped and correct. What has not happened is that anybody has run an analysis since it shipped — so the rows sitting in the database were all written before provenance existed, and computed_from_hash is empty on every one of them. They cannot be back-filled. A row written before the anchor existed has no hash, and inventing one would be fabricated provenance — worse than an empty column, because an empty column is legible as “we do not know” and a made-up hash is not. The practical reading: a computed number in a project that has not been recomputed recently is reported as unknown rather than as current or stale, and Data Trust Report is where you see that count. Running the analysis again is what fills it in.

entries.title: Reproducibility record — What to do if you need a defensible figure today
entries.text: Freeze a dataset version and save a policy version before the run, not after. Both are fingerprinted at the moment you take them, and a run that names them can be pointed at later; a run against unfrozen data cannot, however carefully it was recorded elsewhere. Then export the three workbooks for that run and keep them together. It is assembly by hand, and it works.
