entries.title: Engine versions & changes
entries.text: Engine versions & changes Every version of the simulation engine, what it changed, who it affects, and how to run a result again on the engine that produced it.

entries.title: Engine versions & changes — How to read this page
entries.text: A result is only as reproducible as the engine that computed it. Every run records which engine that was, and this page says what each engine version changed. Engine version The number a person reads, such as 0.8.3 . It moves when the engine's behaviour or its contract changes. Engine build What actually ran, named by the content of its code: scsim-0.8.3+ followed by a 12-character code computed from the engine's source. Two builds of one version are different code. Since build identity arrived, every run records its build, so a result can say exactly which code computed it. Comparable Whether a result from the previous version can be set beside one from this version. “Results unchanged” means every reference run gave the same numbers. “Changed for some projects” names who. “Not comparable” means a result must be re-run before it can be a paired experiment; Compare still shows such a pair, marked not like-for-like. Tier The engineering classification. Tier 1 changes no behaviour, Tier 2 adds something that is off by default or corrects a result, and Tier 3 changes the engine's contract and comes with a design record. A Tier 2 change can still change results for the projects that use it, which is why comparability is stated separately. Of 23 versions, 18 change results for at least some projects. When two runs you compare were computed by different engines, the comparison says …

entries.title: Engine versions & changes — The engine running now
entries.text: The newest version is 0.8.3 (2026-10-27). Safety stock is now a real recovery strategy. For the materials a disrupted supplier ships, a scenario can hold extra days of cover between a start week and an end week: the reorder levels rise only in those weeks, so the buffer is built from orders placed at the start and arrives a lead time later, and its holding cost is charged at the material's own holding rate for those weeks only. The /policies safety stock is unchanged, and a scenario that sets no buffer runs exactly as before. Reading the build ledger…

entries.title: Engine versions & changes — Every version, newest first
entries.text: Each entry is written when the version is made, and a CI check refuses a change to the engine that moves a frozen reference result without a new version and an entry naming exactly what moved. A change made under a version without a new number is appended to that version as an amendment, and nothing published is rewritten. Entries before the record existed were written from the history afterwards and say so. Engine 0.8.3 2026-10-27 · Tier 2 Changed for some projects Safety stock is now a real recovery strategy. For the materials a disrupted supplier ships, a scenario can hold extra days of cover between a start week and an end week: the reorder levels rise only in those weeks, so the buffer is built from orders placed at the start and arrives a lead time later, and its holding cost is charged at the material's own holding rate for those weeks only. The /policies safety stock is unchanged, and a scenario that sets no buffer runs exactly as before. Who is affected. Results change only for a scenario that ticks Safety stock and sets a buffer window; every other scenario runs exactly as before (every frozen reference run kept its digest). Technical. P-P.3 windows ( SafetyStockWindow : material_id, days, start_week, end_week exclusive): E[D_m]·days/7 added to s and S at PH-70 while active (never to a stated level); holding h_m·c_m·units booked in ss_holding for active weeks. The ma…

entries.title: Engine versions & changes — Running a result again on its own engine
entries.text: Every engine build the platform has published stays published, and none is ever deleted. To recompute a stored result with the engine that produced it, install that build with the Python library and run the same frozen inputs: import suresuite as ss api = ss.connect() ss.install_engine(api, version=run["code_version"]) # the exact build the run recorded # or: ss.install_engine(api, version="0.6.0") # the newest build of a version The simulation server always runs the current engine; earlier ones run on your machine. See the reproducibility record for everything else a result is bound to.

entries.title: Engine versions & changes — What this page cannot tell you
entries.text: Runs before build identity name only a version. Several different builds often shipped under one number then, so for those runs the version is known and the exact code is not. Every one of those builds is archived and installable, but the run did not record which it was. The measured report sees only what the reference runs exercise. A change that acts only on fields those runs do not set (a typed replenishment level, MRP, demand per customer row) shows as unchanged there. The entry's “who is affected” line is what says who else is touched. Some history is counted, not described. Where engine changes were made without any record, the entry gives their number rather than inventing what they were. Reference data: contract 62a6e8587a37 , engine 0.8.3 . entries.title: Exporting and deleting your data
entries.text: Exporting and deleting your data Taking your data out, and having it removed.

entries.title: Exporting and deleting your data — The commitment
entries.text: Your data is yours. You can take it out in a format nothing here owns, and you can have it removed. That is one of the five commitments this product is built on — What happens to your data states all five, and this page is the practical half of the last one.

entries.title: Exporting and deleting your data — Getting it out
entries.text: Everything you uploaded is a CSV you already have. What you may not have is everything the system computed from it, and the three verifiable workbooks are the way to take that: the exact rows a version was computed over, the decisions you made, and what came out. They are ordinary spreadsheets. Nothing in them needs this software to be read, which is the point — an export you can only open here is not an export. There is no one-click “export everything” yet The workbooks cover the data spine — inputs, decisions, results. The system holds 94 tables in all, and some of what surrounds the spine (conversation threads, request logs, admin records) has no export of its own. If you need a complete copy rather than the model and its results, that is a request to make of whoever administers your organization rather than a button on a screen. We would rather say that than let you assume the workbooks are exhaustive.

entries.title: Exporting and deleting your data — Deleting a project
entries.text: What a deletion reaches Three tables outlive a deleted project, and all three are facts about the account rather than the project. That is a decision, and it is as hard to lose as the cascade. Two mechanisms do it, and knowing which is which tells you what is actually gone. 55 tables hold rows belonging to a project. Deleting one removes them two ways: 44 tables are wired to the project in the database and go automatically, and a further 5 are deleted by name by the deletion itself, because they were created without that wiring. All tables shows, for every described table, what it points at and what happens to it when the thing it points at goes. 2 things are detached rather than deleted, on purpose Your conversation threads and your rendered files are not removed with the project. They lose their link to it and remain yours — a report you rendered last month is still in your file list after the project it described is gone. That is the right behaviour for something you own personally, and it is worth knowing before you delete a project expecting everything about it to disappear. Deleting those is a separate act, on the file itself. 4 project-scoped tables are deliberately left behind They have no database wiring to the project and are not on the deletion's list, so their rows survive it — and for these three that is the intended answer, not an oversight: ai_chat_events , ai_u…

entries.title: Organizations and members
entries.text: Organizations and members The tenant boundary, and who sits inside it.

entries.title: Organizations and members — The boundary
entries.text: An organization is the wall. Projects live inside one, and nothing crosses between two except a person who belongs to both. It is the coarsest and most important of the access questions, because everything finer — project membership, roles, capabilities — operates inside a boundary that has already been drawn. Organizations are matched by identity, not by name Two organizations can be called the same thing and are not the same organization. Renaming one does not disconnect it from its projects, and creating a second with an identical display name does not give it access to the first's data. That sounds obvious and it was not always true here: a display name used as a join key is the defect this was fixed to close, and it is proved against a real database rather than asserted — a rename still matches, a shared display name does not.

entries.title: Organizations and members — Organizations — every column
entries.text: id uuid The organization's identity. This is the value that must travel — it is what projects.organization_id , approved_users.organization_id and the public /v1 API's p_org_id all mean. Not displayable, and that is the property that makes it safe as a join key (§2.1 uuid-identity ). Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. name text The organization's display name, as an administrator typed it. EDITABLE and NOT UNIQUE — two organizations may legitimately share one. It is a label for humans and it is never an identity. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. slug text A URL-safe form of the name, lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '-', 'g')) at the moment the row was seeded. UNIQUE, and deliberately NOT recomputed on rename — so after a rename it is a record of what the organization used to be called, which is what makes it usable to match rows written before it. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. owner_user_id uuid The approved user who owns the tenant. Advisory today — nothing in RLS or any RPC reads it; ownership is expressed through organization_members.org_role = 'owner' . Two places holding the same fact is an I1 violation waiting to diverge; WP 2.2 owns the…

entries.title: Organizations and members — Belonging to more than one organization
entries.text: One account can belong to several organizations — a consultant working for two tenants signs in once, with one address and one password. An administrator adds or removes an account’s organizations on /admin/users , and each membership takes one of that organization’s user places. You work in one organization at a time: your current organization . The projects you see, the projects you create and the plan shown on your profile are all the current organization’s, so two tenants’ projects never share a screen. Switch from the account menu or from your profile ; the app reloads on the other side of the wall. You cannot switch into an organization whose access period has ended, and if your current one ends while another is still valid, signing in takes you to the valid one. Deleting an organization deletes only the accounts that belong to no other organization. An account that also belongs elsewhere is removed from the deleted one and keeps the rest.

entries.title: Organizations and members — Members — every column
entries.text: id uuid Surrogate row identifier. The membership's identity is (org_id, user_id). Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. org_id uuid The organization joined, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE — deleting a tenant removes its memberships rather than orphaning them. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. user_id uuid The approved user who is a member, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. org_role text The member's standing in the organization — owner , admin or member , CHECK-constrained. This is an ORG vocabulary and it is not the project vocabulary: min_project_role throughout this contract speaks of viewer / analyst / editor / owner, which WP 2.2 creates on project_members . The two share the word "owner" and mean different things by it. Since D303 an owner or admin row of the account's ACTIVE organization lets a user account create projects there ( project_creation_right , read by capabilities_for_user ), and since D304 delete that organization's projects and their data ( project_org_admin , read by delete_project and delete_project_dataset ). Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. …

entries.title: Organizations and members — Rules the database itself enforces
entries.text: These run on every write, from any source. A row that fails one is refused — not corrected, not warned about. CHECK (status IN ('active','suspended')) CHECK (access_period IN ('week', 'month', 'quarter', 'year')) CHECK ((access_period IS NULL) = (access_valid_from IS NULL)) CHECK (project_limit IN (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) CHECK (user_limit IN (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) CHECK ( (storage_quota_bytes IS NULL OR storage_quota_bytes > 0) AND (compute_quota_rep_weeks_month IS NULL OR compute_quota_rep_weeks_month > 0) AND (max_replications_per_run IS NULL OR max_replications_per_run BETWEEN 1 AND 200) AND (max_concurrent_runs IS NULL OR max_concurrent_runs > 0) AND (series_retention_days IS NULL OR series_retention_days > 0))

entries.title: Roles and capabilities
entries.text: Roles and capabilities Understand your project rights and distinguish interface controls from server enforcement.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — Three different kinds of role
entries.text: An account role controls application-level capabilities. Organization membership places a user in an organizational context. A project role controls the rights shown for one project. Being a project owner is not the same as being an organization administrator, and a role on one project does not describe another project. Two rights cross the layers: an Admin or Owner of an organization may create projects in it, and may delete its projects and the data inside them, whatever the account role. Both apply to the organization you are working in, so switch to that organization on your profile first. Different roles, different questions Illustration. The API key gateway and browser simulation path have different checks.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — Account-role defaults
entries.text: These are the same descriptions shown by account administration. Project rights and explicit grants still need a separate check. Super admin Everything, everywhere — the checks below are skipped entirely, and this is the only role that opens the administration area. Admin The full working surface: every workspace, the Project Manager and the Developer API, with every feature on by default. It does not open the administration area — that is super admin only. Modeler The builder's role. The same default surface as admin — the two differ by what older row rules name and by convention, not by their default grants. User Read and analyse. Every workspace opens, but creating projects, editing data and running simulations are off by default. An Admin or Owner of an organization may still create projects in it, and delete its projects and their data, while working in that organization.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — Default project rights in the current source
entries.text: The current migration-defined project roles are viewer, analyst, editor and owner. Their defaults for the four project controls are: Role Edit inputs Edit policies Run simulations Export Viewer No No No No Analyst No No Yes No Editor Yes Yes Yes Yes Owner Yes Yes Yes Yes This is the source-defined default matrix, not a live audit of your account. Account activity, project access, administrative overrides and delegation can affect the effective answer. Project settings and membership administration have separate checks; an editor's four rights do not imply ownership.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — Check and resolve an access problem
entries.text: Open your profile's project-access information and check the effective role and reason for the right in question. Confirm the selected project. If you can view data but cannot edit policies, an analyst or viewer role may explain it. Ask the owner or an administrator for the required right; changing a policy parameter will not clear a permission failure. For upload failures, distinguish landing from promotion. The interface and backend check different stages. Record the action, project and exact error so the administrator can identify the failing boundary. Do not treat a hidden control as evidence that direct requests are impossible.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — What is verified and what remains a gap
entries.text: Some operations, including staged promotion, have database role checks. The public API gateway authenticates keys, checks scopes and project tenancy, and fails closed on authorization errors. These checks do not establish that every browser RPC and edge function enforces the same model. Known browser simulation authorization gap Source review found that the browser simulation endpoint accepts an Authorization header, can continue without an authenticated Supabase user, and checks project existence with service privileges. Its dispatch helper assumes the caller already authorized the request. This path does not establish the caller's project role before dispatch. Interface restrictions therefore must not be described as a complete security boundary. No production bypass test or permission change was performed during this documentation review. Deployment parity remains unverified. The separate engineering review records affected paths and follow-up work. Use the scoped public API for documented integrations; do not build integrations against internal browser RPCs.

entries.title: Roles and capabilities — Related access questions
entries.text: Project access explains project administration. Organizations and members covers organization context. Documentation sections have their own release rules: being able to read a page does not confer access to the corresponding project action.

entries.title: Project access
entries.text: Project access Find who can work on a project and request the right level of access.

entries.title: Project access — Start with the project, not the account label
entries.text: A project has an owner and can have members with viewer, analyst or editor rights. Project roles are separate from account roles and organization membership. The current project-rights defaults are documented in Roles and capabilities ; notably, an analyst can run simulations but does not receive input editing, policy editing or export by default. Resolve access for a particular task Illustration. The role display guides diagnosis; it does not prove server enforcement.

entries.title: Project access — Inspect effective access
entries.text: Use your profile's project-access information to see the effective role and rights for the selected project. Administrators can use the project-access administration screen to inspect ownership, membership and delegation. Access to that administration screen is itself restricted. Ask for a right tied to a concrete task: 'edit input data for Control-unit tutorial' is clearer than 'make me an admin'. An editor can prepare inputs and policies without becoming the project's owner. Ownership and project-setting changes have separate checks.

entries.title: Project access — Delegation and expiration
entries.text: Delegation can grant temporary project access under the application's delegation rules. Check both the effective role and expiry; a previous successful session is not proof that the grant remains valid. When a grant expires, ask the owner or administrator to review the task rather than assuming the project was deleted.

entries.title: Project access — When access and controls disagree
entries.text: Record the project, action, effective-right display and exact backend error. Reloading can resolve a stale interface state, but cannot correct a missing permission. The absence of a button and a denied server request are different evidence. Enforcement has known gaps The current source does not establish uniform enforcement across every browser and backend path. The browser simulation dispatch gap is described in Roles and capabilities . This documentation records it; it does not change access control or certify a live deployment. Documentation release access is separate. Being unable to open a manual section is not itself evidence that your project role changed.

entries.title: Who can see your data
entries.text: Who can see your data The honest answer, including the parts that are not reassuring.

entries.title: Who can see your data — The short answer
entries.text: People in your organization who have been given access to your project, and the people who operate this system. The rest of this page is the long answer, and it is longer because the short one leaves out where the boundaries are actually enforced and where they are currently only described. Three gates, two decisions They ask different questions, and they can disagree about the same action.

entries.title: Who can see your data — Three gates, and only two of them decide
entries.text: A write to your data passes three checks that sound like one thing and are not. Can you reach the project? The database's own row rules. This is the gate that actually refuses people, and it asks about reachability rather than about your role. Do you hold the capability? Resolved in layers from your role, your organization and you. It governs what the application offers you. Do you hold the minimum project role? Declared on all 77 described tables and checked by one live path — the promotion that lands reviewed data. Everywhere else it is a design that has not been made live. The first and third can disagree A person with the editor role on a project, who is not that project's modeler, passes the promotion's role check and is then refused by the row rules on the rows they were promoting. Two gates asking different questions about the same action, and only one of them is the one that decides. “Row-level security: enabled” is not the assurance it sounds like 74 of 77 described tables have row-level security switched on. Switched on is not the same as restrictive: a rule can be enabled and permit everything, and 16 tables do exactly that — every one of their rules permits every row. For 4 more, the static analysis of the migrations cannot determine the answer — a third state, and not the same as “off”. That is not a hedge: the three item-master tables were recorded as having it o…

entries.title: Who can see your data — What is recorded when someone touches your data
entries.text: 43 of 77 described tables write an audit row on every change, naming the actor. Where a write goes through the promotion, the row also names the role the actor was acting under — so the record says the database agreed they could write, not only that they did. The tables that are not audited are named on their own pages rather than collected here, because “which tables are audited” is a fact that changes and a list in prose would not. The public API does not carry a person at all A request authenticated with an API key has no user behind it — a key is issued to a project, not to a person. Three calls in the public API therefore write with no actor recorded. Naming a fabricated user would make the audit trail read as though somebody acted when nobody did, which is worse than an empty field. The gap is real and it is stated rather than filled. Getting an API key covers what that means for a key you issue.

entries.title: Who can see your data — The people who run this system
entries.text: Administrators of your organization can reach your projects. So can whoever operates the hosting for this deployment — a database administrator can read a database, and no application-level rule changes that. There is no encryption scheme here that would put your data beyond the reach of the people who run the servers, and a manual that implied otherwise would be wrong. The 94 tables in the system are the surface that exists; All tables lists every one, described or not. Read permissions are not declared per table 8 of 77 described tables declare a read capability. The rest declare who may WRITE and leave reading to the row rules, so this manual can tell you precisely who may change a table and cannot tell you as precisely who may see it.

entries.title: Audit log
entries.text: Audit log What is recorded when your data changes — and what is not, yet.

entries.title: Audit log — What a row records
entries.text: One row per statement that changed data: which table, what kind of change, when, and who the request said was doing it. Statement grain rather than row grain, deliberately. A load of two thousand rows is one act by one person, and two thousand audit rows would bury it rather than describe it. A data change also names the projects it touched. Three kinds of entry share the log: what an administrator did (users, organizations, projects, access rules, API keys), what changed in your data, and access events — every sign-in, every wrong password for a registered account, and every export, allowed or refused. A sign-in is recorded by the database after it has checked the password, so a browser cannot write one for somebody else. id uuid The row's identity. Returned by the emit functions so a caller can cite what it wrote. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. actor_user_id uuid Who did it. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. action text What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary ( org.update , api_key.revoke ); data-plane rows use the SQL operation ( insert , update , delete ); access-plane rows use export.all…

entries.title: Audit log — What is covered
entries.text: 43 of the 77 described tables write an audit row on every change. The promotion that lands reviewed data also records the role the person was acting under, so the row says the database agreed they could write. 34 described tables write no audit row. Each says so on its own page, because which tables are audited changes and a list in prose here would not. An audit row names the identity the client presented This application signs you in against its own approved-user list rather than a managed identity provider, so the user id that arrives with a change is asserted by the browser. The database checks that this user can reach the project — a real constraint, checked server-side — and it does not verify that the person is who the request says. So the log answers what changed, when, and under whose asserted identity . It does not answer who in the sense a court would want. Who can see your data is the fuller version of that. Some writes reach the database without naming anybody A request authenticated by an API key has no user behind it, so what it writes is recorded with no actor. Naming a fabricated user would be worse — an audit trail reading as though somebody acted when nobody did — so the field is left empty and the gap is stated here. Nothing in the log can be edited or deleted — and you can check The database refuses to change or remove an entry once it is written. Each ent…

entries.title: Audit log — Rules the database itself enforces
entries.text: These run on every write, from any source. A row that fails one is refused — not corrected, not warned about. CHECK (plane IN ('admin','data','access'))

entries.title: Admin screens — Who reaches these
entries.text: Administrators. 13 of the described tables can only be written by one, and they are the ones that decide what everybody else can do. Changing something here changes it for other people, which is the whole reason the surfaces are separate from the product.

entries.title: Admin screens — The 10 screens
entries.text: /admin The landing page for the administrative area — where the other screens are reached from. /admin/users Who may sign in, and the way into each person's own entitlements. Worth knowing: The role picker sets the platform role, and the person's member/admin role in their active organization follows it (an organization owner stays owner; their other organizations are untouched). It does not change what decides above or beside the role: a grant or denial set on the person or their organization still decides, a project role still limits the four project rights on that project, and admin does not open this administration area — only super admin does. After a change the page lists each of these that still applies, with a link to the person's page; an account left an organization member while its platform role is admin is marked, with a one-click fix. The entitlements themselves are on the per-user page below, not here. Suspending an account can be undone; deleting it cannot. A deleted person's uploads, analyses and lanes are kept with the author shown as unknown, and an account that still owns projects cannot be deleted until they are transferred. /admin/users/:userId One person's access: the organizations they belong to and their role in each, every project they can reach with their role and rights on each, their capability grants and denials, and their permitted AI models. entries.title: Account & password
entries.text: Account & password Managing your own sign-in.

entries.title: Account & password — Your account
entries.text: Your account is an entry in this deployment's list of approved users. It carries your identity, your organization and your role, and it is what every access question resolves against. Accounts are approved rather than self-registered: somebody grants access, and access can be removed.

entries.title: Account & password — If you forget your password
entries.text: Choose Forgot password? on the sign-in page and enter the email you sign in with. That sends a request to the platform's administrator. It does not change your account, and the page shows the same message whether or not the email has an account. The administrator confirms with you through contact details already on file, then sends you a temporary password. Sign in with it and you are taken to /profile to choose a new password before you can open anything else. Nobody needs your current password to reset it. If someone asks you for it, do not give it.

entries.title: Account & password — What your account record holds
entries.text: id uuid The user's identity, and the value every other governance table joins on — organization_members.user_id , projects.modeler_id , the _user_id argument of capabilities_for_user() and of get_current_user_org_id() . Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. name text The account holder's full name, as entered when the account was approved. Their identity for accountability: its owner cannot change it (§4 D209) — update_own_profile has no parameter for it — and only the administrator paths write it. first_name / last_name are a reading of it. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. email text The sign-in address, UNIQUE. Also a second identity path: the fallback branch of get_current_user_org() and get_current_approved_user() locate the row by auth.jwt() ->> 'email' when the session GUC is unset. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. password_hash text The bcrypt hash of the account's password. A credential, and the reason the contradiction recorded in governance.note above is a security finding rather than an untidiness. Blank means blank: nothing substitutes a value for this column, because nothing validates it on the way in. role public.app_role The account's global role…

entries.title: Getting an API key
entries.text: Getting an API key Create a key scoped to one job, make a read-only request, then submit and fetch a run. In short Create the key in Developer API › API keys . Copy the secret now — you won't see it again. Give it only the projects and scopes it needs, and an expiry. Prove it works with a read before you let it write.

entries.title: Getting an API key — Create a key
entries.text: 1 Open API keys /developer Developer API › API keys › Create API key . Any user can create a personal key with the read scopes ( read:data , read:policies , read:runs ); an organization key, or any write scope, needs an administrator or modeler. 2 Name it for its job Create API key Pick test or live, restrict it to the projects and scopes it needs, and set an expiry. 3 Copy the secret Create API key It's shown once. Later views show only a prefix. You should see the key in your list, showing its prefix, scopes and expiry. Start with a scoped read Illustration. Source-checked request flow; no live authenticated call was made. Scopes used in this guide. Scope Allows read:data Listing projects and reading data — the first request read:policies Listing saved policy versions read:runs Listing scenarios, polling a run, fetching replications write:runs Creating a scenario or submitting a run What a key can and can't do Keys carry an organization and optional project restrictions. What a key can reach also depends on its owner's current eligibility — a stored scope list isn't a permanent entitlement. GET /key returns the scopes the key may use now; the notebooks check it before they start. The test/live label controls limits. It isn't proof that the key points at a separate database.

entries.title: Getting an API key — Make your first request
entries.text: Set SURESUITE_API_BASE (your gateway URL, ending in /functions/v1/api/v1 ) and SURESUITE_API_KEY in your local environment. Never commit the secret. This request needs read:data . curl --fail-with-body \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SURESUITE_API_KEY" \ "$SURESUITE_API_BASE/projects?limit=10" Success is a data array and a next_cursor . A key that can see no projects gets a valid empty page: { "data": [], "next_cursor": null } Follow next_cursor until it's null. An empty data array is not a simulation result. The request and response shape are checked against the current handler; this guide doesn't claim a live authenticated request was run.

entries.title: Getting an API key — Submit a run
entries.text: 1 Find real IDs read:policies · read:runs List saved policy versions and scenarios in the authorized project. Don't copy example UUIDs into production. 2 POST the run write:runs POST to /projects/PROJECT_ID/runs with scenario_id and policy_version_id . Leave acknowledge_warnings and force_rerun false unless you mean them. Set a unique Idempotency-Key , and reuse it only to retry this same request. 3 Poll until it's done read:runs A run_id and status means accepted, not finished. Poll GET /runs/RUN_ID , then fetch GET /runs/RUN_ID/replications . You should see status done, the versions you expected, the replication count, and the conversion notes. { "scenario_id": "UUID_FROM_SCENARIO_LIST", "policy_version_id": "UUID_FROM_POLICY_VERSION_LIST", "acknowledge_warnings": false, "force_rerun": false }

entries.title: Getting an API key — If a request fails
entries.text: 401 Missing, malformed, expired or revoked key. Check the error code and replace the key in Developer API. Never paste a key into a support message. 403 or 404 A missing scope, or a project or run the key can't reach. A 404 can deliberately hide something inaccessible. 400 or a validation response Read the error body for malformed IDs, unsupported fields or invalid input. Run-readiness findings mean fixing the model, not the auth header. 409 reuse_available A compatible result already exists. Inspect it; force a rerun only when you really want fresh computation. 429 or 503 Quota, rate limit or a service that's down. Respect any retry information, retry a bounded number of times, and keep the same idempotency key. Keep the response's X-Request-Id and error code for diagnosis. Details: Endpoints & schemas and rate limits and idempotency .

entries.title: Endpoints & schemas
entries.text: Endpoints & schemas Every endpoint, the scope it requires, and how the surface is shaped.

entries.title: Endpoints & schemas — The shape of the surface
entries.text: 22 routes, under /v1 , over three resources: projects and what hangs off them, runs, and keys. Everything is scoped to a project by its id, and the id is checked against your key's organization before any handler runs. A key cannot reach a project it was not issued for, whatever the path says.

entries.title: Endpoints & schemas — The routes
entries.text: /engine GET /v1/engine read:data /keys GET /v1/keys admin:keys POST /v1/keys/{id}:revoke admin:keys /projects GET /v1/projects read:data GET /v1/projects/{id} read:data POST /v1/projects/{id}/datasets:freeze write:data GET /v1/projects/{id}/dataset-versions read:data GET /v1/projects/{id}/dataset-versions/{version} read:data GET /v1/projects/{id}/policy-catalog read:policies GET /v1/projects/{id}/policies read:policies PUT /v1/projects/{id}/policies write:policies POST /v1/projects/{id}/policy-versions write:policies GET /v1/projects/{id}/policy-versions read:policies GET /v1/projects/{id}/policy-versions/{version} read:policies GET /v1/projects/{id}/scenarios read:runs POST /v1/projects/{id}/scenarios write:runs POST /v1/projects/{id}/runs write:runs /runs GET /v1/runs/{id} read:runs GET /v1/runs/{id}/replications read:runs POST /v1/runs/{id}:cancel write:runs POST /v1/runs/{id}:add-reps write:runs GET /v1/runs/{id}/validation read:runs A colon in a path is an action, not a resource Routes like :freeze , :cancel and :revoke are things you do rather than things you fetch. They are always POST, and they are named that way so that a URL cannot be mistaken for something you can GET.

entries.title: Endpoints & schemas — Reading a list
entries.text: Lists are cursor-paged, not offset-paged. A list response carries its rows under data and a next_cursor beside them; pass that value back as ?cursor= to get the following page, and stop when it comes back null. ?limit= takes 20 by default and 100 at most. A larger number is clamped rather than refused, so a client asking for a thousand rows gets 100 and a cursor, not an error — which is worth knowing, because a loop that stops when it receives fewer rows than it asked for will stop on the first page. A cursor is a position, not a snapshot. Rows created while you are paging can appear or shift, so for anything you intend to reconcile later, freeze a dataset version first and read against that.

entries.title: Endpoints & schemas — Every error this API can return
entries.text: Failures carry a stable machine code beside the HTTP status, and the code is what a client should branch on: statuses are shared — four different things return 429 — and only the code says which. 32 codes exist, and they are read from the dispatcher's own throw sites rather than listed by hand, so one that stops being thrown leaves this page. Status Code What it means 400 invalid_cursor cursor must be a replication index 400 invalid_json request body is not valid JSON 400 invalid_request request body failed validation 401 expired_key this API key has expired 401 invalid_key missing or malformed API key (expected Authorization: Bearer sk_… ) 401 key_owner_inactive this personal key's owner is no longer active in its organization 401 org_suspended the key's organization is not active 401 revoked_key this API key has been revoked 402 quota_exceeded ${e.message} 403 missing_scope this key does not have the ${scope} scope 403 replications_exceeded ${e.message} 404 dataset_version_not_found no such dataset version in this project 404 engine_version_not_published engine ${wanted} was never published; published versions: ${publishedVersions(versions).join(", ")} 404 key_not_found key not found 404 policy_version_not_found no such policy version in this project 404 project_not_found project not found 404 route_not_found no such route: ${req.method} /v1${subPath} 404 run_not_found run n…

entries.title: Rate limits & idempotency
entries.text: Rate limits & idempotency How often you may call, and how to retry without doing something twice.

entries.title: Rate limits & idempotency — Limits
entries.text: Every response tells you where you stand, so a well-behaved client never has to guess. X-RateLimit-Limit What your key is allowed, per minute. X-RateLimit-Remaining What is left in the current window. X-RateLimit-Reset When the window rolls over. Retry-After On a refusal, how long to wait. Honour it rather than backing off by guess. Read the headers rather than assuming the numbers. A limit is resolved per request from three places, in order: a row for your key , then a row for your organization , then the default for the key's environment. So two keys in the same organization can have different ceilings, and neither has to match the table below. If nothing is configured Per minute Per day Runs at once sk_live_… 120 5000 5 sk_test_… 30 300 1 Raising either is an administrator's decision rather than something a client can negotiate. It takes effect on the next request — there is no deploy behind it.

entries.title: Rate limits & idempotency — Three more ceilings that are not requests per minute
entries.text: The per-minute limit is the one everybody meets first and the one least likely to stop a real integration. These three are the ones that do. Simulations running at once, per organization Counted across everything your organization has queued or running — the API, the application, everyone's browser tab. Exceeding it answers concurrent_runs_exceeded with a Retry-After of 60 seconds, and the message tells you how many are active. This is the limit a batch script hits, and the fix is to finish a run before dispatching the next rather than to raise the ceiling. Replications per run, where your organization sets one A scenario asking for more than your organization allows is refused with replications_exceeded before any compute starts — a 403, not a truncation, so you never receive a run quietly shorter than the one you asked for. Under that there is a hard global clamp at 200. 512 KB per request body Over it is payload_too_large . There are no bulk endpoints, so the only way to approach this is a very large policy document; a request that hits it is usually a loop that meant to send one override and sent every override. Failed authentication is throttled by address, not by key 30 failed authentications a minute from one address answers too_many_failed_auths — a 429, for what is really a 401. It exists to make key-guessing expensive. It catches an honest client too: a deployment th…

entries.title: Rate limits & idempotency — Idempotency
entries.text: Starting a run is the call you must not accidentally make twice, because the second one costs real compute and produces a second result that looks like a disagreement. Send an Idempotency-Key header with it. If a request carrying that key already started a run, the original run is returned rather than a new one started — so a retry after a timeout you are not sure about is safe. You can tell the two apart: a replayed request comes back with Idempotency-Replayed: true , and the body is the original run's id and current status rather than a freshly queued one. A client that wants to know whether it actually caused the run should read that header. The record lasts 24 hours , and the key is scoped to your API key . After that window the same header starts a new run, and two keys using the same string never collide with each other. Use a key that means something Derive it from what the request is about — the project, the policy version, the scenario — rather than from a fresh random value per attempt. A key generated per attempt makes every retry a new request, which is precisely what the header exists to prevent. The other protection against a duplicate run costs you nothing to ignore Dispatching a run whose inputs, policy version and scenario exactly match a completed run answers reuse_available — a 409 — instead of computing it again. It is not an error: it is the API telling yo…

entries.title: Request log
entries.text: Request log What your key did, and when.

entries.title: Request log — What each request records
entries.text: Every request, successful or not, whether or not it reached a handler. Which key And which organization it belongs to. Method and route What was asked for. Status and error code What came back, and why if it failed. Scope used Which permission the route required. Latency and bytes How long it took and how much came back. Request id Returned in X-Request-Id on every response — quote it when asking about a particular call.

entries.title: Request log — What it is for
entries.text: Two things, and they are different. Debugging: your client says the call failed and this says what the server saw. And review: which keys are active, what they are doing, and whether a key is being used for something it was not issued for. The API keys tab of Developer API is where the second one is answered without reading rows: each key shows its request count over the last 30 days and when it was last used. A key with no traffic for months is a key to revoke, and a key with traffic nobody can account for is the question this log exists to answer.

entries.title: Request log — Reading a failed call
entries.text: Three fields together tell you what happened, and reading only one of them is how a debugging session goes wrong. Status Not enough on its own. Four different failures answer 429, and three of them are not rate limits. Error code The stable name, and the one to branch on. Endpoints & schemas lists every one the server can produce. Scope used Which permission the route demanded. On a missing_scope refusal this is the field that says what to add, and it is recorded even though the call never reached a handler. Set your own X-Request-Id on a request and it is kept rather than replaced, so a request id you generated in your own logs is the same string here. Send none and one is generated and returned to you. Either way the response carries it, so the id in your client's log is the id to quote. Nothing you send in a request body is recorded here The log holds the method, the route, the status, the size of the response and the timing. It does not hold what you sent or what came back, and it never records the Authorization header. That is right for a log that will outlive the request, and it means this log cannot answer “what did that call change”. For that you want the audit log , which records the change rather than the call. Logging never delays or fails your request The row is written after the response has been handed back, and a write that fails is reported to the server's own …

entries.text: All tables Every table in the system, and every column of every table the contract describes.

entries.title: All tables — How to read this page
entries.text: This is the detailed index. For the shape of the system rather than its detail, The data model at a glance is the map; for a single field, Field index lists every one alphabetically. 94 tables exist. 77 are described here in full — 1026 columns. The other 17 are listed at the bottom, each under the work package that will describe it. Columns lead with the name you type Where a column is one you upload, the CSV header is the name shown first and the stored name follows underneath. They are usually the same and occasionally not — a products file says sell_price where the engine says unit_price . Leading with the engine's vocabulary is what made the previous manual unusable to the person holding the file. Every row has a stable address: #table.column . Linking someone to one exact field is a link, not an instruction to scroll.

entries.title: All tables — audit_logs
entries.text: Tier G platform 14 columns One recorded action, on one plane. admin is what a super admin did, data is a tier transition — a write to tier 2, 3 or 4 — and access is a governed decision such as an export being allowed or refused. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor. action not uploaded text What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary ( org.update , api_key.revoke ); data-plane rows use the SQL operation ( insert , update , delete ); access-plane rows use export.allowed / export.refused , and since 20260929000001 auth.sign_in / auth.sign_in_failed , written by authenticate_approved_user after the database has checked the password (throttled to one per person per minute; a failed attempt names the ACCOUNT as target and no actor). entries.title: All tables — capabilities

entries.title: All tables — customers

entries.title: All tables — ingest_files
entries.text: Tier 0 data-ingestion 11 columns One file as received, in one run: the manifest for bytes held in storage — where they are, how many there were, and the SHA-256 of exactly the sequence received. Write-once: the row records an event that has already happened and cannot be edited into a different one. Columns of ingest_files Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key for one landed file. never empty key ingest_run_id not uploaded uuid The run this file was landed for. NOT NULL: a file with no run is a byte-stream nobody asked for, and making the run the owner is what keeps a landing attached to a project, a source kind and an approval. required source_kind not uploaded text csv, orbit-mrp or api — what kind of source produced these bytes. The same closed vocabulary as the run's. required original_filename not uploaded text The file's name as the user's machine gave it, verbatim. For display and for the person's own recognition — never a key, and never parsed for meaning: two projects upload inbound.csv on the same afternoon (G1's rule, applied to filenames). required storage_bucket not uploaded text The storage bucket the bytes live in. Recorded rather than assumed, so that moving a bucket is a data change and not a code change. required storage_path not uploaded text Where the bytes are inside the bucket. entries.title: All tables — ingest_runs
entries.text: Tier 1 data-ingestion 23 columns One ingestion attempt, from any source — a connector sync, a CSV upload or an API push — with the counts and the mapping report it produced. The unit a person reviews and approves: staged rows belong to a run, and promotion is a decision about a run rather than about a row. Columns of ingest_runs Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. Not the grain: a run is identified by what it did, and nothing joins to this except the staging rows and the landed files. never empty key link_id not uploaded uuid The ERP link this run used, or NULL for a source that has none. NULL means 'this source needs no link', never 'the link was lost' — a CSV upload and an API push have no credential to point at. triggered_by not uploaded text manual or scheduled. A manual run was asked for by a person; a scheduled one was started by the cron sweep against the link's sync_schedule_cron . required triggered_by_user_id not uploaded uuid The person who asked for a manual run, in auth.users . NULL for a scheduled run, where there is no person — stated rather than back-filled to a service account, because 'nobody asked, the schedule did' is the true answer (G4). status not uploaded text running, staged, applied, failed or skipped. staged is the state that matters: rows are in tier 1 and a human has not approved them. Nothing reaches tier 2 before applied…

entries.title: All tables — ingest_staged_rows
entries.text: Tier 1 data-ingestion 11 columns One row of one uploaded file, in one run: the cells as received beside what validation made of them, and the findings that explain the difference. The unit a reviewer reads when a number looks wrong — and the only place in the system where the left-hand side of a parse survives. Columns of ingest_staged_rows Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key for one staged row. never empty key ingest_run_id not uploaded uuid The run these rows were staged in. entries.title: All tables — materials
entries.text: Tier 2 data-ingestion 16 columns One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing. Columns of materials Column Type What it means project_id not uploaded uuid The project this material belongs to. Half of the primary key. Checked: set from the selected project, never from the CSV never empty material_id text The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to the BOM and to every inbound arc that supplies it. Checked: non-empty; unique within the project required name text A human-readable name for the material. Display only. If missing: the material_id — NULL or blank (shown as default) cost numeric in currency per unit of material What one unit of this material costs to buy. The master value; where it is unset the engine values the material at the volume-weighted average price of its inbound arcs — what the project actually pays, which is usually what the user wants and is why leaving it blank is not an error. Checked: numeric > 0 If missing: the volume-weighted average of the material's inbound unit_price values, each weighted by that arc's weekly volume (grading.ts::volumeWeightedInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first) — NULL or <= 0, with at least one inbound arc carrying a vol…

entries.title: All tables — model_validations
entries.text: Tier 4 policy-ui 38 columns One VALIDATED MODEL: a decision about how a project's model may be used, bound to the exact policy content, graph version and scenario world it was established on and stating the run protocol every decision-grade run must follow — how many seeds, the week steady state begins, horizon, analysis window, CI level and stopping rule — with who validated it and when. Immutable: only its lifecycle (status, supersession, revocation) changes. Matched by CONTENT, never by id (WP 10.2). Runs stamp it ( simulation_runs.model_validation_id ); a person sees name and version_no . never empty key project_id not uploaded uuid The project it validates. never empty policy_version_id not uploaded uuid The policy version row it was recorded under — for display and the foreign key only. Matching is by policy_hash (WP 10.2, §4 D242). never empty policy_hash not uploaded text The policy CONTENT it was validated on — the policy half of its identity. never empty dataset_version_id not uploaded uuid The graph version ("Graph vN") it was validated on. Required on every model written since WP 10.3 (a BEFORE INSERT trigger); NULL only on cards older than that. graph_hash not uploaded text The composite graph it was validated on — the whole snapshot, kept beside hash_simulation . entries.title: All tables — node_list
entries.text: Tier 3 analysis 22 columns One node of one project's supply chain, derived from BOTH edge tables — supply_chain_data AND supply_chain_data_multi_tier — by refresh_node_list_for_project . The multi-tier half is WP 8.1's widening: until then the derivation read the flat table only, so 104 deep-tier nodes had no row here and therefore no type any page could read (D132). Like network_nodes it is two things (D56): the derivation and the geocoder write some columns, the criticality prediction others. SCOPE LIMIT, stated because supply_tier makes it visible: this is the projection of the two EDGE tables, so a firm that appears only in tier2_suppliers / tier3_suppliers is not a node here and its tier is reachable only through node_supply_tier . Folding the deep-tier FIRM graph in is a different node universe ( network_nodes.uid against material ids is D137) and is owned by no package yet. entries.title: All tables — org_capabilities
entries.text: Tier G platform 5 columns One grant or denial, for one org_id and one capability. The org layer: a tenant-wide override of the role default. Columns of org_capabilities Column Type What it means org_id not uploaded uuid the organization the row grants for. never empty capability_key not uploaded text The capability, naming a row in capabilities . Checked: must exist in capabilities never empty allowed not uploaded boolean Whether this layer grants the capability. TRI-STATE in effect: a missing row means "inherit from the next layer out", false means "deny here". They are different answers and the resolver's COALESCE depends on the difference. If missing: the next layer out decides; the chain ends in false — no row exists at this layer (shown as default) never empty created_at not uploaded timestamp with time zone When the row was created. Server-stamped. never empty updated_at not uploaded timestamp with time zone When it was last changed. Server-stamped. never empty

entries.title: All tables — organization_members
entries.text: Tier G platform 6 columns One user's membership of one organization, and the role they hold IN that organization. An account may hold several — one per organization it belongs to (§4 D210). Org-level only: it says nothing about which projects inside the organization the user may touch, which is what WP 2.2's project_members is for. Columns of organization_members Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate row identifier. The membership's identity is (org_id, user_id). never empty key org_id not uploaded uuid The organization joined, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE — deleting a tenant removes its memberships rather than orphaning them. never empty user_id not uploaded uuid The approved user who is a member, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE. never empty org_role not uploaded text The member's standing in the organization — owner , admin or member , CHECK-constrained. This is an ORG vocabulary and it is not the project vocabulary: min_project_role throughout this contract speaks of viewer / analyst / editor / owner, which WP 2.2 creates on project_members . The two share the word "owner" and mean different things by it. Since D303 an owner or admin row of the account's ACTIVE organization lets a user account create projects there ( project_creation_right , read by capabilities_for_user ), and since D304 delete that organization's projects and their data ( project_org_admin , r…

entries.title: All tables — organizations
entries.text: Tier G platform 18 columns One tenant. Every project, every dataset and every simulation result in the product belongs to exactly one of these rows, and the boundary between two of them is the boundary the whole access layer is built to hold. Columns of organizations Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid The organization's identity. This is the value that must travel — it is what projects.organization_id , approved_users.organization_id and the public /v1 API's p_org_id all mean. Not displayable, and that is the property that makes it safe as a join key (§2.1 uuid-identity ). never empty key name not uploaded text The organization's display name, as an administrator typed it. EDITABLE and NOT UNIQUE — two organizations may legitimately share one. It is a label for humans and it is never an identity. Checked: non-empty after btrim — admin_update_organization never empty slug not uploaded text A URL-safe form of the name, lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '-', 'g')) at the moment the row was seeded. UNIQUE, and deliberately NOT recomputed on rename — so after a rename it is a record of what the organization used to be called, which is what makes it usable to match rows written before it. Checked: unique never empty owner_user_id not uploaded uuid The approved user who owns the tenant. Advisory today — nothing in RLS or any RPC reads it; ownership is expressed …

entries.text: Tier 2 data-ingestion 18 columns One demand arc as the user uploaded it: this customer buys this product from this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. Columns of outbound_logistics Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing. never empty key project_id not uploaded uuid The project this row belongs to. Every read is scoped by it. Checked: set from the selected project, never from the CSV never empty plant_name not uploaded text The focal plant this row belongs to, by NAME. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid. Checked: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise If missing: the selected project's projects.plant_name — the CSV omits it (shown as derived) never empty customer_id text The customer's code as the user's own systems spell it. Checked: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8) required product_id text The finished product's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to products and the BOM. Checked: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8) required volume numeric in units per time_unit How much of this product the customer takes over on…

entries.title: All tables — password_reset_requests
entries.text: Tier G platform 6 columns One "Forgot password?" request for one account, from the moment the person asks until a super admin resets the password or dismisses the request (PLAN.md §4 D251). Columns of password_reset_requests Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate id, gen_random_uuid() . never empty key user_id not uploaded uuid The account the request is for — the active approved_users row whose email was typed. Deleting the account deletes its requests ( ON DELETE CASCADE ). never empty status not uploaded text open until a super admin acts; then resolved (the password was reset) or dismissed (the request was not genuine, or was handled another way). CHECK-constrained, and closed_at is set exactly when the status is not open . Checked: open | resolved | dismissed never empty requested_at not uploaded timestamp with time zone When the person asked. Server-stamped. never empty closed_at not uploaded timestamp with time zone When a super admin resolved or dismissed the request; NULL while it is open. closed_by not uploaded uuid The super admin who closed it; NULL while open, or once that account is deleted ( ON DELETE SET NULL ). Rules the database enforces CHECK ((status = 'open') = (closed_at IS NULL)) CHECK (status IN ('open', 'resolved', 'dismissed'))

entries.title: All tables — policy_overrides
entries.text: Tier 4 policy-ui 10 columns One patch against the project bundle, for one target: this supplier, this material, this customer/product pair. The only tier-4 table with a real natural key — (project, scope, target, family) is UNIQUE, so a target cannot hold two conflicting patches for the same family. Columns of policy_overrides Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate row identifier. The natural key is the UNIQUE constraint, not this. never empty key project_id not uploaded uuid The project this override belongs to. never empty scope not uploaded text What KIND of thing the override targets — a supplier, a material, a plant, a customer/product pair. Decides how target_key is read. Checked: one of the stage scopes the policy grid emits never empty target_key not uploaded text WHICH thing, in the scope's own spelling — a supplier_id, a material_id, or a composite like customer::product . Checked: must name a row that exists; an override for a deleted entity is silently inert never empty family not uploaded text Which policy family this patch belongs to — the same vocabulary as policy_defaults' jsonb columns. Checked: one of sourcing / inventory / transport / fulfillment / production / recovery / demand never empty patch not uploaded jsonb The fields this target overrides, and only those. A field absent from the patch keeps the bundle's value — which is exactly why…

entries.title: All tables — policy_presets
entries.text: Tier 4 policy-ui 9 columns One named policy bundle a user can apply to a project — the DECISION plane's catalog of starting points. A system preset ( is_system ) ships with the product; a user preset belongs to its owner_id . Columns of policy_presets Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. The natural key is (slug, owner_id) below. never empty key slug not uploaded text The preset's stable name — lean_jit , make_to_order . Half the natural key, so one owner may not hold two presets under one slug while two owners may each hold their own. never empty name not uploaded text What a person reads — "Lean / JIT". The slug is the key; this is the label. never empty description not uploaded text One sentence on what the preset does to a project. NULL where nobody wrote one; there is no default sentence, because an invented description of a decision is worse than none. is_system not uploaded boolean TRUE for a preset that ships with the product and FALSE for one a user saved. It is the only thing separating a catalog entry from somebody's own work, and owner_id is NULL on the system rows. never empty owner_id not uploaded uuid The user whose preset this is, or NULL for a system preset. Half the natural key — and the NULL half, which is why the pair behaves the way NULLS NOT DISTINCT indexes elsewhere in this contract had to be made to behave (§4 D5): without that…

entries.title: All tables — policy_versions
entries.text: Tier 4 policy-ui 15 columns One saved snapshot of a project's whole policy bundle, with the bundle it replaced and the hash of both. The audit trail of the /policies grid: what the policies WERE at a moment somebody chose to record, which is what makes a simulation result reproducible from the policy side. Columns of policy_versions Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. entries.title: All tables — project_members

entries.title: All tables — project_role_capabilities
entries.text: Tier G platform 5 columns What one project role may do — one row per (project_role, capability). The project layer of the four-layer resolver, shaped exactly like role_capabilities so all four layers read the same way. entries.title: All tables — recovery_playbooks

Columns of recovery_playbooks Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. entries.title: All tables — run_item_series
entries.text: Tier 5 engine 7 columns One item's weekly series from one INSPECTION run: a material or a product of the project, and a map of named weekly arrays for it (on-hand, in-transit and orders for a material; demand, production, fulfillment, backlog and lost units for a product). Tier 5 — a RESULT of one run, input to nothing; a row is superseded by re-running, never edited. Columns of run_item_series Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. The row's identity is natural_key_intended ; nothing reads or joins on this. never empty key run_id not uploaded uuid The simulation_runs row this series belongs to. A third of the natural key, and what the explorer filters every read on. never empty project_id not uploaded uuid The owning project, denormalized from the run so a project's rows can be reached without the join. It decides which measures series carries. never empty item_id not uploaded text The mate…

entries.title: All tables — run_replications
entries.text: Tier 5 engine 12 columns One replication of one simulation run: the seed it used, the KPI row the engine computed for it, and its weekly series. A run has as many rows here as it has replications, and rep_index orders them. Tier 5 — a RESULT, derived from a tier-2 dataset by a named engine version, never an input to anything. Nothing downstream reads it except the result surfaces; a row is superseded by re-running, never edited. Columns of run_replications Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid Surrogate key. The row's identity is natural_key_intended ; this exists because the table predates that rule. never empty key run_id not uploaded uuid The simulation_runs row this replication belongs to. ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting a run takes its replications with it, which is right for a result — a replication of a run that no longer exists is not evidence. never empty project_id not uploaded uuid The owning project. Denormalized from simulation_runs so RLS and the per-project reads do not need the join. never empty rep_index not uploaded integer This replication's position in the run, from 0. entries.title: All tables — run_series_orphans
entries.text: Tier 5 engine 4 columns One series object in the run-results bucket whose run no longer exists, waiting to be removed. A deleted run queues its object here instead of deleting a storage row with SQL — which would orphan the stored file, and which hosted Supabase refuses — and the next series sweep hands the path to the worker, which removes it through the Storage API. Re-uploading duplicates these rows One row should be identified by path , and the table does not yet enforce it. Uploading the same file twice adds the rows twice. See Known limits . Kept as NULL when the run is deleted, so the month's compute it used stays counted. rep_weeks not uploaded bigint in replication-weeks Compute, in replication-weeks: at dispatch the reservation (replications × ceil(horizon days / 7)); at complete what actually ran (replications done × the same weeks — a cancelled or failed run counts what it computed); 0 at expire . entries.text: Tier 4 engine 15 columns One shipped starting point for a scenario: a named disruption shape with its schedule, its suggested playbook and the run settings that go with it. entries.title: All tables — scenarios
entries.text: Tier 4 engine 23 columns One what-if a person set up and can run: the horizon, the warm-up, the replications, the seed, the demand model, the disruption schedule and the recovery overrides. entries.title: All tables — sim_engines

entries.title: All tables — simulation_results
entries.text: Tier 5 engine 13 columns One result of one run of the RETIRED batch pipeline (the "Legacy Sim" path: simulation-runner → external-simulation-processor → the Render-hosted ml-service ), for one project, one plant and a set of legacy disruption profiles: a status and a metrics blob. entries.title: All tables — simulation_runs
entries.text: Tier 5 engine 40 columns One simulation run: what it was bound to (engine, graph version, policy version, scenario run spec, Validated Model, deviations), its status, and the run-level KPIs. Tier 5 — a RESULT. Its replications are run_replications . Since WP 10.4 every binding of a NEW run resolves from this row alone ( run_spec , run_key , engine_id , model_validation_id , protocol_overrides , exploratory ); runs dispatched earlier carry the three content hashes, the seed and the schedule, and say so in the record. Columns of simulation_runs Column Type What it means id not uploaded uuid The run's id. Replications, item series and the reproducibility record hang off it. never empty key scenario_id not uploaded uuid The scenario the run was dispatched from. entries.title: Units & conventions
entries.text: Units & conventions Every unit the system understands, what each one means, and where the definition lives.

entries.title: Units & conventions — Time periods
entries.text: Wherever you give a period — a lead time, a rate, a window — you may spell it any of the ways below. They are understood identically, and anything not on this list is rejected at upload rather than guessed at. 24 accepted spellings, 5 distinct periods. One table, read by the browser, the database and the engine alike. Accepted unit spellings and their length in days Period In days Ways you may write it d 1 d daily day days w 7 w week weekly weeks wk m 30.4375 m mo month monthly months quarter 91.3125 quarter quarterly quarters annual 365.25 annual annually y year yearly years yr Why a month is 30.4375 days It is a year divided by twelve, and a year is 365.25 days — the average that accounts for leap years. Using 30 or 31 would make a monthly rate drift against a yearly one, and the drift would show up as a small unexplained difference in a result nobody could trace. The quarter follows from the same arithmetic.

entries.title: Units & conventions — One table, three languages
entries.text: Conversion is defined exactly once, in TypeScript. The database's version is generated from it, and the engine's Python copy is checked against it on every build. Adding a unit to one and not the others fails CI. This is a fix, not a design flourish There used to be three conversions. Two agreed; the third lived in a database view as a handful of pattern matches with a catch-all, so a row quoted in quarter matched none of them, fell through to the catch-all, and was read as weekly — thirteen times its real value, silently, on that product's demand. Nothing failed. The number was simply wrong. Conversion happens once, when data is promoted into your project, and nothing downstream converts anything again. That is what stops a value being converted twice — the failure that turns a week into a month and looks entirely ordinary on screen. See How your data flows .

entries.title: Units & conventions — Other conventions
entries.text: Money Prices and costs are plain numbers in one currency of your choosing, consistently across a project. The system does no conversion and holds no exchange rates — a project mixing currencies produces arithmetic nobody should act on. Percentages Fields named as a percentage are given as a percentage, not a fraction: a holding cost of 20 % is 20, not 0.2. The field's own entry in All tables states which it expects. Quantities Counts of physical units, consistent within a material. The system does not convert kilograms to units or pallets to cases. The simulation clock The engine advances one week at a time. Periods you supply in other units are converted to weeks on the way in, so a lead time of 10 days becomes a lead time the engine reads in weeks. Dates Calendar dates are ISO — four-digit year, two-digit month, two-digit day. Consistency is yours to keep Nothing checks that every price in a project is in the same currency, or that every quantity counts the same kind of thing. The unit table settles time; money and quantity are conventions the software trusts you to hold. That is a real limit and it belongs on Known limits rather than in a footnote.
